VIE PILLAGED NEST. In gentle April's pleasant days. When trees put out wee shoots a green, Two tiny birds tang happy lays Of home, the sweetest ever seen. "We'll build a home," they joyful sang, Till all the woods triumphant rang. The soft round nest was lined with down, And safely hidden 'midst the boughs. And soon three white:eggs speckled brown Were laid therein; each bird avows No sweeter eggs were ever laid, No softer nest was ever made. And often when the night wind blew Across their borne so safe and fair, They'd wake to see if it were true, And count each egg kid snugly there, Beneath the rno, her's brooding breast, Within that warm and lovely nest. Alas! one fatal day they left Their home awhile; some though Glens bays. In just five minutes have bereft The little birds of all their joys. Broken the eggs I sorrow's iu vain; No tears can build that nest again. Oh I boys, what would your parents say, If some one, when their :backs were tr.rned, Took all their little ones away? Think of their cries when they returned. Then pause awhile era you again Give God's sweet singers such keen pain. ..—Litt2e Folks' Mesznzine.

- _ - The most manifest sks-rt of wisdom is continued cheerful- ness. A judicious silence 13 better than truth spoken without charity. When you have oeclsion to utter a rebuke, let your words be soft and your argatnerits hard. Such men should be placed in authority as are least ambi- tious of it, and thee kept out who prees forward to it. Is there any -fixed rule or writing poetry ?" wrote a isorrespondent to a country editor. His reply was--'. There is, Don't." . .

"Manners meketh man," is an excellent proverb to act upon; but surely it is going a little too far when a person -can't drink a cup of tea without using refined sugar. Mark Twain is of opinion that any gifted person ought to learn English in thirry hours, French in thirty days, and German in thirty years. There are no moral blanks, there are no neutral characters. We are either the sower th*.t sows and corrupts, or the light th It splendiily illuminat,s, or the salt that silently operates ; but being dead or alive, every man speaks.—Chemers. We never know through what divine mysteries of com- pensatiin the great Father of the Universe may be carrying out His sublime plan ; and tho,e three words," God is love," ought to contain to every doubting soul the solution of all thin gs.—Miss Mulock. I would rather be what God chose to make me than the mast glorious creature I could think of. For to have been thought about, born in God's thought, and then made by God, is the dearest, grandest, and most precious thing in all thinking.—George .31-Donald. • In one of the earliest trials before a coloured jury in Texas, twelve gentlemen were told by the Judge to retire and "hod a verdict." Tney went to the jury-room. Toe Sheriffs and others stand:rig outside heard the opening and shutting of doors, and other sounds of unusual commotion. At last the jury came back into the court, when the foreman rose and said—" Massa Judge, we have done looked every- whar in the drawers and behind the do', and can't found no verdic'. It warn't in de room."

The danger of "being in the wrorg box" was curiously Illustrated once at the Surrey Sessions by a bewildered jure, man who had the serne name as one of the prisoners about to he called up for judgment. Hearing himself called, as he supposed, he meekly answered. "Go into the dock," said the Judge, and into the dock he was shoved. "It's all a mistake," cried the hapless man, only to be sternly silenced with "Bead the charge." The charge was read, and the astounded juryman was told to hold up his hand and plead. "But my Lord!" he cried again; and again was silenced, and told he must answer " guilty " or "not guilty." I'm not —" the wretched Briton stammered our, whereupon again he was ordered to be silent, and a plea of "not guitty" was duly entered. A little more, and he might have found himself sentenced and locked up ; but gathering bremh from despair, he broke forth at last with the explanation that be was really a juryman, and not a prisoner. AMERICAN TRAVELLING.—RaiIvray travelling in America is most loan lone, and cheap as well; a little slower, per- haps, than it is in this country, but a person in smirch of health will hardly grumble at this. Dinner and refreshment's of all k;nds can be had on board, and at whatsoever town or city he halts the invalid will find the hotel system all that heart can desire. The hotel porter, too, awaits the arrival of all trains, and into his hands you hind your "baggage checks," and the next you see of your luggage will be in your own bedroom. This system of checking the baggage is a very good one, esp,cially for long journeys, as the pas- senger bee no care or worry about anything except the hand-bag he may take into the car with him, Travelling by train is as cheap, if not more so, than it is with us, and there are no fees to pertere, expected at all events. Tnere are sleeping-cars on all long routes; in a word, railway travelling in America has been reduced to a eystern, and the comfort of the traveller in eoneldered paramount to all other coasiderations.—Cosse,l's TEE BLARNEY STONE.—Five miles to the west of the city of Cork, in a valley where two streams meet, is the little village of Blarney, with its castle, whose fame is vFide- *prea d. For high in the northeastern eide of that castle is a stone, and he who is adventurous enough to reach it, and has faith enough to kiss it, will be sure to possess thence- forth a gift of marvellous efficacy. Honeyed words will flew from his lips; pereuesive power will hang on his utter- arose; he will win his way ellerywhere and with every- body. ; and when mankind, and much more wornaekind, are tiken captive by the witchery of his tongue, they teiy, "He has ki.sed the Blarney Stone." There are two stones which each claim to be the real taliernan— one on the summit of the castle, being about two feet seuare, with the date of 1703; the other, that which records the date of the build- lag, 1446. Thanks to Mr. Jefierey, any one may kiss the former. To kiss the latter the votary must be let down twenty feet by a pulley and tackle. Try the first. If it works the charm, well; if not, let no amount of "blarney" induce you to attempt the other.—Picturesque Eitrope. LONGFELLOW'S RECEPTION DT THE QUEEN.—An account of Longfellow's description of his reception by her Majeety, in the Thronemocm at Windsor, is worth extracting An imposing lady in black, with flowing drapery, came quickly forward to greet me. It was her Majesty Queen 'Victoria. She extended her hand, and I offered to take it. "What," I interrupted, " did you not bend and offer to kiss it?" "No," said he timidly; "I was not then familiar or ac- quainted with Court etiquette, as I am now. She offered me her hand evidently to shake, and I shook it." "Why," said I, "she is the most inexorably caggeante of all sove- reigns. You mast have horrified her." "I presume I did." said he simply. "Now I think of it, she was disconcerted, I suppose for that reason; but she rallied graciously, and asked me about America and myself. She explained, We speak of America first, because you are America's poet. Tennyson is ours.' 'Tennyson is the world's poet, madam,' said I, bowing gravely. She smiled in gratified acenies- eence, and conenued : You are very generous,' Her

_ Majesty was then pleased to converse on general topics, but persistently got back to the subj Pct of myself. I felt she was piquea about something at first, and her last words were, • We shall not forget you;' adding, with a laugh, 'why, even all my servants read your poems!'" The poet then glanced up, and, with an alroont c3tnlc4l express:on. he said; "What do you think she intended by it? I was non- plussid ; and to-day, although many years have passed away, I am undecided as to what.her Majesty's real meaning was."

THE MOT DEGRLDED RACE IST SOUTHAMERICA.—The people are known as the Picherays, or, from the name of their country, more commonly the Tierra del Fasgians. The country which they inhabit is wretched and bleak in the extreme; but unlike the Eskimo hod of the North, a few dwarf trees and bushes enable Vie inhabitants to obtain some shelter from the storm, materials to warm themselves, and mains of building a canoe. Yet notwithstanding the superior advantages in natural resources of country which the Tierra del Faegian possesses over the Eskimo, in com- fort and physical and intellectual character he is not com- parable to the fur-clad denizen of the snow-lands on the shores of the Arctic Ocean. In stature the Puegian is Ahmed; his lower jaw projecting, and with long straight black hair hanging down his back and cheeks. For this hair he has a superstitions veneration, and conceives that the prssession of a scrap of it by any one else will entail all manner of disaster on the original owner. Everything about the Faegian is disgusting, animal, and almost brute-like. The spectator turns away from him in the belief that surely now man, created in the Maga of his Maker, has reached the lowest type, or brute ascended to the highest stage. Be . moves about in a crouching, et oping posture, his person is covered with the filth of generations, and his long mane-like locks, which his vanity or superstition induces him now and then to rake out with a comb made of a porpoise jaw, almost without any alteration, are crawling with a detestable in- sect, which though it has family relations in the locks of people all over the world, is yet said to be a species peculiar to this race. Though living in a country where sleet, snow, rain, and frost are of almost every-day occurrence, the male Fuegian wears no clothing, except a small piece of sealekin thrown over his shoulders, and moved now and then so as to shelter his person in the direction from whence the blast may be blowing. When in his canoe or engaged in any active exercise, he considers even thia limited amount of wardrobe ' altogether superfluous, and tosses it aside. The women have quite as little clothing, the claims of modesty being satisfied by the presence of an apron of sellAin. 'Vet the country supplies abundance of the far-searand various land animals, the hides of which would sn only excellent materials ler clothing. The skins of this race seem, however, to be almost insensible to cold, and though they seem to strangers t) be always shivering and chilly, yet this most have be- come a second nature with them, for they may be seen mov- ing about from place to place, or sitting in their canoes, with the whirling snow betting against their naked persons, or gathering about their limbs, seemingly without caring about it, or even being conscious of it.— The Peoples of the World. " Spring's delights" can only h, actually realized by those who live in healthy house, and who comb'ne known sanitary measures for the prevention of such infections disenes as small- p ,x, scarlet fever, and mea,s'es. The remedy actually becomes a luxury when the washing of toilet, bath, arid nuri.ery is con- ducted with Wright's Coal Tar S.ap. Refuse ell im*ations which are but dsnge^o4s counterfeits.—Advt.

A com- pany is being started in Paris for the imlustrial appAcatioe of Meret's process. It is said that the albamen is bleached if It is exposed to electric fight either in the dry state or ie selntion.—Textile Ma7ZUfactnrer. Professor Renisch, addressing a meeting of the Victoria Institute, bas.developed a new theory of the formation of coal. He has given great attention to the subject, and has cnme to the conclusion that coal has not bets:l formed by the alteration of accumulated land plants, hut that it consists ot microscopical organic forms of a lower order of protoplasm. Plants of a higher order have contributed only a fraction of , the matter of coal wine. From the Tyrol comes news of a newel application of the microphone, by- Coact von Eugenberg, at castle Fratzberg, who has used it to trace underground water-courses. At several different pieces on a hill-nide he planted micro- phones, and connected each with a telephone and battery. In the quiet hours of the night the faintest murmur of water und.,§tetround could be detected, and its coarse traced by listening at tho telephones. Use or BA.R7TA IN FiNiSEING FABRICS.—M. In this, way, it is Said, the7eizad goods do not show the yellowish cast which is observable on goads where sulphate of barium has been used by the old process. For the preparation of his size M. Chaudet uses 40 gallons water. 1001 e. farina, 101 b. to 201 b. olive oil, Wlb. to 201 b. chloride of :atrium, and enough sulphate of soda to decompeee ail the chloride of barium. All these ingredients are mixed at' the &erne time, and boiled in the ordinary way for size-making.—Textile Manttfacturer. Tan TELEGRAPH IN CHINA.—We are glad to observe that the telearaph is making rapid way in China. The Shanghai-Tientsin line has been working now for a few months, and a line is being constructed in the south between Canton and Hongkong—a distance of about 100 miles. The first section is to connect Canton, which is practically the commercial capital of China, with the frontier of British Kowloon, situate opposite the town of Victoria. after some consideration it has been decided that a hand-line is prefer- able to a submarine cable, as it will be more economical, and the latter also would seriously interfere with the anon won' junk traffic and fishing operatione in the estuary of the Canton river. It is interesting to remark that this line is purely a private undertaking of a company of Cairese merchants in Canton, who, doubtless, want to be on a level with their brethren in the north in rapidity of communica- tion with the markets of the world. The line, ae above stated, will for the present terminate on the confines of British territory. It seems hardly credible—but the fact is state] in the Honakong journals—that onpoeition is made by the British authorities to the further construction of the line, and especiatly to the cable across the harbour neces- sary to connect Kowloon with Hongkonaesunless it is con- structed by a British company. his illiberal demann seems also illogical and unfair, because one of the telegraphic cables between Hongkong and the outer world belongs to a foreign company, the Danish Great Northern Telegraph Conmeny.—Nature. A Nom. Bemoote.—A new steerahle balloon, the inven- tion of Herr Baumgarten and Dr. %halter; was recently tried at Charlottenburg, in Germany. It is of huge size, having a capacity of about 473 cahic yards, and is ellipsoid in form, the longer diameter about 531 t. It differs in prin- ciple from all other aerostats in that, although billeted with hydrogen, it has no ascensional force; its total weight is about 2 1-Ib. aboveghat of the air it displaces. The means of displacement, in the horizontal or the vertical direction. are a helical system of vanes actuated by machinery in the car. Hence in making land, the balloon does not require to be partly emptied, and on reaching the ground it has nearly the same quantity of gas as when it rose. Another novelty consists in the mode of connection of the car. This is rigid Thus the dangerous bounds or jerks to which the ordinary balloon-car is liable in landing are to some extent avoided. The car being esaally suspended by ropes, the system is suddenly relieved of its weight when it touches the ground, se that the balloon shoots up. again, giving a series of violent shocks. With a rigid connection the total weight cannot thus be temporarily diminished. The mechanism has a double action, one helix of vanes or screw propellers, driven in one direction or the opposite, produces ascent or descent, while a couple of screws give horizontal propulsion ; in pretty calm atmosphere the horizontal direction may be modified by working one of the couple alone. The first ex- periments, it appears, were quite saccessful. The weather was exceptionally calm. In a second trial a slight accident ruptured the envelope of the balloon, and the car mechanism was also injured. The experiments are soon to be resumed The motor, it may be mentioned, has a force of four-horse power and weighs 80 lbs. The cost of charging, each time the balloon is filled anew, is about L'2o. THE HARDENING OF STEEL.--Profmor Roberts, the chemist to the Mint, in his memorandum appended to the annual report of Mr. Fremantle, gives particulars of some very interesting experiments he and others have carried on with the view of determining what i€ the true cause of the hardening of steel. Varicue theories have been pronounced to account for this phenomenon, one of the most feasible being that the heating of steel expels certain gaseous matter absorbed from the atmosphere. This gaseous matter would tend to keep the constituent particles of the steel asunder, and the sudden cooling of water wool,' have the effect of bringing the particles together while the gas W.l. keot out. Mr. Roberts quotes an experiment by Weer-our which quite upsets this very plausible theory. A piece of steel Was cooled in the nearest approach to a perfect vacuum that could be secured, and under ce,nditions, therefore, which precluded the possibility of atmospheric gases having any- thing to do with the prevention of the particles compacting closely together as they cooled. He focnorl that tinder such conditions the steel remained soft. The result of the most recent experiments of various kinds is, it appears, to leave the true solution of the questien still to be discovered. It is not dam to the introduction of any new substance into the metal, nor apparently to the expulsion of anything from it. It is believed that the cause must be sought in the changes occurring in the structure of the steel, or In the mode of existence of carbon in it. How these changes are brouht about nobody knows. One very important communication to the French Academy of Science hi' referred to by Mr. Roberts. It has been found that if a piece of steel be heated to about 900 dep. Centigrade, and then stahjected to greet pressure till quite cold, it acquires extreme hardness, and it is thought probable that by properly regulating the pres- sure, the hardness may he regulated, and thus hardening and tempering may be effected in a single operation.— Globe. NEW METHOD OF MINING i.COAL—VALUABLE Die- COVERY.—Not many days ago Mr. Paget Moeley read a paper "on a new method of mining coal" to "The Iron and Steel Institute." He explained that at Shipley Col- lieries, in Derbyshire, which is very liable to gas, the sys- tem of wedging bad been tried, but it was found that more accidents had occurred even than with gunpowder. The managers of the collieries some time ago set to work upon experiments with a view to utilising practically the power of lime. After the lapse of nearly two years it has been ascertained that a cartridge, two and a half inches in diame- ter, made from mountain limestone ground to a fine powder. and consolidated by the application of heavy pressure, is likely to revolutionise the entire system of coal-gettMg all over the world. These cartridge 3 are thruit into shot boles, drilled by means of a light boring machine. An iren tuba. about half an inch in diameter, having a small external channel or groove upon the upper side, and provided also with perforatiors, is then inserted along the whole lzngth of the bore hole. This tube is encleeed in a bag of calico, covering the perforations and the further end, while to the near end a tap is fitted. The cartridges are then put in and lightly rammed, so as to ensure their filling the bore bole. After the cartridges have been firmly fixed by tamping, in the same way as if gunpowder were being need, a small force-pump is connected with the tap at the end of the tube, by means of a short flexible pipe, and a quantity of water, equal in bulk to the quantity of lime used, is forced in. The water driven to the far end of the shot hole through the tube escapes along the groove and through the perfora- tions and calico, flowing to wa,ds the t unplug and saturating the whole charge of lime, while the air is expelled before it. The tap is then closed, so as to prevent the escape of the steam generated by the action of the water on the lime, and the flexible pipe attached to the force pump is disconnected. The immense ircreaso in pressure obtained by thus slaking the lime causes the coal to split away, and it COMES down by tons without the danger of flame or of the wedges. For each of the last thirty years it has been computed that at least one thousand human beings have perished annually in the coal mines of Great Britain alone; and if this mournful drain of life can, as is believed, be arrested by the expansive force of wetted lime, the sooner it is universally used the better. On the 28th of April Professor Abel, during a lec- ture which he gave at the Royal Institution, burst one of these lime cartridges by applying water to it before his audience, thereby showing them the amazing power of ex- pansion which, like exploded gunpowder, the dinsolideted mineral contains. It is claimed for the new process that it saves time, and enables the coal to be cot in large masses, in addition to relieving the collier from the laborious exertion of "in-wedging." It secures immunity from the explosion of gas; no smoke or noxious smell of any kind arises from its use; the roof is not shaken; the coals in falling produce much less dust; skilled labour is unnecessary; the appara- tus is simple and inexpensive, and can easily be carried about and kept in order; and, lastly, any number of holes can be loaded with the lime cartridges, and by applying the water to them in quick succession, a.continuous and gradual pressure is brought to bear along the face, which causes the coal to fall in large masses. It is thus brought to bank in a better condition for stacking or carriage than by any other means, and the result, when compared with wedging or employing gunpowder, shows a considerable increase in the percentage of coal got. Out of all these alleged advan- tages there is, of course, none to compare in value with the increased security to human life which seems to be fore- shadowed ; and if the new method of getting coal be half as full of promise as Mr. Mosley thinks, we trust the time is not far distant when every coalowner in the United King- dom will be compelled by law tn employ lime instead of gunpowder and other explosives in his subterraneous opera- tions.

This determination to do deavour to get as much of it as possible. justice to Ireland led first to the secession frem the Ministry of Stanley, Graham, Richmond, and Ripon, and after a few more weeks to the downfall of the Reform Administration. When Sir Robert Peel became First Lord of the Treasury O'Connell used his influence in cutting short his official career. Ireland proved ones more Peel's "chief difficulty." It was on an Irish question, that of the Church, that he and his Administration stumbled and fell. It was with much reluctance that King William entrusted to Lord Melbourne the task of forming a new Administration. The task proved by no means an easy one It was on the Bth of April, 1835, that Sir Robert Peel and the Duke of Wellington announced their resignations, but not until the 18th Was Lord Mel- bourne able to announce that his Administration was virtually complete. Great snrprise was felt by the Irish people that in the Cabinet O'Connell was conspicuous by his absence. For six months he had cordially arid without bond or bargain lent his aid to reinstate the Whigs in power, aid without which that reinstatement must have been deferred for many a day. It was also understood that O'Connell himself was not unwilling to accept office under the newly formed Liberal Administration "to try how far England could legislate for Ireland in a manner that would content the people." But though "to six millions of people his ap. pointment would have been the visible embodiment and positive realisation of the statute of 1829," and though it would "have shortened by at least a decade the tedious and shameful struggle to make that law a reality." yet no sooner was his possible appointment communicated to tieb leading membere of the proposed Cabinet, than it threatened to cause its premature disruption. As for William IV., his anger and fear knew no bounds when rumour reached the palace that the man whom he had been advised to denounce from the throne as an incendiary was about to be proposed to him as Attorney-General for Ireland. Lord Melbourne WAS therefore obliged to fling O'Connell overboard, and the Liberator saw the prize of his profession fall to another. But while O'Connell gave free • expre•sion to his feelings when Mr. Ellice, the veteran whip, made known to him the unwelcome news, he did not by word or look betray his dis- appointment publicly. He was too astute to let the world without, or even the circle of his own immediate followers, know how he had been thus summarily compelled to stand by. What he really thought of the transaction we shall never know, brit that unresenttully and magnanimously he bore hie mortification is beyond dispute. He retained his seat below the gangway on the Opposition stde after the House re-assembled, declaring that his future course would be guided by the composition of the Irish Executive. It was but natural he should desire that after a century and a half of exclusion one of the ancient faith shouid be named chief of the Bar. The Attorney-Generalship for Ireland was given to Mr. Perrin, and the Solicitor-Generelship to Mr. O'Loghien. The moment the appointments were announced to the House of Commons, the Liberator rose, and followed hr his son and other Parliamentary friends, crossed the floor in token of his satisfaction, and took his seat on the Minis- terial side, a position never quitted by him during the six succeeding years.
TRE STATE ()F IRELAND.

Mr. Michael Davitt sailed from Queenstown for New York on Friday. In taking leave of his friends he de- nounced the continued outrages. A Parliamentary return shows that the number of" sus- pects" now detained under the Protection Act is 263, as compared with 512 in February, 587 in March, 511 in April, and 386 in May. A parliamentary return issued on Tuesday shows that the number of families evicted thr mghout Ireland during May was 698. In the cases mentioned tenants refused to piy their rents. A Dublin correspondent says, notwithstanding the state- ment to the contrary, it is a fact that the Lord Lieutenant received a threatening letter last week. The police have had the matter in hand since last Friday. The Irish correspondent of the Observer states that Mr. Davites scheme for the riortionalisation of the land has not at all received general approval amongst the ranks of the Nationalist party. In fact, already many of the Land League leaders have pronounced strongly against sit, and letters, it is stated, will appear on the subject immediately. Mr. Sexton, M.P., speaking at a meeting on the land ques- tion, held in Dublin on Saturday evening, referred to the amelioration effected in the condition of the tenant farmers of Ireland daring the past two years, and said that if the Irish people continued to use their strength as they had done there was nothing which they could not wring from the preponderating power with which they were connected by an evil and fallacious union. The detailed report of the attack on the man Hickey, near Castleisland, is a horrible story. Hickey, who was care- taker on a farm from which his brother Michael had been evicted by another brother, and who was returning from the petty sessions court, where he bad been prosecuting Michael for trespass, was met by two men armed and disgaised, ac- cused of being a "land grabber," and deliberately shot twice in the leg. Four men are in custody on suspicion of being concerned in the outrage. .

On Saturday the ten-ants of the Duke of Leinster met his grace's agent, Mr. Charles It. Hamilton, in the Town Hall,. Athy, for the purpose of considering the rents proposed in the revaluation of the estate just completed. The result, as announced, is that a substantial reduction on the present rent has been made. It varies in each case, but all round, so far as the revision has gone, it is about 24 per cent , the tenants acquiescing in the proposed arrangetnent, and nearly all, who have done so have signed a form of originating notice for the Land Court, where the rent agreed upon will be declared the judicial rent. His grace's action is the sub- ject of very favourable comment. hum Meats-rnkrEs.—A parliamentary return moved by Mr. Callan, was issued on Saturday, showing the names ot the lords-lieutenant of each county, and of the local magis- trates, with the dates of appointment, distinguishing resident from nonresident, and giving the amount of property for which each magistrate appeards rated for the relief of the poor as occupier and as immediate lessor. Among the names of magistrates in this return is that of Mr. Walter M. Bourke. of Curraghleagh, Claremorris county Mayo, who is described as "usually resident." He was appointed on October 11th, 1879, by Viscount Massareene, Claremorris being the petty sessions district he usually attended. The amount of property in the county for which he was rated for the relief of the poor as occupier was £ll4 be., and as immediate lessor £B5 Gs. It does not appear that the de- ceased was also a magistrate for Galway, in which county he held property, and where on Thursday he was murdered.

The Lord Lieutenant of Ireland made reference to the pre- valence of outrage, in replying to an address presented to him on Saturday by a deputation of teachers. He said that the atrocious crimes committed in Galway, Mayo, Roscom- mon, and Kerry proved, though proof was abundant before, that organisations existed in Ireland which maimed and murdered in open defiance of the law. It was the duty of society to destroy these organisationa and this was an object which the Government and all law-abiding classes of the community must strain every nerve to secure. As an essen- tial means of attaining that obj,)ct, he earnestly hoped that the bill now ly.tfore Parliament would speedily be passed. If law and order were actively supported and maintained by the people, the Government would be able without :lindrance to devote themselves to the congenial work of developing the resources of the country, and extending the system of education which civilised and elevated a nation.

MR. P. J. iiMYTH AND Mn. DAvrrfs SCHEME.—Mr. P. J. Smrrn, " enters his emphetic protest again Mr. Davitt's as- sertion that the programme unfolded by Mr. Davitt ztt Liverpool last week was the demand of the whole Irish race. " Nationalisation of the land," says Mr. Stnith, " sounds well, but would it be nationalisation? No ; it would be the opposite. It would b 3 the denationalisation of the land for ever, the acknowledgments and ratification of conquest, the formal surrender of the country, and her title deeds to liberty. The land for the people. 'is a taking cry. But I say that under Mr. Dayitt's programme it would be the land for the Government, which, once in possession, would bestow it on whom they thought fit, and regulate it as they deemed best in the interest of Government and not of the people. If Mr. Davitt anti this Mr. Henry George do really wish to reform the human, race, why do they not begin in America? There is, ready made, a national 6r;oVernmeut in the best sense. There are wide lands, occupied and unoccupied. Clearly there is the proper field for the nationalisation experiment. Ireland is not the field ; and I trust the Irish race in America will reject this programme of ruin and dishonour."

ADVANCES UNDER` ME LAND ACT.—A parliamentary paper just issued shows that there have been 347 applica- tions by occupiers of land in Ireland to the Board of Works for advances under section 31 of the Land Act, 1831. Of these 107 have been rejectdd, not being within the terms of the Treasury minute of December 21, 1881 ; and there re- main for consideration 209 applications. The number of loans sanctioned to the 30th April, 1832, was nine. (The power to sanction loans rests with the Treasury, not with the R,ard of Works.) The amount advanced on account of such loans to the same date was nil. The estimated annual cost of the staff specially employed to give effect to the pro- visions of section 31 of the Land I aw Act, 1881, is £2,856. The following note is appended to this return :—" The regulations, which were framed in order to give effect to section 31 of the Land Law Act, required very careful pre- paration, and were not issued until the 21st of December, 1881. The inspectors were appointed on the 27th of the same month, and commenced their duties at their respective stations as soon as possible after that date. Some time must necessarily be occupied in local inquiries and in the preparation of plans and estimates, and a period of six weeks is required by the Tteasury regulations between the adver- tisement of the application and the advance. It is estimated that a period of from 70 to 75 days, on the average, must elapse between the date of application and the date of ad- vance; and the information furnished by the applicants for loans has often been of so incomplete a character as to cause prolonged correspondence and inquiry, and consequent delay." MANIFESTO BY THE IRISH PRELATES.

A.vigorous manifesto, endorsed by Cardinal Maceabe, two archbishops, and 25 bishops, has been issued with special reference to the present crisis in Ireland. It &elates that what is morally wrong cannot be politically right, and while cluntenancing lawful. agitation,' condemns without reserve the refusal to pay just dells that people are able to pay, the prevention of others from paying debts, the injury of a neighbour in his person, rights, or property, the forcible re- sistance of the law or incitement to such resistance, and the formation of secret societies for the promotion of terror or other like objects. The people are solemnly urged to con- demn and oppose these criminal resources, and when the National movement is purged of these evils the hierarchy promise it their hearty support. THE MURDERS IN GALWAY.

A proclamation has been issued in the Dublin Gazencl offering a reward of £2,000 for information leading to the conviction of the persons who murdered Mr. W. M. Bourke and Corporal Wallace on Thursday. A reward of £l,OOO is offered for private information leading to a similar result; and £5OO for information, followed by the conviction, of any person who harbours the murderers. Further details of the murder of-Mr. Burke and the sol- dier who accompanied him show that five men had secreted themselves inside the gate at Castle Taylor and had loop- holed the wall, and when their victims had approached they fired a volley through the loopholes and killed them, and saw the men pick up their rifles. Thinking they were poachers he approached them, but a rifle was presented at him, and he then stood still, while the murderers walked away. The inquest on the bodies was held on Monday. The evidence showed that the crime was committed with the greatest deliberation, and that the murderers subsequently took possession of the arms of Mr. Burke and the soldier and quietly walked away. Mr. Taylor was within a hundred yards of them, but could not identify them. An examina- tion of the bodies revealed the fact that both Mr. Burke and Wallace had been shot through the head at a distance which showed that the assassins were well skilled in the use of their arms. The most terrible statement at the inquest was, however, that of Constable Charleston, who said that a man called Martin Kane, when he carije upon the scene, laughed over the bodies of the murdered men. The jury re- turned a verdict of "Wilful murder against persons un- known."

div.head: SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT RADCLIFFE.
div.p: SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT RADCLIFFE.
DOUBLE MURDER AND SUICIDE.

Yesterday night week, a dreadful tragedy was committed at Chapelfleld, Radcliffe. A man named Rebert Booth, 32 years old, a miner, drowned two of his children (boys), one abut five years old and the other four months, and afterwards cut his own throat, almost severing the head from the body. It appears that about seven o'clock Booth sug- gested that his wife should go to market, which is about three-quarters of a mile distant, and when she bad gone he e.ined the little boy, who was playing in the street, to come into the house. At the time there was a little girl named Sandiford nursing the younger one, and he told her to go home as it was bed time. She went home, and, apparently after the nurse had gone oet, Booth locked the doors and then committed the deed. He appears to have filled a dolly tub full of water and put the elder child in, and then filled a washing mug full of water and put the younger child in that. After doing this he cut his own throat with a razer in a most shocking manner. The dreadful affair was not dis- covered till his wife returned from the market about half-past eight o'clock, when she found the doors fast. She got the :Mkt:MC.l of some neighbours, and one of them got a ladder and entered the house through the bedroom window. He afterwards went downstairs, and in-the kitchen was presented to bins the shocking spectacle described above, Booth lying on his back in a pool of blood. It appears that the man had been out of employment for eleven weeks, and in conse- quence had got into a very desponding statb of mind. The aff,ir caused great excitement in the neighbourhood. An inquest on the bodies was held on Monday afternoon. The evidence was to the effect that Booth was a collier, and having been out of work eleven weeks was depressed. On Friday morning his wife, on returning from Radcliffe, found the door locked, and on an entry being forced it was dis- covered that Booth, after drowning the children in a large basin, had cut his throat. The jury returned a verdict that the children were killed by the father, who committed suicide whilst temporarily insane.

POLITICAL ITEMS.
It is stated that steps are bout to IA taken to celebrate in a iittiDg manner tho Parliamentary jubilee of Mr. tilad- stone.

The suit initiated by Mr. Bradlaugh against the Deputy Sergeant-at-Arms is being pressed to a decision. The plead- ings will challenge the legality of the resolutions by which the House of Commons has excluded Mr. Bradlaugh from his seat.

Sir Thomas Brassey, Mr., writes I desire to state that I have no intention of retiring from the representation of Hastings. lam deeply sensible of the obligations which I owe to my constituents, and so long as I an able to bear the strain of public life it will be my greatest pride to remain one of the members for your borough."

Much amusement has been created in the House of Com- mons by the discovery that Mr. J. G. Hubbard, in sending out a private " whip in favour of his Income Tax Resolu- tion, inadvertently sent an invitation to Mr. Bradlaugh to be in his place. Mr. Rfadlaugh replied that he would'be most happy to attend if the right hon. gentleman wauld move and carry a resolution rescinding that declaring him incapable or ,sitting. Mr. Hubbard has always taken an animated part in bringing about theexclusion of the member for Northampton.

In one of the recent suits brought against Mr. Bradlwagh in connection with the attempt to take his seat, the hon. member was ordertd to pay into court a penalty of £5OO pending appeal. This sum has now been raised by public subscription in sums varying from twopence to five pounds. The principal number of donations was in shillings. In the division on the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, in the House of Lords, on Monday evening, the Prince of Wales, the Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke of Albany, and the Duke of Cambridge voted for the bill, as also did the members of the Government, except the Lord Chancellor. Last session the Protection Act occupied the time of the House for twenty-six days, that is, first reading six days (from which point the urgency rules came into force), second readinc, four days, committee eight days, considera- tion as amended three days, and third reading one day. The Crime Bill at present before the House has taken up for first reading one day, for second reading two days, for mov- ing the Speaker out of the chair three days, and for committee eight days—in all fourteen days; but, as only the fourth clause has as yet been reached, it is pretty clear that if urgency is not soon declared the bill will consume in the a,gregate more time than was the case with the Protection Act of 1881.

Seventeen members of the Episcopal Bench voted against the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill on Monday night, and not one in its favour. The Bishop of Ripon paired in favour of the bill. In the minority /were forty-three Conservatives, whilst twenty-three Liberals voted with the majority. The Conservative party issued a strong whip against Lord Dalhousie's bill for legalising marriage with a de- ceased wife's sister. The whip was so far effectual that the Imijority in the House of Lords on Monday night included all the known opponents of the bill except six, who were either abroad or absent from illness. Several Conservative peers admitted that they abstained from voting for the bill under party pressure. It is worthy of remark that sixteen bishops voted in the majority against the bill. The num- ber of absentees—chiefly from unavoidable causes—among the supporters of the measure was thirty. The division was the largest ever yet taken on this subject in the House of Lords. In 1879 the bill was rejected by 101 votes to 81, in in 1881 hy 101 to 90, and in 1882 by 132 to 128. The Daily News hears that negotiations with the railway companies on the subject of the proposed parcels post have been resumed, with considerable prospect of a satisfactory result.

The Daily News understands that Lord Kimberley has intimated that the lOyal assent will be given to the Mar- riage wiQl a Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, which passed both Houses of the Canadian Parliament.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY AFFAIR NEAR LIVERPOOL. A SERVANT SHOT DEAD BY HER MASTER.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY AFFAIR NEAR LIVERPOOL. A SERVANT SHOT DEAD BY HER MASTER.

Crosby, a pretty village in the northern suburbs of Liver- pool, was on Sunday afternoon thrown into a state of excite- ment by the report of the shooting of a young woman named Mary Cremen, aged 20, by Arthur Golding, a well- known Liverpool estate agent, in whose service she was. Golding and the girl were alone in the kitchen at the former's residence, Queen's-road, when a report of firearms and screams were heard. Golding's wife, running to ascer- tain the cause, met him on the stairs, and he said, "I have shot the servant." He immediately gave himself up at the police station, and was locked up. The police on going to the house found the girl lying on the floor dead, with a bullet wound in the foreheat Death appeared to have been instantaneous. A six-chamber revolver, five barrels loaded and one recently discharged, was found on Golding, who is only 23 years of age, carried on business in North John street, Liverpool, and resided at Aston House, Queen's-read, Great Crosby. The prisoner was on Monday charged at the County Magistrates' Court, Basnett-street, Liverpool, with haying murdered Mary Cremen, a domestic servant in his employment, at his residence at Great Crosby. The priso- ner was represented by Mr. Sykes, solicitor. Superintendent Walsh, who appeared to prosecute, stated that about three o'clock the previous afternoon (Sunday) the prisoner went to the police station at Crosby, having in his possession a revolver, which was loaded in five chambers, one having been recently discharged. He said to the sergeant on duty, "I was staudinss at the scullery door conversing with my servant Mary "Cremen, waiting for my shoes to be cleaned, when she said to me, What would you do if they went to shoot you first?' I put my hand to my hip pocket and pulled out my revolver, which I purchased, and for which I had a license to carry it for self-protection from my next door neighbours, and presenting it towards her—not think- ing at the time it was loaded—l raised the hammer and tired, killing her on the spot. I immediately went upstairs and told my wife I had shot Mary, and that she was dead. It was spite an accident, ash would not have laid my hands on her for anything at all." In cansEquence of this stetement the sergeant took him into custody, and proceeded to the house, where he found the &ceased lying on the scullery floor and a pool of blood nedr her head. There was a wound on her forehead, and some of her brains were on the floor near to where she was lying. Oa being shortly afterwards formally charged with causing the young woman's deafly, the prisoner said, "I must reserve my defence ; it was purely accidental." After that the prisoner made another statement which, Superintendent Walsh said, was of an important nature and needed enquiry into, as, if trne, it sup- plied a motive for the crime. It would be brought forward at a later stage of the enquiry., It would be shown that the prisoner loaded the revolver the same morning, for the pur- pose, as he stated after the tragedy, of shooting a dog. Evidence having been given in Support of the above state- ment the prisoner was remanded. An inquest on the body was opened at Crosby en Tues- day. The statement made by the prisoner was again read, in which be said the occurrence was accidental. Police- superintendent Walsh denosed that the prisoner stated at the police station that he had bought the revolver to defend himself against two neighbours. The witness found in the deceased's box seven letters ,from Mrs. Golding bearing strongly on the case. The inquiry was adjourned until Tuesday next.

The Local Government Board have issued a return of the number of able-bodied paupers in receipt ef relief on the Ist January 1882, as compared with the corresponding date of 1881 in each Union in England and Wales, and we extract the following In the Warrington Union there were 4 males, 21 females, adults indoor, and 5:5 children under 16 years of age. Out- door 38 males, 141 fetnales, and 349 children, as compared with 18 males, 18 females, and 35 children indoor, and 32 males, 128 females, and 369 children in 1881. THE CRISIS IN EGYPT: MINISTERIAL STATEMENT.— A livery afternoon was spent in a miscellaneous cross- questioning of the Government upon the situation in Egypt. Proceedings commenced with a request by Mr. BOuRKE that the Government would either to-day or to-morrow make a statement which would enable a debate to take place on their Egyptian policy; and when sir CHARLES Dimes explained that this could not be done, as members must see the papers which he had promised for next week before they could understand the position, Sir H. 1). WOLFF moved the adjournment of the House in order that a debate might. be taken there and then. His special desire seemed to he to attack the alliance with Franc., and by references to Dulcigno, Smyrna, the action of France in Tunis, and other matters, to prove that the French alliance had led to bad feeling between England and the Sultan.—Baron DE WORMS seconded the motion for adjournment.—Sir C. DILKE then gave a little further information, the pith of which was that Sir H. D. Wolff's statements were both erroneous and mischievous, England's relations with the Porte and all other Continental Governments being "friendly in the extreme," and that Sir B. Seymour, who had "a very large force indeed," was at liberty to land as many soldiers and marines as he pleased when Tver he thought such action necessary.—The debate once turned into this channel, was not easily diverted into another, and Baron de Worms, in attacking the French alliance, matte jealous allusion to Germany's influence in the East.—Sir GrEORGE CAMPBELL thought it might not be Parliamentary to say that Baron de Worms talked nonsence, so he contented himself with saying that he had made some very rash statements. Mr. GLAD- STONE said- he did not complain of the interest ex- cited by late events, but he thought the House would with greater advantage approach a discussion of this subject had they before them the papers which would furnish informs- time on the whole case. The Government would have been departing from their duty if they bad given to questions categorical answers which would have the effect of limiting the liberty of action of this and other countries, especially of Turkey. The business of the Government was to reserve liberty of action—to indicate the ends in view, not the means by Tfhich those ends were to be attained, These ends were the maintenance of established rights in Egypt, whether of the Khedive, of the Keyptian people, of the foreigrabondholders, or of whosoever else relight have estab- lished rights. He greatly regretted the attacks which had been made on the Government of France. The Government of France had declared in strong, and unequivocal terms its intention to labour loyally and heartily with the Government of Eng- land, and it was not for the Government of England to be behind in reciprocating that feeling. If ever there was a moment when the spirit of co-operation was strong, clear, and unequivocal between the Government of Turkey and this country, it was the present. Sa far as their informa- tion went, Her Majesty's Government agreed with the French Minister, that the origin of the disturbance was ac- cidental and extraneous to the present Egyptian crisis. Within the last few days Germany had actively supported the representation of the other Powers—that it was for the interest of all parties that a Conference should assemble at Constantinople —Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE expressed a hope that the Government would in a day or two be able to furnish some real information as to the condition of affairs in Egypt.—Mr. GOSCHEN said a premature statement of the course it might be deemed the duty of the Government to take might not only frustrate the object they had in view, hut also in the meantime jeopardise the lives of the Europeans resident in Egypt. The Government oould not speak in that-House without speaking at the same time in Egypt, and it was scarcely fair to choose a moment like this, when they could not give the answer they would other- wise make, for indulging in an attack on thern.—Sir H. D. Wolff agreed to withdraw his motion for adjournment. EVICTIONS IN IRELAND.—CoIoneI NOLAN called attention to the question of evictions in Ireland, and the Chief Secretary made an important statement.—Mr. TREVELYAN said the evictions during the last month were formidable, and during the first week of this month they were appalling. He thought it most unpatriotic and cruel at a time like the present, when the Government were engaged in promoting' legislation for bettering the condition of the country, that the Irish landlords should use the right they possessed in the manner they were using it. He put it to the Irish mem- bers that in order to getat the Arrears Bills it was their duty to try and get the Crimes Bill passed as speedily as possible. When this was done the Government would press the Arrears Bill forward with the same energy that had been applied to the proceedings on the Crimes Bill. THE PREYENTION OF CRIME BILL—The House after- wards went into Committee on the Prevention of Crime Bill, and considered amendments to the clause which gives power to prohibit illegal meetings. No concessions were made. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THERSDAY. THE CluSis IN EGYPT: ATTACK UPON THE GOVERN,- MENT.—A fierce attack upon the Government on their Egyptian policy was made by the Marquis of SALISBURY, who in the first instance asked for information especially with regard to the course which Her Majesty's Government intended to take.—Earl GRANVILLE briefly replied that the Khedive and Dervish Pasha were maintaining public order, though there was considerable panic among Europeans; that arrangements had been made to put refugees on board merchant vessels, and that the military were keeping order and were apparently in earnest. As to the measures to be taken in concert with the European Powers and Turkey it was not in hii power to give any information.—The Marquis of SALISBURY then in a vehement speech urged that we were free to attain the objects of English policy alone if we could not attain them in concert with other Powers. There were, he said, other matters going on with respect to which the reticence of the British Government was misplaced. He demanded to know what measures were being taken to pro- tect the imperilled interests and lives of British subjects in this moment of acute crisis, and he also expected some ex- planation as to the position of the fleet and the functions which it is supposed to perform. :Having asked if the naval "demonstration," as it was called, demonstrated anything else than the impotency of Great Britain and the feeble- ness of her councils, he contended that upon those who, sent the fleet to Alexandria without a reso- lution to follow up their action and without the necessary force at hand to give effect to their policy rested the responsibility of the blood which was shed by the passions which the presence of the fleet pro- voked. It would, he admitted, be a very humiliating thing to withdraw the fleet, but to leave the fleet there to look on helplessly whilst British menaces were being disregarded and British policy was being frustrated and British subjects were being slaughtered was a deeper and lower depth of humiliation still.—Earl GRANvILLE pointed out that the noble Marquis in his violent attack had not given any indi- cation of the measures he would wish to be taken, except first that it would be desirable to separate from the French and not to rely upon the other Powers, and secondly that we should withdraw our fleet from Alexandria. He denied that our fleet was either helpless or, pa,sive. The Govern- ment would act in the manner which appeared to them to be most judicious, but would not be driven by taunts to do anything which they though injudicious in regard to the to the lives of Europeans in Egypt. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TITHRSDA.V.

EGYPT.--Notice was given of several new questions on Egyptian affairs, and a great variety of queries were pro- pounded for Sir Charles Dilke's iininsdiete reply. In resPonse to Mr. Arthur Arnold, Sir CHARLES Said it was quite true that in September last Mr. Cookson had told the military party that they might have to meet the combined military forces of the Sultan and the Kuropean Powers, and that the Government approved his language ' • and in answer to Mr. Bourke's question as to whether the Government had made any claims for British losses in Egypt, he gave the very conclusive reply that the Government had not yet had any claims sent in. Steps had, however, been taken to look after the property of the Manchester gentlemen who had been killed, and arrangements had been made for the conveyance from Egypt of persons who could not pay their own passage- money. The foreign population of Egypt, Sir Charles added. numbered 30,000 Greeks, 15,000 French, 15,000 Italians, 4,000 British, and 4,000 Austrian and German subjects. 0 ROUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY.
