div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 17, 1882. MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 17, 1882. MISCELLANEOUS.

At a special meeting of the political committee of the Reform Club, held on. Tuf sday, a resolution of admiration at tit:? services of General Garibaldi, and sympathy with his family, was passed and ordered to be transmitted. While a young lady was purchasing a book of music in the NA-folk Market Hall, Sheffield, a thief cleverly suc- ceeded in cutting off the whole of her back hair, which hung in a plait down her hack, and made off with the prize. The trial of Mr. James Nicol Fleming on charges of fraud in the affairs of the City of Glasgow Bank will commence in Etlinburgh oa the 3rd of July. The late manager of the wrecked concern and all the directors who are living will be e,amined as witnesses.

The Observer says that a.t.a meeting of the Irish Roman Catholic Archbishops and Bishops on Saturday, Mr. Errington's mission to Rome was under consideration. It is said that three-fourths of the Bishops were in favour of having an English Embassy at the Papal Court. The other fourth, who disapproved of this course, consisted of some of the most influential members of the Hierarchy. A painful elopement is reported from Haslingden, near Manchester. A married man, aged thirty-three; eloped with a neighbour's daughter, a young woman of seventeen, and rather pretty. The young woman was frustrated in the morning, as her father and the butcher's wife appeared at the roadside station. She effected her escape at night, and was list seen at Manchester with the man above alluded to, who leaves a wife and five children.

FUNERAL EXTRAVAGANCE —Several dukes and many other members of the aristocracy, as well as 15 of the bishops, have signified their approval of the objects of a Church of England Funeral and Mourning Reform Association, in connection with which a meeting was held on the 16th instant, at Grosvenor House. One of the objects of the as- sociation is to discourage ostentatious and expensive arrangements at funerals, such as the use of crape, scarves, plumes, mourning coaches, and the like, which involve un- profitable expenditure. STABBING A SISTER-IN-LAW.-At Hull, on Tuesday, a a cabinetmaker named John Barnfather, an elderly man, was committed for trial on a charge of attempted murder. The prisoner stabbed his sister-in-law, a domestic servant named Hannah Atkinson, in the neck with a large clasp-knife. Im- mediately afterwards he gave himself up to the police, and, producing the knife, said he bought it for the purpose of stabbing the prosecutrix. He was under the influence of drink at the time, and was locked tip on a charge of being drunk and disorderly.

The appointmentby Mr. Gladstone of a Ritualist" priest" to the living of St. Matthew's, in Sheffield, has excited quite a storm in the town, and at the meeting of the local Church Conference it was resalved, by a majority of one, to with- draw the grant in aid which has been given to the vicar of St. Matthew's for some years. Ritualism has not made much progress in Sheffield, and Mr. Ommanney, who goes to that town from Bristol, will find that his membership of the "Confraternity of the Blessed Sacrament " will not be a powerful recommendation.

RECOYEHABLENESS OF SCHOOL FEES.—The North Staf- fordshire County Court Judge, Mr, H. Holroyd, sitting at Newcastle-under-Lyne, on Tuesday, in a case brought for- ward by the Newcistle School Board, for the recovery of arrears of school fees, gave judgment for plaintiffs, remark- ing that although there was a difference of opinion as to whether the fees were recoverable, and the judge of Green- wich Court had recently given elaborate judgment that they were not, other judges held the other way, and his view was in accoidance with theirs.

Replying to a letter of congratulation addressed to him on his 85th birthday on behalf of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, Sir Thomas Bazley writes that for mote than 50 years he has been identified with the proceedings of the Chamber. To have been permitted to join the earliest members in unshackling the new-born and grow ng industry of our country has been a source of the greatest gratifica- tion to him, and to have aided the relief of our commerce in British interests in India, and in the colonies, and in the wide world, have been sources of great pleasure to him. ' About 300 gas engineers, from all parts of the United Kingdom, assembled on Tuesday, in the hall of the Civil Engineers, Great George-street, Westminster, at the nine- teenth annual meeting of the Gas Institute, under which name the British Association of Gas managers will now be known. Mr. George Wilson Stevenson presided, and in his inaugural address referred to what he described as the scan- dalous conduct of the daily Press in persistently endeavour- ing to depreciate gas property, and to exalt the merits of the electric light. The Birmingham gold medal, for originality in corinection with the manufacture and applica- tion of gas, 6' as awarded to Mr. George T. Livesey, of London.

THE ErrreusTs.—The English Church Union at its an- nual meeting on Tuesday Bounden a bold note of defiance of the secular coutts. A resolution approving of the conduct of the Rev. S. F. Green was passed. The Hon. C. Wood intimated that if deprivation were to be substituted for im- prisonment as the punishment for contumacy the question would be fougHt vigorously in the courts of law. He claimed that the Church should be regarded as "supreme" in every- thing that pertained to "the supernatural end of man." The Union has upwards of 20,000 members on its books. It was stated that the subscription in aid of Mr. Green had al- ready realised .E9OO.

DISMISSAL OF A SCHOOL BOARD BY THE PRIVY COUNCIL. —The Lords of the Committee of the Privy Council on Education have made an order dismissing the members of the School Board for Barmby-on-the-Marsh, near Howden, Yorkshire. and have themselves appointed a new Board of five members. It appears that the department have been making inquiry into the working of the Elementary Educa- tion Act within the district"of Barmby, and have satisfied themselves that the members of the old Board have failed in their duty as a local authority, inasmuch as they have neglected to carry out the provisions of the Act respecting the employment of children.

PRISON GOVERNMENT.—Sir W. Harceurt and the Prison Commissioners on Monday received a deputation from the Prison Conference' including Lord Leigh and Sir U. J. Kay-Shuttleworth, Sze. The speakers explained the various reforms and improvements recommended by the recent con- ference. The Home Secretary, in reply, said the new system of prison government bad thrown an enormous responsibi- lity upon the central executive authority, and had occa- sioned some jealousy at the supercessiodof local authority and jurisdiction. He was glad the suggestions made refe.red to minor details, and he would give careful consideration to the recommendations emanating from gentlemen so perfectly familiar with the subject. THE DUKE OF ALBANY AND THE MAYOR OF MANCHESTER. —The Duke of Albany, on being informed that the Council of the Corporation of Manchester had agreed upon an address of congratulation to him on his marriage with the Princess Helen of Waldeck-Pyrinont, and that the Mayor would either forward it to his equerry or himself attend and present it, at once invited the Mayor to Claremont, and made an ap- pointment for Saturday last. The Mayor attended the appointment and presented the address, and afterwards had the honour of lunching with his Rnyal Highness. The Duke gave the Mayor the opportunity of sbeing the horse and the extensive pleasure grounds, with their grand old trees. The Mayor was received with every courtesy, anddriven frein and to the station in one of the royal carriages. COERCIVE CIARITY : IMPORTANT TO MASTERS AND MEN.—At the Birmingham Police-court, on Tuesday, the stipendiary decided an important test case instituted by the National AmaLeamared Association of Brassworkers. It was stated on behalf of the association that great dissatisfaction existed among the operatives of the town at being corn- pelted by their masters to contribute towards the Hospital Saturday collections, and it had consequently been decided to test the question as to whether the employers ceuld make deductions from the wages without the authority of the men. The stipendiary megistrate ordered Messrs. Baker & Sons, hrassfounders to refund the three shillings they had de- ducted without authority from a workman for the col- lection, and to pay the costs. This decision will rule some hundreds of cases where the masters have deducted sums from wages for the hospital collections. THE BISHOP OF MANCHESTER ON THE SALVATION ARMY. —Speaking on Monday at the annual meeting of the Lon- don Diocesan Home Mission, the Bishop cef Manchester referred to the Salvation Army. He said just now all Churchmen, clergy and laity alike, were saying that they were unable to reach the masses of the people. He found, and he was sorry for the fact, that there was a large number of the clergy and laity content to leave those masses to the care of the Salvation Army. 11,p thought that was a great reproach to the Church of England, and one which they ought to remove. Without desiring to say a word against any agency used in the cause of Christ, his mind was full of apprehension about that particular type of sensuous and emotional relieion which was now so popular. He was afraid there would be a terrible reaction, and that the results would he such as at present they could hardly appreciate. When he heard of people adopting the methods of the Sal- vation Army he always exclaimed, "Let us s.e.e whether we cannot produce the same results in our own lines," and the experiment was about to be tried in some large poor and populous parishes with which he was acquainted, a state- tnent that was received with cheers.

ANTI-COERCION DEMONSTRATION.—On Sunday afternoon, a demonstration by the Democratic Federation was held in Hyde Park to discuss the new Coercion Hill for Ireland. It was estimated that there were about 30,000 persons in the park. Bands and banners of various Democratic organisa- tions and of the Magna Charta Association were conspicuous in the assembly. Several English and Irish members of Parliament watched the proceedings from the outskirts of the crowd, but Mr. Joseph Cowen was the only English member who spoke. Mr. Cowen explained that the meeting was entirely arranged by Englishmen to discuss Irish affairs. Ireland barred the path of political progress and disturbed the administration and legislation of the country. When an important portion of the United Kingdom was in a state of serious and chronic disturbance, every other poction suf- fered. The condition of Ireland was a national humiliation, a direct reflection on our mode of rule, and a scandal to civilisation. The interests of both countries were :he same, , and he believed the bulk of the people desired to live on terms of goodwill. Ireland was disturbed because she was suffering, and Englishmen were ignorant of the extent and intensity of her suffering. Coercion in the past had proved a failure, and would be a failure in future. It was proposed to abrogate trial by jury, to give the Executive power to stop pubrc meetings, and to suppress newspapers. He pro- ceeded to review the powers given by the bill to police and magistrates, and appealed to Englishmen to protest against such an infringement of liberty. A resolution was passed strongly condemning the tyrannical policy of the Liberal Government towards Ireland, and protesting against the CoerciOn Bill now beitzg forced through the House of Com- mons as tending to strengthen secret societies, foster out- race and embitter the feeling between the two peoples. The I proceedings were orderly throughout.

The death is announced of Mr. Robert Platt, one of the largest cotton spinners in Stalybridge. Tlv will of the late Sir Francis Lyec•tt has I.ycn disputed by one of his nephews, and the Cause was tried in the Pro- bate Court on Wednesday. There was no proof whatever that Sir Francis was mentally incapable of making a will, and the jury found a verdict to that effect. The Disfranchisement Bill now before Parliament was discussed by the Chester Town Council on Wednesday, and it was resolved to ask the House of Commons to refer it to a Select Committe, before which the Council might be heard. On Monday fhe Nottingham police reported the finding of the body of a young man named Charles Cooper in the Trent, at Nottingham. He had been missing for a week, and is supposed to have committed suicide through a quarrel with his sweetheart.

The annual rifle shooting match of the " Twenties " of England, Scotland, and Ireland for the International Trophy took plice at Cowglin, near Glasgow, on Saturday. Scotland won by 19 points, the scores being—Scotland, 1,753; Eng- land, 1,734; Ireland, 1,546.

Late on Sunday night a fire took place in Spitalfields, London, in the course of which Ellen M'Conley, aged 14, was burned to death. Her parents and brother were rescued soon after the fire was discovered, but no attempt was made to save her, as it was thought there was no other person in the house.

The Duke of Cambridge visited Pontefract on Saturday afternoon, and was present for a couple of hours at the East of England Horse Show. The Right Hon. H. E. C. Chil- ders, Mr. Sydney Woolf, M.P.' Lord Houghton, and other gentlemen received His Royal Highness, who left for town in the evening. At Warwick, on Monday, a sergeant in the let battalion of the Royal IVarwickshire Regiment, flamed Charles DevonpOrt, a native of Coventry, made a desperate attempt to commit suicide. Placing his rifle against his mouth he discharged the contents, shattering the lower portion of his face in a shocking manner. He was reamed to the Warn- ford flovital. Hopes are entertained of his recovery. A Nottingham telegram states that on Saturday evening a boating fatality occurred on the river Trent at Stoke, near Nottingham. Five young men were rowing in a pleasure boat, which suddenly capsized. The river was in flood, and one named John Chater, a warehouseman, was drowned. The others had a narrow escape. The wife of a working man at Willeahall on Wednesday took out her two young children for an airing in a perambu- lator. Her attention was called away for a moment, and she left the perambulator at the top of an embankment. It wae blowni by the high wind down the incline and into a pond, and both the children were drowned. THE PRINCESS LOGISE.—A Renter's telegram, dated Quebec, Tuesday says :—" The Marquis of Lorne's yacht on approaching the wharf to-day came into collision with a schooner, in consequence of which the flagstaff on the bow of the former broke and fell on the deck. It was only pre- vented from striking the Princess Louise by the Marquis, wbo warded off the blow with his arm." THE MURDER NEAR ROTHERHAM TWENTY-SIX YEARS AGO —Leedham and Siddall, the two men charged on the confession of the former with the murder of John Whittaker, a farmer, at Dalton Brook, in 1856, and robbing him of £lBO, were en Monday remanded at large by the Rotherham magistrate. the police having failed to obtain evidence cor- roborating Leedhatn's confession., Siddall appeared to have recovered from the dekcted appearance which he presented after his recent attempt to commit suicide.

THE CHURCH AND THE SALTATION ARMY. ---.- General Booth, writing to a Manchester clergyman, says that the Bishop of Truro and Dr. Westcott have called at their head- quarters to inquire about the question of the relations of the Salvation Army to the Church; and he adds that there is evidently a very friendly feeling, and an earnest desire to establish the bcst relations possible with them, but it re- mained to he seen whether the Church would be willing to recognise, bless, and help them just as they were. CHURCH ATTENDANCE IN TIDE ORMSEIRIC DISTRICT.— Our Ormskirk correspondent sends returns of the church attendance in that district, as ' ascertained by order of the Bishop of Liverpool. The places included were Aintree, Anghton, Bickerstaffe, Birkdale, Cburchtown, Crossens, Formby, Halsall, Lydiate, Newburgh, Maghull, Ormskirk, Scarishtick, Sefton, Southport, and Westhead, containing altctgether a church population of 22,182. The attendances on the day of enumeration (yesterday week) were—morning, 5,667; evening, 3,446 ; afternoon (not general), _1,993. THE POISONING NY HOT CROSS BUNS. Since Good Friday the hot cross buns which contained poison, and which were sold in Inverness on that day, have been in the hands of a chemical analvst employed by the Crown. Ac- cording to the report of the Crown Office, no arsenic was found in the buns or in any part of the matter of which they were made; neither was any trace of arsenic discovered, or any trace of metallic poison. There was, however, an alkaloid substance possessing irritant qualities. This was present in a recognisable quantity, but its exact nature has not been determined.

COCKFIGHTING NEAR ACCRINGTON.—At an early hour on Monday morning, a cockfight occurred in the village of Huncoat, near Accrington. A large number of persons from Oswaidtwistle, Blackburn, and Burnley assembled beneath a hill in a rather secluded spot, though not far from the high- way. Three mains, it is believed, were fought, and one cock was killed and two others badly injured. Police Sergeant Sinclair, of the borough police force, heard of the affair, and went to the Accrington Station, where he apprehended three men, all of Guide, Oswaldtwistle, one of whom had in his Possession the winning cock. The feathers were stripped from the head and tail, and there bad been steel spurs used. The men were handed over to the county police at Church, and one or more will be summoned. THE ATTEMPTED MURDER AT WAKEFIELD.—At Wake- field, on Wednesday, Alfred Thompson, a coachbuilder's apprentice, was charged with committing a murderous assault on Mr. Joseph de Trosier, a homcepathic chemist. The greatest interest was taken in the ease, and the court was crowded. On Wednesday evening, the 24th ultimo, the prisoner, who lodges with his brother in Southgate, went into the prosecutor's shop for two pennyworth of ointment, and whilst Mr. de Trosier was placing it in a box the pri- soner struck him on the head with a hammer, and after- wards made several serious gashes on his neck with a pocketknife. He then ran off, leaving -his victim in a very critical state. The lad was apprehended the same night, and remanded until the sufferer was able to appear in court. He was now committed for trial.

SYMPATHY WITH A 6SASSINS —At the Conway Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, a case of assault arising ont of the assas- sination of Lord Frederick Cavendish was heard. It ap- peared that a married woman named Mary Every was charged by Mary Williams with threatening her. Com- plainant, in the presence of defendant, remarked to another woman that it was to be regretted that the murderers had not been captured. Defendant, who is of Irish extraction, felt indignant at this, and at once got hold of complainant by the throat and threatened that whenever she had the opportunity she would do for her. Complainant gave evi- dence to this effect, and was supported by other witnesses. A cross-summons was taken out by defendant against com- plainant for assault, the evidence of defendant being corro- borated by a Mrs. Ffoulkes.—The Bench dismissed the last summons, and for the assault upon Mary Williams fined defendant 20s. and costs. SIR S. NORTHCOTE ON POLITICAL AFFAIRS.—Sir Stafford Northcote, speaking at the annual meeting of the Constitu- tional Union at St. James's Hall, London, on Wednesday, said it was of the highest importance that the Conservatives should at the present moment be collecting their strength and be prepared for the great struggles. With tegard to the Egyptian question, the right hon. gentleman said they could not but feel that the information which had been received was very incomplete, such as caused Conservatives to look with very considerable anxiety and some distrast upon the course which the Government has been pursuing, and which they might pursue in future. It would, however, be quite wrong and premature to discuss such a question now. As to Ireland. it was the duty of Conservatives to strengthen the hands of the Executive Government in maintaining order and preserving life and property if they would do it. There was very great anxiety as to the present condition of society in Ireland, and very many things were said by and on be- half of the Government calculated to increase, rather than to alleviate, the anxiety. THE LIBERATION Socirrv.—At the monthly meeting of the Manchester and District Committee of the Liberation Society held at the offices, 4, St. James's Square, on Mon- day, Mr. J. H. Crosfietd in the chair, it was moved by Mr. Hugh Booth, seconded hy'Mr. R. C. Richards, and resolved —"That this Committee expresses its hearty approval of the Cemeteries Bill introduced in the House of Commons by Mr. Henry Richards. and is of opinion that the conse- cration or non-consecration of burial grounds should in no way affect burial services, whether conducted by the clergy of the Church of Prigland or byNonconformists. and that the application of this *principle to all places of public inter- ment is an eseential additioa to the Burial Laws Amend- ment Act, 18Sq. The Committee also hope that Burial Boards, and political clubs and associations throughout this district will pronounce in favour of Mr. Richard's Bill." It was moved by Rev. James McDougall, seconded by Rev. Jos. Freeston, and resolved—" That this Committee calls upon Liberal electors to urge their members to vote for the intended motion of Mr. Dick Peddie, M.P., on Friday, 23rd June, in favour of the Disestablishment of the Church of Scotland, on account of its bearing on the general question of .Disestablisliteent, and because Scottish Liberals have uniformly supported English measures for promoting reli- gious equality." A " DFCANING " WELSH MARKET TOWN.—Some surprise has been caused in Holvwell, which in a recent guide book has been described as having " thriving shops and substan- tial houses, some of which are elegant, giving indication of great prosperity and opulence." by a report just issued by the Local Government Beard, from their medical inspector, Dr. H. Franklin Parsons. The report describes Holywell itself as "an old and decaying market town," and adds that "only a single new house has been erected there during the !oast twenty years." The town in 1875 was inspected by i Dr. Blaxail, his repert pointing out serious sanitary defi- ciencies. Dr. Parsons remarks that the state of matters ldescribed in that report remains substantially the same at the present day. A letter from the Local Government Board,,,accompan;c ing the report, was read at a meeting of the Lecal Board on Tuesday, in which it was stated that : the duties of the Sanitary Authority had been almost !entirely neglected, and cdiing upon the board to improve I the drainage of the town, provide a wholesome and sufficient water supply, and to make a itisfactory arrangements for the ' removal of house refuse. The question was referred to the Stnitary Coininittee, it being explained that the medical : officer (Dr. Kell Lloyd) was preparing a special report on , I the subject. The Chah men observed that with the rates at I present 6. in the pound the demands of the Local Govern.- 1 punt Board were alarming.

(' A Cheshire carresp:mdent reports that the potato plant is blackened and cut up by the severely cold winds recently 1 prevailing. Mr. Tennyson has written a letter in wh!cli he says he thinks it would be an excellent thing for the isle of Wight if the public-houses were closed on Sundays. The Corporation of Balton have resolved from the let of July to reduce the price of gas from 3s. to 23. Bd. per thousand feet. This makes a reduction of 10d. in five years. • ...

After a long adjournment for the Whitsuntide holidays the Select Committee appointed by the House of Lords to inquire into the working of the Irish Land Act resumed its investigations on Thursday, Earl Cairns presiding. Some men w3re engaged casting a cistern at Messrs. Jackson's foundry, Bolton, on Wednesday, when through the pressure of hot metal the clamps were fo,c.!cl off the mould, and the fiery contents were scattered over five men, two of whom had to be taken to the Infirmary. On Thursday morning, a communication was received from the Local Government Board intimating that the township of Rishton had been formed into a local board district. The population of the township is over 4,000, and the local board is to consist of nine members. The first election is fired for August 11.

The wife of a man named William Smith, of Clyffe Pypard, near Wooton Basset, Wiltshire, has presented her husband, an agricultural labourer, with four children (still born) at a birth. Within eleven months she has been the mother of six children.

At Oldham, on Thursday, Mary Broadbent and Sons, cotton spinners, were mulcted in fines aud costs amounting to .£25, for allowing a number of females to work durin dinner time on the 25th. Eleven minutes had been taken out of meal hour. The factory impector said this was had case, adding that the practice was very prevalent in Oldham, and he was determined to put it down. Mr. Cane, Local Government inspector, attended at the Buraley Board of Guardians on Thursday with reference to a decision come to by the Board three weeks ago that Catholic children in the workhouse should not be allowed to attend their own church on Sundays. Mr. Cane, on behalf of the Local Government Board, requested the guardians to reconsider their decision, and notice was given for this to b-,?, done at the next meetinc%

• On Thursday the body of George Bochlen, porter, in Glas- ovi, t. Enoch's-street Hotel, was found fearfully smashed at the folt of the heist. He ascended the hoist 1 tte on Wednesday night, and is supposed to have stepped off at the seventh storey-, but apparently he had fallen from that height, coming down with such force as to have burst through the floor at the bottom of the hoist.

The-Marquis of Lansdowne, speaking at a Liberal meet- ing-at Chippenham, on Wednesday, said his recent action in retiring from the Government had been taken as indicating that he was about to sever himself from the Liberal party, but this was not the case. He thoroughly agreed with them on their general policy, and hoped the day would soon come when he could unite with them in carrying those great liberal measures which the country needed. The inquest as to the recent fatal explosion of fireworks at Hanley and the death of two girls named Cook was con- cluded on Thursday. The evidence of Dr. Dupre, professor of chemistry at Westminster Hospital, who examined the fireworks found on the premises after the explosion, showed that some of them were of a dangerous character, and liable to spontaneous ignition under certain atmospheric condi- tions. The jury found that there was no evidence to show how the explosion occurred. REVIEW BY THE DUKE OF CAMBRIDGE.—OH Thursday the Duke of Cambridge reviewedthe Staffordshire yeomanry and .militia, who for a week past have been encamping on Whittington Heath, near Lichfield. The weather has been very unfavourable for good soldiering during the ' whole time of the encampment, and on Thursday both wind and rain combined to render the review as unsuccessful as possible. Nevertheless many thousand spectators were pre- sent and witnessed the manoeuvres of the men. SID ACCIDENT ON THE Ter.—A sad accident happened on the Tay on Monday, by which two of the crew of H.M.S. Unicorn were drowned. One of the ship's yachts, under the charge of John Tuppin, who was accompanied by Abram Pepperal and William Sisk, able seamen, left Dundee in the yacht to bring Captain Cameron from Newport. The boat was capsized by a squall about midstream, and Tuppin and Pepperal sank before assistance 'reached them. Sisk was rescued in an exhausted condition.

On Thursday, at the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the sittings were commenced, and in the list ap- pears the case of " Harris and Clay v. Perkins and Enraght " on appeal from a judgment of Lord Penzance, as Dean of Arches, whether Mr. Harris and Mr. Clay, as new church- wardens, who are underevod to be favourable to the Rev. Mr. Enraght. can be substituted in the suit which was com- menced by Mr. Perkins, who is now neither churchwa, den or petitioner. Their lordships have appointed the case for Tues- day, the 4th July, when two or more Bishops, as "ecclesias- tical assessors," will attend.

At Birmingham on Thursday, Charles William Miltorr, 26, Princess•ro td, was committed to the assiz.?s for forging cheques upon Lloyd's Basking Company Limited 'The prisoner managed to obtain several cheques from the cheque-book of the Midland Farmers' Club, and filled the same up for different amounts. Cheques for small sums were paid upon presentation, but upon the presentation of a cheque for £5l us. 61. the forgery was discovered. The prisoner was also committed for trial for forging a cheque purporting to have been signed by Samuel James Mason upon the Birmingham and Dudley and District Banking Company Limited. An application for bail was refused.

THE FULHAM TRAGEDY.—Richard Wells, accountant, was again charged at Hammersmith, on Thursday' with the murder of John Carlisle, at Moore Park-road, on the evening of the Oaks race. The principal witness was Mrs. Sykes, at whose house the alleged murder was committed. She stated that on returning from Beam in the evening the prisoner and deceased had some whisky. She asked de- ceased to come out and see the garden. Prisoner some minutes after followed and struck deceased. Fighting took place and she sent for the police. She heard deceased call out that he was stabbed. Witness denied having lived with the prisoner as his wife. The case was adjourned. SHOCKING Erne OF A SHOCKING LIFE.—The turnkey at the Sheffield Police Station was considerably startled, at midnight on Tuesday, on going into one of the cells, where he found a prisoner, named Walter Sellers, bad committed suicide by hanging himself by his drawers to one of the window bars. The man, who had led a, most dissolute life, had been arrested on a charge of committing a rape on dais own child. When apprehended he was very excited, and smashed the cell window. He was a roll turner by trade, and earned £5 a week. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OF A CLERGYMAN'S SON—On Wed- nesday morning a determined suicide was attempted by a youth, who says his name is Herbert A. Bell, and that be is the son of a Norfolk clergyman. A coastguard and a fisherman heard a report on Daddy Hole, and on proceed- ing to the spot discovered the young fellow lying on the grass with a large bullet wound in the temple and a portion of the skull mid brain shot away. A large six- chambered revolver was lying near. Five of the chambers were loaded, but one had been recently discharged. He said that the previous night he had tried to shoot himself, and bad snapped his pistol eight times, but the caps were old and missed fire. Ho had, however, bought a fresh supply, aud had shot himself. A PERENNIAL LEGACY.—It may be well to note, for the cot red t ion of fallacies which are being sedulously prop igated in certain quarters, that Mr. Gladstone would have been able to make a very handsome remission of taxation if he had not had to pay the post-obits of Jingoism. This was equally the case in 1880 and in 1881. In 1880 the charges incurred by the policy of the late Administration cost us £2,347,000; in 1881 they rose to £3,842,000. This year they amount to £2,170,0.00 made up as follows :—The six millions war vote, £1.400.000. The Afghan war, £500,000. The Indian loan, £120,000. Cyprus, £90,000. Altogether, Mr. Gladstone has had to find £8,359,000 to meet the bills incurred by the spirited foreign plicy of his predecessors. No wonder there is no surplus. It is easier to get rid of an Administration than to escape payment for its liabilities. ALARMING BOATING ACCIDENT.—An exciting scene was witnessed on the river Lime, about a mile from Lancaster, about eight o'clock on Wednesday evening. A four-oared race in outrigged boats had been arranged to take place between two crews of the Lancaster Rowing Club, in the Wyre and Lune. Shortly before the appointed hour the crews were proceed- ing up the river to the starting point. There was a heavy "fresh," and a very strong wind at the time. The Lune crew were leading, and when they had reached Halton bend a huge breaker swept over the boat, causing it immediately to sink. Almost at the same moment the We're was struck in a similar manner, and both crews were immersed. A large number of perscns had assembled on the banks of ..the river, and when they saw the eight rowers and two cox- swains struggling in the water the greatest excitement pre- vailed. The whole of the young men forming the crews were, with one exception, good swimmers, end although they were about 20 yards from the side, nine of them soon got on shore, and the other young man was picked up by a pleasure-boat party, who at once went to his assistance. Upon landing the drenched crews ran as quickly as possible to their boathouse, about a mile distant, and changed their clothing. Great.was the enthus;esm displayed at their narrow escape, but the general opinion was that they ought not to have ventured on the river on such a rough evening. The boats were re- covered on Thursday. THE WORKING OF THE BURIALS Acr IN WALES.— " A Welsh Vicar" writes to the Globe protesting against the at- tempts which have been made to misrepresent the conduct of the clergy in Wales in reference to the Burials Act. He says:--" In my own case—with a population of over 4,000 --six burials only have taken place since the passing of the Act, and some of those were not quite free of 'moral pres- sure' outside the bereaved family circle. In one case tile father of a deceased child, in banding me the 'notice of burial,' voluntarily stated that he was ae.ting under outside impulse. He asked me if I would, in accordance with a Welsh custom, 'start' the funeral from the home with an appropriate prayer, &c., to afford evidence, so he said, that unity and brotherly love were not extinct. Not to be be- hind my Nonconformist friend in Catholicity, I consented to atterid at the house as desired, and offeied as a further compromise to read the part of the burial service in church, his wen minister to read the lesson and,conduct service at the grave according to his own method and discretion. The bereaved father expressed his warm approval, and added, 'lf Mr. —, my minister, agrees, it shall be so; and if be is as Christ:an-like as von are, he will do so.' But he did not do so. A note was sent by the father notifying th,e minister:a refusal. Shortly after a tombstone was set up oeer achlds grave with this inscription: ereis was the first buried in ' this churchyard under the new burial law.' Thie was a sly slap on, the cheek; but I held my tongue, and said nothing."
FoREIG N INTELLIGENCE.
THE EGYPTIAN QUES HON. GREAT RIOT -IN ALEXANDRIA : UPON EUROPEANS. TWO MANCHESTER MEN KILLED.
AT rscii-

A situation more serious than any that has preceded it has now arisen in Egypt. On Sunday a formidable riot— said to have arisen through a quarrel between a Multese and an Arab—broke out in Alexandriaond, almost without an effort being made by the Eeyptian authorities to suppress it, raged for five hours. A desperate attack was made upon the European population, in which unfortunately Mr. Cookson, the British Consul, was severely wounded, and an engineer of Her Majesty's ship Superb was killed. Several other Europeans were killed or wounded, and some of the wounded taking refuge in the French Consulate, the rioters proceeded thither and made hostile demonstrations. After five hours of rioting a body of military appeared upon the scene and dispersed the mob. The following is an extract from the Consular official re- poet: " Being summoned by the Governor, we proceeded to the great square in a carsiage, where we soon noticed the wild looks and excited gesticulations of the Arabs who were ' thronging the streets. Nearly all of them carried bludgeons or crowbars, which from time to • time they brandished in the faces of inoffensive passers-by. We met people coming back with their heads streaming with blood. Others were knocked down before our eyes, including two Europeans of respectable appearance, whom we took to be English naval officers in plain clothes. A Greek was shot at and killed by a soldier five yards from us, and at three paces tlistant to the right and left others were knocked down and stabbed. The crowd then forced us to turn round again, the carriage of the Greek Consul-General being before us. After we had proceeded a few yards an Egyptian soldier made a cut with his sword at the Consular kawass, on the box of our carriage. The weapon, however, only touched the man's arm; but the force of the blow drove several splinters of wood among us. The carriage of the Greek Consul- General was then suddenly stopped by a number of soldiers, who held the horses heads and dragged out all the occu- pants, whnn they seriously maltreated. The Greek Consul was immediately beaten with sticks and his companions re- ceived blows on the heal, causing the blood to flow, while struagling with the mob. Almost immediately afterwards an attempt was made to stop our own can iage, but the coachman lashed his horses and succeeded !fa cretting off. Mr. Cookson was struck over the head and had hia arm broken. lbs Italian Consul at Alexandria was injured by a stone at the commencement of the outbreak. The wife of the Austrian Consul-General was attacked and insulted in the street while returning from a drive." Unofficial reports differ as to the number of persons killed and wounded. One account estimates the number of Europeans killed at 67; while another states that 49 Europeans and five natives were killed, and that 80 persons in . all were wounded. The official returns of the riots - give as 3Q.0 the number of killed and wounded. Of these between 60 and 70 Europeans were killed. England and France took prompt action. In a communica- tion to the Powers they asked for an immediate assembly of the proposed Conference, and if the Porte still objected pro- posed that it should he held elsewhere without the presence of a Turkish representative. ln a situation so serious and critical further delay is obviously impossible, but meanwhile some precautionary measures at Alexandria are also required. The Khedive and Dervish Pasha, "acting in pursuance of orders from the Sultan," left Cairo for Alexandria on Tues- day, where they are under the immediate protection of the squadrons; and Arabi Pasha is left master of the situation at the Egyptian capital. The Khedive was accompanied to the railway station by Arabi, and as it is well known that he would got out of love choose the company of the rebellious Pasha, lwe can only infer that Arabi's presence was naces• aary to secure the Khedive's personal safety. All the Consuls-General too, except Sir E. Malet, haveJeft Cairo for Alexandria. The last proceedings of the Khedive: Derv:sh Pasha, and the Consuls-General, before leaving Cairo, ate not a little suggestive. All assembled, at the Palace, where Arabi was also present, as well as other prominent Egypt- ians. Aralsi then undertook to effect faithfully all the orders of the Khedive, to stop the preaching of a Holy War which he had ordered in the mosques, and to stop sedition at public meetings and in the Press; and Dervish Pasha agreed jointly with Arabi to execute the Khedive's orders—all of which means that Arabi Pasha is the only man in Egypt who can execute an order, and that so long as the Khedive's orders, received through Dervish Pasha, are agreeable to him, he will execute them. It seems to have been the preaching of a Holy War that caused the K-hedive to leave Cairo.

Latest accounts state that Sir E. Malet quitted Cairo on Wednesday in obedience to instructions from Earl Granville, and at the time of writing there is no further news from that city. In Alexandria great uneasiness prevails, although the Khedive has assured the leading European residents and the native officials that there is no fear of another outbreak. The view of the situation which his Highness takes is not shared by many who are on the spot, and it is stated that all Europeans who can obtain shipping are quitting Egypt. At Cairo the soldiers are quiet and obey their officers, but at Alexandria they are "insolent and triumphant." The Earl of Duff,rin and the French Ambassador have "insisted" that the Conference shall meet without delay, but the reply of the Sultan is not known. The telegrams from Alexandria contain full accounts of the terror which prevails there, and descriptions of the massacre on Sunday. An eye-witness gives an awful account of the scene. He states that the heads of Europeans were in many cases beaten tek a pulp, while other; victims were subjected to shocking outrages. Everywhere the bodies of the dead- were plundered. The shops were also pillaged. Another spectator saw three Europeans killed in the square. Their heads were battered against the paving stones until they were dead, and then the bodies were stripped of their clothing. This witness sa natives in official dress (green) encouraging the Arabs in their brutality. Little doubt is now entertained that although the first signal for the riot was given by tbeaffiay between a Maltese and an Arab, the outbreak was precon- certed. The rabble was uniformly armed with heavy sticks, and appeared in force at many points simultaneously. Moreover, a fanatic wearing a green robe was seen driving about in a carriage haranguisg the mob. The soldiers and the police looked on passively for five hours, and when the military were finally called out the rioters dispersed. Another "frightful " panic broke out in Alexandria on Wednesday among the European population in consequence of a street quarrel, but fortunately no serious disorders fol- lowed. The flight of the Europeans continues, and large numbers of ships have been sent to Alexandria, both by Governments and private companies, for the purpose of carrying away the refugees. The Khedive is reported to have said that he felt inexpressibly humiliated and ashamed, and that "if it were not for his family, he did not care to live."

div.head: MURDER OF BRITISH SUBJECTS.
div.p: THE MURDER OF BRITISH SUBJECTS.

Information was received in Manchester on Tuesday that two of the persons murdered on Sunday night in Alexandria were natives of the city. One was the son of Mr. J. B. Dobson, of Gresham Shipping-house, 46, Bloom-street, Man- chester, who carried on the " Manchester House," Place de Consuls, in Alexandria. Four years ago he went to Alex, andria to take part in the business there, and. 1S months ago he was joined by Mr. Reginald John Richardson, son of Mr. Richardson, head, of the firm of Richardson and Co., paperhangers and house decorators, Thomas-street, Man- chester, who took the management of the business. About six weeks ago Mr. Dobson went over to Alexandria, and seeing the state of affairs, advised them- to have an inven- tory taken of the stock in hand, to get the Consul to verify it, then lock up the place and come home, but both the young men declined to accede to his suggestion, young Dob- son stating that he was "not going to run away from the ship like a nigger." On Tuesday, in answer to a telegram which had been sent, a reply was received by Mr. Dobs.on from Mr. Whittaker that Mr. Dobson and Mr. Richardson had been murdered. From the report of the Consul, which was published on Tuesday, there is little doubt that the deceased are the two gentlemen who were "knocked down before the eyes" of the Consuls, and who were described as "two Europeans of respectable appearance, whom we took to be English naval officers in plain clothes." The proba- bility is that after being knocked down they were murdered by the Arabs, who were armed with heavy clubs. The casualties among British seamen in consequence of the riots at Alexandria on Sunday are as follow :—Killed : Mr. Pibworth, engineer of the Superb; George Strackett, admiral's domestic ; and Alfred Horne, flag lieutenant's - servant. Slightly wounded: Mr. Joyce, surgeon of the Superb; and John Cable, wardroom steward of the Monarch. No other casualties are reported among the fleet. •

div.head: KHEDIVE'S BEHAVIOUR.
div.p: THE KHEDIVE'S BEHAVIOUR.

The Times Alexandria correspondent writes 7-4 have seen the Khedive, who is behaving admirably. He said" I can- not express the disgrace which Heel. But for my wife and family I should n)t care to live." He is giving sensible direction for the preservation of order, and sinking all per- sonal feelings of dislike towards the rebel officers to ensure it. But orders, however sensible, are useless unless they are obeyed, though it is just to say that the superior officers are now behaving well. We cannot say how long this docility will last.

A blll has been brought forward in the Chamber of Deputies at Madrid for the immediate abolition of slavery. In Tuesday's sitting of the French Chamber of Deputies, the bill re-establishing divorce was read a second time by 344 to 143. . .

It is asserted by the Vienna Pressc that great opposition is presented by Ufa Russian authorities to the return of the fugitive Jews. , The Spanish Senate has agreed, by GO- against 31 votes, to discuss a bill for the mocation in a liberal sense of the oath required from members of the Legislature. Steamers arriving at American ports still report the pre- valence of icebergs in the Atlantic. Some vessels have en- countered iaefields which they estimate at not less than I, 300 square miles in extent. There is reported from Tunia the death of Mr. Levi, the claimant, in the famous Enfida case, whose claim was the in- direct :muse of the recent French-Tunisian campaign. From Vienna we learn that a violent gale has broken eczat at Moscow, and has done great damage to the exhibition bulidings there. During the storm a tire took place %thick destroyed about a hundred buildings.

lii the French Chamber at Deputies on Saturday, the bill for the reform of the judiciary system was discussed, and a clause abolishing the irremovability of the judges was adopted, as was also a proposal in favour of the principle of judges being Chosen by election. A manifesto has been issued by the 11,adica1s in Seryin in which the impeachment of the Alinistm is deed. Tha

Idispute between the Progressists and the Opposition is assuming grave proportions and as the peasants are provided , with rid e and .itum,:nition, it i:i yob:this that we shall hear t 1 of serious disturbances.

TREES ON ROADi.—St Ilie:tics have been published by the French Department of Peblic Works relative to the planting of trees along tbe high roads of the country. The total length of the Routes Nationales is 39,938,126 metres, of which 23,731,928 metres may be bordered with trees. Of this dis- tance 14,335,311 metres are planted, while 9,396,617 metres remain to be slone. Tlie, number of trees used to form the welcome avenues is 2,091,698.—A ichitect. GAMBLING AT MONA CO.—Th e evils inflieted by the Monaco gaming tables upon the Italian Riviera continue so grievous, says the Paris correspondent of the Times, that the Municipality of Ventimiglia is again petitioning the Italian Parliament to take action in the matter. The Inte) - national Aseociation for the Suppression of Gaming Tabb s is preparing for a vigorous campaign next season. In- fluential accessions have been secured to the Continent., committees, and cordial svrnpathy has been expreved in quarters from which great weight should be exercised. FIGHT IN THE HUNGARIAN PARLIAMENT.—A fight took place in the lobby of the Lower House 'of the Hungarian Parliament the other day, in consequence of a difference during a debate on lhe immi,iation of Russian Jews, be- tween a Jewish deputy namecrWahrinann caused Istoczy to send him a challenger, which was refneed, and subsequently Istoev made a personal attack upon I'Vahrmann, which led to the interference of the bystanders. The event naturally caused great excitement, and a vote of censure was passed upon the belligerents. The West Coast mail brings word that there had been no settlement of the dispute between Oko Jumbo and the people of New Calabar; but there had been no fighting for some time. From Sierra Leone it is reported that Governor Havelock had gone up to SherLoro with IW soldiers to cover a British flag which had been forcibly taken on the occasion of a recent" palaver." The Si eeboro chief and his followers are said to be very troublesome, and it was "probable their town would be destroyeel.." RECOMMENCEMENT OF HOSTILITIES IN TUNIS—The re- commencement of hostilities in Southern Tunis is reported. A despatch from Gabes says it is feared that the events of last summer are about to be repeated. The fighting near Zergis lasted several hours, with heavy loss b,:th among the Arabs and the "insurgents" who attacked them. A remark able and ominious fact in ref,,rence to this encounter is that a number of men from the Tripolite.n territory joined in the attack on the nominal allies of the French. European troops tied it almost impossible to move in Southern Tunis owing to the heat, which is said to be of "almost unprecedented severity."

GENEnAL TONATIEFF.—GeneraI Ignatieff, who for some time past has been gradually receding into the background of Russian politics, has now taken another step to the rear. It is announccd that he has voluroynily resigned the office of Minister of the Interior, and accepted the presidency of the Academy and a senatorship, retaining his position as a- mem- ber of the Council of the Empire. His retirement may be more apparent than real, but, so far as it goes, it is favour- able to a pacific policy on the part of Russia.

div.head: ZULU AFFAIR,.
div.p: ZULU AFFAIR,.

A telegram from Durban, which comes from a source avowedly hostile to Cetewayo, says that "all sorts of alarm- ing rumours come from Zululand, where the intrigues fomented by Cetewayo's sympathisers in Natal threaten to bear fruit in serious bloodshed." The Zulus, we are told, have been led to believe that Bishop Colenso is more power- ful than the Resident or the Governor. Another rumour is to the effect that Cetewavo will return and ally himself with the Boers against the English. John Dunn is reported —probably on his own authority—to be using his utmost influence to prevent an outbreak, but strife is believed to be imminent.

div.head: FUNERAL OF GARIBALDI.
div.p: FUNERAL OF GARIBALDI.

Amid a storm of wind and rain, which raged the whole time, Garibaldi's remains were on Friday interred in the little cemetery on the island of Caprera. Garlands of flowers covered the coffin, which was followed to the grave by the representatives of the Royal Family of Italy, the Senate, the Chamber of Deputies, and delegates of 300 Italian associa- tions. Numerous speeches were delivered at the grave, and as the coffin- was lowered salutes were fired.. Imposing as was the funeral there is much displeased comment on the disregard of the dead hero's wish that his body might be burned. The idea of cremation was abandoned because of the flood of telegrams addressed to Menotti Garibaldi by Italian municipal councils and friends of Garibaldi, and more particularly, it is said, through the influence of Signor Canzio, and unfortunately there are rumours'now that Sig- nor Canzio's motive in proposing to convey the body to-- Rome was not altogether pure, but that he hoped thereby to be enabled to raise himself to the position of leader of the Republican party in Italy. It is thought that the body will not be removed to Rome until the national monument that is to be built is ready to receive it, but the idea of removal at any time is deeply resented by the inhabitants of Mad- dalena, who say that rather than this they will burn tho body according to Garibaldi's commands.

div.head: KHOND OUTBREAK.
div.p: THE KHOND OUTBREAK.

The Calcutta correspondent of the Times says :—The last - telegram from Rajpore states that the Khonds are dispersing.. and no fresh murdels of Kultas are reported. The 23rd, Madras Infantry were expected on the Bth. We have every-, reason to hope that the disturbances are being successfully grappled with. The Chief Commissioner of the Central Provinces has been fully empowered to call to his aid such troops as- may be necessary, and he has made military arrangements for the entry of the troops into Kalahandi, from four different directions. The Gurgot police have. already done some good service, and their success gives reason to hope that there will be no difficulty in dealing with the armed bands which may be met with. The monsoon, makes it urgently necessary to close the operations as soon as possible. I have received the following telegram from Simla explanatory of these disturbances :—" The Khond outbreak in lialahandi, in the Central Provices, has practi- cally been repressed. The prompt energetic actionof Mr. Morris, the Chief Commissioner, and the concentrating movements of the troops appear to have deterred the leader.‘ of the outbreak, whose efforts were directed against the Kul- tas, or Hindocr cultivators. The absolute cause of the out- break is not yet definitely ascertained."
AUSTRIA AND THE PORT.
APPROACHEIG ANNEXATION OF BOSNIA AND,.
HERZ EGOVINA.

A special telegram says :—lt has been persistently re- ported for some time past that the Austro-Hungarian Ambassador at Constantinople has been charged to sound- influential Turkish circles confidentially upon the idea of a voluntary cession of the occupied provinces to the Emperor of Austria. Notwithstinding official denials, these rumours - are considered in well-infortned circles as receiving strong confirmation from the passive attitude of the Porte in regard, to the recruitment in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and more especially to the oath demanded from recruits, which makes no mention of the supreme authority of the Sultan. Not- withstanding the restricted character of Baron Calice's

mission in this matter, a certain accord is already believed to- exist between the Vienna Cabinet and the Porte rezarding the &Unitive settlement of the political relations of the oc- cupied provinces •towards the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. The indication on which this belief is based refers not only to the manner in which tke Porte has tolerated the Austrian military measures which virtually ignore the sovereign rights- concede-4i to the Sultan in the occupied provinces, but also to: the friendly attitude of Austria towards the Porte in the latest phase of the Egyptian question. This accord is looked, upon as the motive which principally contributed to Herr von KaHay's acceptance of the Common Ministry of Finance. and the supreme direction of the administration of Bosnia. Moreover. Hungarian public opinion zonsiciered that states- man as pledged in accepting office to some speedy tangible. act in regard to Bosnian affairs.

HORRIBLE TREATMENT OF LADIES IN BURMALL The. Daily Nelcs correspondent. at Rangoon writes:;-- " Th 3 latest accounts from up-country relate. only .to the King's treatment of the ex-liullah Woon (i.e., Governor for Foreigners) and his family. The Woon's disgrace is the result of a suspicion which Theebaw entertained that he was- in secret correspondence with the refugee princes In Cal- cutta, and that he was reporting for the benefit of the Ran— goon Press all the events of tha palace. The Woon and his family, with some others, were Thrown into prison, and there- every one was subjected to Ih3.most barbarous cruelty. The Woon's wife and anotbsr lady, were tied by cords to upright posts, and then cruelly beaten with clubs .until they were senseless, while his daughte:s were subj,cted to still greater indignities. The latest inf=mation of the unfortunates is that they have all been btnished to various unhealthy places in the King's dominions. Theebaw hnowa.that it would be hardly safe to Lill these people outright, but all the s.^ane he intends to accomplish his.purpose, life in the places referred to not being worth a month's purchase." FALL OF A BRIDGE::—NINE PERSONS DROWNED.

A New York telegram. says :—A br:dge across a, swollen stream at Indianopolia, Indaru, gave way while some people were on it, nine of whom were precipitated into the water qind drowned. GARIBALDI'S DEATH SENTENCE. It my not be generally known that Garibaldi was once sentenced to death. with ignominy (namely to be shot in the back) under the same Royal House of Savoy to which he subsequently readered such signal services. It was in the reign of the la:a Carlo Alberto, "'King of Sardinia, Cyprus, and Jerusalem." and father, of Victcr Emanual. The Gaze ta Pietwattse,the then Gificill joumal•of the kingdom, published tlz'o sentence on thalith Jur,e,, 1834.

div.p: STATE OTI THE CROPS.

Grass l za.a rule is light,, but seems to be thickening in the bottom , , Iteeter the late rains. Potatoes are only doing middling, i particularly rreagnume, which are very much missed. Oats are looking well, and are promis- ing more than an average crop. Of barley there are some I good fields, hat the majority of them are not doing well. 1 Hay grass is promising for a good average croo ; a mild winter and a nice spring being favourable for clover. Pete- , toes, on the whole, are not tneking • their appearance above { ground nearly so strong ne last year, and there are many complaints of magnums rotting- in the ground. A Bo— 10 ...A.MITSD TO DHANII AT WARLINGTON. —A bo— .# named Richard Harnblett, aged six years, son of John ' liamblett re..-tding at 68, Winwick-street, died on Tuesday .t-vet.ing, under the following circumstances :—About seven o'clock on Monday morning the deceased proceeded down stairs unknown to his parents, and commenced to light the tire. Whilst doing so his shirt caught fire, and he was very badly burnt !bout the body. Dr. Lees was immediately eilled in, and did all in his power to save deceased, but his efforts were without avail.—Mr. Driffi,ld (County coroner) held an inquest. on the body at the Old Bull, Winwick-street, ion Friday morning. Evidence having been given, the jury I returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

The frret statuf,cry meeting of the creditors cf Geo. David Wenham, Brown-street, Manchester, and Wilson- Patten-street, Warrington, bookseller, stationer, and news land general advertising agent, was held on Tuesday at the offices of Messrs. Lees and Graham. accountants, Manchester. The statement of affairs presented by the receiver, Mr. Mainwaring, of Warrine:ton, showed liabilitiss amounting to £2,276, and assets £753. Lividation by arrangement was resolved upon, and Mr. J. J. Graham was appointed trustee with a committee of inspection. THE COMET WELLS.—A local gentleman writes :—This comet in its parabolic orbit has passed the sun, and is now on its farewell journey to return no more. Last week the sun was clear from spots for two or three days, but during the last four days there has been one large spot on the left lower limb, which by usual measurement is 30 000 miles in di meter. During last Wednesday two more spots almost equal in size have made their appearance close to the first one named. Astronomers .and others believe these spots to be the chief cause of the cold and wet here ; of the snow in Scotland, Vienna, and other places, just now; and of the hun dreds of miles of ice and icebergs in :he Atlantic, and that they possess influences affecting the general economy of the ordi- nary physical and natural conditions, through loss of heat, on the principle of dead black places in the tire.

THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For 'week ending 10th June.—The mean temperature was 51-9 Fahrenheit, and therefore 1.3 degrees lower than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 66 P. was re- corded on the 4th inst., and the minimum 'temperature 40 F. on the 9th inst. The rainfall trieasnred slightly. The general direction of the wind was West. During the week, which was the 21rd of the current year, 31 births and 23 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 28.4 per 1.000, against 34 6 the average of the previous four weeks and against 25 2 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 6 from measles, 2 from sctrlet f ever, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from discontrol, 4 From Jung disease, 4 from old age, and 2 from vielence.—Three cases of infectious diseases were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parlia- ment, JOHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health. LANCA.SHERE AND CHESHIRE ASSOCIATION OF BAPTIST CHURCHES.—The annual meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association of Baptism Churches took place on Wednesday, at Bacup. The Moderator, the Rev. C. Williams, of Accrington, delivered an address, which bore chiefly on evangelistioeffort and the essentials to its success. From a report which was presented, it appeared that 27 churches are at the present time without pastors. Never- theless there are throughout the denomination signs of real progress. There are now in association 106 churches with a membership of 16.324, as against 102 churches and a membership of 15,927 last year. The receipts from the church for associational work have been larger than usual during the past year. At a public meeting held in the even- ing, presided over by Mr. E. Hoyle, a favourable account was given of the home mission work undertaken in connec- tion with the asoociation. The meeting was resumed and concluded on Thursday. It was decided to bola the next meeting in the church at Fishergate, Preston, and Dr. Hodg- son, of Crewe, was appointed Moderator for the year. Reso- lutions commanding the subject of temperance and express- ing sat;sfaction that a bill was about to be submitted to Parliament by Mr. Henry Richard, M.P., to apply to ceme- teries generally the principles of the Burial Law Amendment Act, 1880, were proposed and carried, as was also one renewing the Association's expression if confidence in Mr. Gladstone and his Cabinet.

PRESCOT RURAL DELNDF.Y.—A. conference of the members of the Prescot Enrol Deanery was held on Wed- needay afternoon, in the Grand Jury-room, St. George's Hall, Liverpool; the Rev. Canon Fielden (rural dean) pre- siding. The Rev. E. Snowden Smith read a paper on " Mission rooms and Non-litnrgical Services," in 14'4-lien he spoke of the value of these rooms as a means of attracting people to worship who would not otherwise attend churches, a.nd made a number of suggestions for the better and more effective carrying on of -informal services. After some dis- cassn)n, the following resolution was moved :—" That,while not excluding extempore prayer, it is most, desirable that tbe. services generally in mission rooms should be liturgical." An amendment was moved as follows :—" That all prayers used in mission rooms should be taken from the Book of Common prayer, and that the service should fellow as much as possible the order of the Church service." This amend- ment was carried by 21 votes to 6. SALE OF A CU/MP:BLAND bedutiful property known as the Derwentwater Bay Estate, near Keswick, for many' years the residence of the late .Major- General Sir John George Woodford, K.C.8., was solamitted to public competition the other day by Messrs. chinnock, Galsworthy, and Chinnock, of London, at the ,Grosvenor Hotel, Manchester. The property was divided into nine lots. Lots 1 and 2, comprising the house and a small pro- perty adjoining, known as House End, etb ntaining together 154 r. lr. 14p., realised £16,000. A small •cottage at , Portinscale fetched ee2so, and two little islands, known as Lingholmes, sold for £55. Two sPeculative properties, . known as Scale Thorns and Saltwell Park, near Borrowdale, under.which there are veins of lead and a mineral spring, did not come up to the reserve prices and were bought in. The eix lots sold, comprising together about 263 acres, realised a total of £22,910, exclusive of timber, which has to be taken at a valuation. The purchaser was Lieutenant- Colonel Greenall, a relation of the late member for War- rington.

IMPORTANT MRETING OF MUSIC/ANS. IN 3fIANCaRSTRR. —A correspondent writes :—On Monday evening a large meeting of the musicians of Lancashire, Yorkshite, and Cheshire was held in this city, to celebrate the •inaugura- tion of a national astociation of qualified professere of the art. Hitherto a great hindrance to the spread of trausic and to the recognition of th,..3 social and educational influence it exercises has been caused by the comparative isolation of its teachers, and the want of a representative body du!' quali- fied to present to the public in an authoritative manner their views and aims. Probably the present agitation ronpecting the proposed Royal College of Music has convinced the leaders of the profession-ef the advisability of no longer de- laying a fuller organisation of the large body of tighly- qualified musicians in thin country, and it cannot be doubted that for the advantage of the great body of teachets,-for the improvement and %ystematiaing of modes of tuition, anal for the concentration and utilising of the resources of executive talent which our larger towns afford, the society now estab- lished ought, if wisely managed, to be able to effect much. Lt the meeting on MendayDr. Hiles, of this city, was called La the chair; and resolutions were passed set ling the government and defining the objects of the association. On Saturday evening, July 1, an adjourned meeting will be held at -87, Barton Arcade, and in tbe autumn tie regular monthly gatherings of the members will commence. Mr. James Dawber, of Wigan, has (pro tern) und.rtaken the duties of secretary, awl will afford all necessary information as to membership.
