On the evening of the sth inst., two men waned Mat,on and Burrows were drinking together at the Britannia Inn, Irwell-street, Widnes. Mason asked Burrows to-come out- side and settle a quarrel of long standing 'between them. Both the men are stated to have been considerably under the influence of liquor at the time. Burrows, at fist, appeared unwilling to engage in a tight, but at last he consented, and they went down to a spot near the river Mersey. Here Mason hit Burrows on the nose, and a struggle took place between the two men, Mason falling backwards a distance of about two feet. Burrows immediatQly got up, and called upon his cotnpanion to "come on," but Mason said he could slot move, as his ankle gave him great pain. A cab was , sent for and he was taken home. Up to Friday night he went about the house with a stick, but refused to have the doctor sent for. His wife at length ...sent for Dr. Cooper, who pronounced the ankle broken. Deceased gradually grow worse, and daring Saturday and Sunday he was totally unconscious. He expired on Sunday night. The man Burrows was subsequently taken into custody on a charge of manslaughter. THE PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
Burrows was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday morning, charged with killing and slaying Richd. Mason.

Inspec'or Barnett, in open;ng the case, observed that deceased died on Sunday night. On the evening of the sth inst., about lialf•past five, the prisoner and the deceased were at the Britannia public-house, Irwell-street. It ap- peared that there was an old grievance existing between them, and after a passage of words, which only added fire to the dispute, they adjourned to the river side and com- menced to tight. After the exchange of some blows they seized hold of .each other. Mason fell, and immediately complained that he could not get up, as his ankle was injured. He was assisted to rise, but it was then found he was quite unable to walk. Deceased was carried into a house, and afterwards removed home in a cab. There he remained several days without medical assistance, but his wife afterwards went to Dr. McLennan and consulted him in respect to her husband. He advised her to fetch Dr. Cooper, the poor-law medical officer for the district, and that gentleman paid deceased a visit on Friday last. Dr. Cooper, who found that several of the banes in the man's ankle were broken, attended deceased up to the time of his death,which took place on Sunday evening last. The difficulty in which the police were was how to account for Mason's death, as the broken ankle could not possibly be considered a satisfac- tory explanation of his decease. Mr. Lewin, magistrates' clerk, asked the inspector if he wished to apply for the remand of the prisoner. Inspector Barnett replied that he did. The police had written to the coroner, and it was quite likely the inquest would be fixed for the following day. Samuel Snelson, waterman, sai.4 that on Monday, the sth inst., he was in the Britannia vaults, in Irwell-street, with the prisoner and the deceased. He had to leave the house, and when he did so the two men were quarrelling.
Inspector B anett: Was there any proposition- that they should go out and fight?
Witnesi: Not then.

Inspector Barnett:But was that proposition made at all? Witness went on to say that about five Minutes afterwards Burrows begged of deceased to let the matter drop, as it was three years since the cause of the quarrel arose, but he said he was not agreeable to that course, as he fancied "he could lay on him" (Burrows), and "they must have it out." Bur- rows remarked that he did not 'lay upon him for nothing." He also said they could "go out and try it." The two men then left the house' and went down to the river side, where they commenced to fight. Mason took off his coat, in order to have freer play for his limbs, but the other man did not remove any garment. Nothing of particular moment hap- pened in the first round, but in the second Mason hit Burrows under the nose, and drew a little blood. Barrows then said, "I shall have to shape better than that, or I shall get a lay- ing on," and went into the contest with more energy, the result being that immediately afterwards he hit Mason on the mouth. They struggled with one another further, but no blow was struck, and Mason fell close to the edge of the declivity formed by the ground on which the fi At occurred, rolled over, and exclaimed, " Oh, my foot! " Witness said to Mason," Host thou hurt thy ankle? Let me pull thy boot off" After doing so, he (witness) remarked, "It is out," but the deceased said, "It isn't. He then put his arms round Mason's neck and carried him, with the assistance of Isaac Spruce, to the Britannia lon, where they put him upon a chair. They offered to carry deceased home, but he de- clined, and said he would go home in a cab. Witness then went to Mr. Lee's for a conveyance, in which deceased was taken home. _ _ _

Mr. Lewin : What state where these people in when they were in the pub!ichouse ? Witnes: They were far gone in drink. Mr. Lewin : Prisoner, you have heard the evidence given against you. Have you anything to say? The Prisoner : Yes, it is about true so far, only a little before that--
Mr. Lewin: You had better not make any Btatemont now.

sergeant Robinson said he had seen the deceased Richard Mason, of whose death a report had been made to him. .In consequence of this, he apprehended the prisoner, and charged him with ()lining the man's death by fighting with him, and striking him over the face, on Monday the sth inst. Bnl-rows replied "I Imaye had to resist him for more than two years, in order to keep from 'fighting with him. have nofhing azainst the man."
Mr. Lewin: Do you wish to ask ;the witness any ques- tions ?

The Prisoner said that whr!ri Sergeant Robinson appre- hended him, he reminded him thatthe charge he had broutfct against him was one of ca-using the man's death, .bat it would be dearly proved, as soon t'S all the evidence hadteen got together, that he could 'not possibly have caused Mason's decea.se.
Witness: You replicd that -Tou had resisted him ler two years.

The Prisoncr said that deceased had had a trricvance Ugainst him during the whcle of that time. Mr. Lewin (to prisoner): Have cog anything to say why you should not be remanded until after the Corcner's in- quest has been held? The Prisoner: "Wht else is there-," if I don't be re- manded ?

Inspector Barnett: The Joctor cannot at prtsent give evidence as to what has caused deuased's deativautil there has been a post nzo;•tem examination made. Mr. Lewin asked Sergeant Robinson if thrresult of his enquiries proved to him that the injured man -did not leave his house from the time that be was taken there after the fight, up to the time of hie death, and that 4o that day he was under the doctor's etre.

Inspector Barnett.: Yes. Mr. Lewin: To when do you ask for a remand? Inspector Barnett : To Thursday. Prisoner was accordingly remanded until Thursday. Burrows was again brought b4ore Mr. Holbrook Gaskell on Thursday morning. Inspector Barnett-stAted the result of the Coroner's investigation, and said bedid not offer any evidence against•the prisoner. His worship formally discharged Burrows. TEIE INQUEST.
On Wednesday afternoon, Mr. Barker4.deputy coroner, held an enquiry touching the death of,tieceased, at the West Bulk Hotel, IVezt Bank, Widnes.

The Coroner, in opening the proceedingei said the enquiry was one which might, or might not involve serious conse- quences to the man who was in custody, bat upon this point he did not propose to express any opinion, as he should leave them to form their own opinion upon the evidence which would be placed before them. It appeared that the deceased and the prisoner were on the evening of the sth inst., drinking in the Britannia Inn, near the river side. There was some grievance existing between them—he did not exactly know what it was—but it seemed that the de- ceased invited tite-man who was in custody to fight him. It was only fair to Burrows to say that he appeared to have been very reluctant to accept the challenge thrown out, for be remarked that the cause of the (petrel -arose some time ago, and he thought the lapse of time wae:quite sufficient to have allowed any angry feeling to subside. Unfortunately, deceased, appeared to have been determined "to have it out" in a trial of strength. He did not put it before them , that Mason had any ill-feeling against the prisoner, for it seemed to him to have ben more a ceate inavhich there had been some angry feeling, and for the purpose of te4ing their physical power rather than from any maliciousness, the two men went out upon some ground near the river side. They were then so much advanced in drink, that bet for the nature of the ground upon which the struggle took place, it was highly probable that no serious results would have happened. The ground was, however, of a peculiar formation at the place named, and deceased appeared to have fallen over the embankment during the tight; and cs he did not rise again, a man -named Snelson, who was-watching the combat, went to him, and asked him what was the matter, and offered to take-his boot off, when it was found that Mason's ankle was broken. Deceased was afterwards taken home in a cab, and told a story to his wife to the effect that he had had "a hit of bather with a man, and had fallen into a gutter and sprained his ankle. When she eked him what "the bother" was about, deceased dido not blame anyone ; but said "It was only a drop of drink, and two fools together." Therefore, it appeared that deceased had no ill- feeling against the prisoner. The only question for them to :consider, as a jury, was what was the cause of death. De- ceased declined to have a doctor for several days, as he appeared to have thought that he was only suffering from a sprained ankle; but on last Friday he became much -worse. :t was certainly a matter for regret that medical assistance wag not called in earlier, because if this course had been adopted the doctor would have seen what was the matter, and then, in all probability, the result would not have been of se serious a nature. Mason became semi-unconscious on the Friday, and died on Sunday evening. Under the cir- cumstance, as a mere strain, or fracture, of the ankle was not of itself eufficient to cause death. he had ordered a post wzoPtem examination of the body to he made, for the satisfaction of the jury. If, after they had heard the evidence of the doctor, they could trace the death to the encounter between the two men, then, of course, the man in custody latfore them would be responsi- ble, and, in point of law, guilty of manslaughter. If, on the other hand, they thought the death nets not atttibutable, either directly or indirectly, to the occurrence on the Mon- day, then, it mieht be, they would-have to return a simple verdict of "Died from natural. Causes." ljatherine Mason, !Yigew of deceased, said 313 e lived at

No. West Bank-street. Her husband was a flatman, and tel t home on Monday, after breakfast, quite sober, and in good health. In fact, deceased, who was 35 years of age, had always been a healthy man. At times he was in the habit of taking considerable drink. It- was 12 years since deceased was attended by a doctor. She had been married to him eight years. It was about nine o'clock in the morn- ing when deceased left the house, and he returned about seven o'clock in a cab. He said he had "been having a bit of bother- with Win. Burrows, and had sprained his ankle by falling in a gutter." He did not blame anyone for the injury to his ankle. Deceased was under the influence of drink when he came home, but wasnot intoxicated. Sae bathed the ankle carefully each day, and on the Friday sent to Mr. MacLen- nan, who came to the house and examined deceased's ankle, which ha said was broken. On the same day, and previous to sending for the doctor, her husband became partly uncon- scious, and could not speak. He remained in the same con- dition until his death, which took place on Sunday night at half-past nine. Before his death she asked deceased how the accident had occurred, and he replied, "It was only a drop of drink, and two fools together." Mr. D. U. MacLennan, physician and surgeon, practising in Widnes, deposed that, by the direction of the coroner, he made a post-niortent examination that inornin. On the left leg, near the ankle, he found a bruise, but, with this exception, no marks of violence. Inside the bead, he found a small clot of blood in one of the arteries of the brain. The surrounding brain tissue was undergoing degeneration, ow- ing to the clot of blood having stopped the circulation. The heart was fatty and degenerated; the liver and kidneys were also soft and flabby. From the appearance of the body, he considered deceased to have been a man addicted to drink- ing for some time past. He cut down to the left ankle bone, which he found to be fractured. The cause of ueath waa a clot of blood forming in the heart, being pumped up to the brain, and so stopping the circulation in the latter organ. The Coroner: Do you think the fracture of the ankle in any way, directly or indirectly, causcd death? Witness: I do not.

The Coroner: 'lO what do you think the formatiou of the clot was due? Witness : To the condition of the valves of the heart. When the valves of the heart are degenerated in that way such clots are formed.
The Coroner: Assuming the heart to be in a fatty state of degeneration, would any excitement, or fall, be likely to cause that clot of blood Witness: I don't think so.
The Coroner: Then you do not think that clot was due to external violence or excitement? Witness: No.
The Coroner: Then, in your opinion, you say that the formation of this clot was due to natural causes, and that it caused death. Witness: Yes.

The Coroner: Supposing the deceased had been engaged in some sort of tight, or struggle, as we understand he was, do you think that could possibly have caused his death in- directly? Witness: It might have increased the circulation, but I don't think it would have caused death.
In answer to a juryman, witness said he thought the clot of blood would had caused death independently of the fracture.

The Coroner: That semi-insensibility, or state of coma, would be due to the 'stoppage of the circulation in the brain? Witness: Quite so. The Coroner: I euppose that there is no chitibt that he had been drinking for sotne years past? Witness thought there could not pos,sibly be any doubt of this, judging from the appearance of the internal organs of deceased's body. The Coroner : Then you do net attribute the death to the fight at all ? Witness: I don't. Death from the cause I have referred to, is quite a common occurrence. I was very particular in investigating the point now under consideration, and care- fully examined all the vessels of the brain to see if any of them were ruptured; and I found they were not. By a juryman It must be remembered that in this case the vessels were not ruptured, but simply clogged. Samuel Sn?lson, waterman, said he had known deceased twenty years; and he was a man who was ye; v " touchy " in drink. Sometimes deceased would have a week's drink- ing, but go on working during the whole of the titne. The Coroner: Then he was a very good man. Witness (proceeding): Between four and 11,P o'clock on the evening of the sth inst. he saw detelLsed and Burrows there. He had met Mason some short time previously in Runcorn. He (witness) had to leave the house for some- thing, and on his rout n he found deceased quarrelling with Burrows about an old grievance. Witness then repeated the evidence which he gave before the magistrates, as reported above. He'added that Burrows and Mason fought four rounds. After Mason's ankle had been examined he heard Burrows say he was very sorry that the affair had happened. He bad never in the past heard of any animosity to deceased on the part of Burrows. On the c,mtrary, they were al- ways great friends when clear of drink. During the fight he observed no unfair conduct an the part. of Burrows.
Mrs. Snctson was also called, but her evidence was not material. -

Isaac Spruce, flatman, employed on the same vessel as deceased, gave evidence as to seeing the latter part of the fight. He admitted that deceased would s'irne times have a drinking bout extending over a month, .bat all the time he would continue to follow his work.

James Bogie, barman at the Britannia, nest give evi- dence. The Coroner then briefiy reviewed the evidence, and directed the jury on the points of law. The jury immediately returned a verdict of "Died from Bat ural ca uses."
During the proceedings a large crowd assembled around the hotel anxiously 7,-altiog for the result.

Mr. DATMICEY said he had aarew observations to addresa to the members before they separated. The Guardians would be aware that the Local Government Board had received a memorial from some of the inhabitants of Appleton, asking that their township might have an additional Guardian ap- pointed. It -seemed to him that the inhabitants of Appleton had very good.ground for the recalest they hail made. Ap- pleton had a population of 3,300, and a rateable value of £11,269, whereas Frodaham, with a population of 2,400, and a rateable value of £lO,OOO had two Guardians. A commu- nication bad been forwarded to the Guardians by the Local Government Boaad, stating that they would ba ready to consider any proposal from the Board as to amalgamating some of the smaller townships. There were at present 42 Guardians for the ;Union, the population of which had only increased 3,400 in ten years, so that there did not seem to be very much ground for increasing the number of the rate- payers' representatives. On the other hand, the papulation of some of their parishes had decreased .considerahlv. For instance, Aston Grange, with a population of 33, and a rateable value of £1,079, returned one Guardian. Baiting- ton, with a population of DC, and a rateahle vain,. of £987, oae ; whilst Appleton. with a Population ..of 3,310, and a rateable value of £11.2.69, only returned one ; with a Mpulation of 196, one; Kekewiek, with a population of 83, and a rateable value of 923, one; Stockham, with a population of 25, one guardian. He did not know whather the representative of Stockliam was present that day or not, but he trust say that it seemed absurd to him that a place containing so few inhabitants should return one guardian. The DPPITTY CLERK said that the guardian in qneztion had only attended once this year. Mr. DAITNCY proceeded to say that this did not Round very well. Steel:ham in 1871 bad 43 inhabitants, but it hail since gone down to 25. There was another p utah which seemed almost entitled to another guardian, viz, Westin, which had a rateable value of £11,609,and a popula- tion 1.282. It would, he thought. be adviaable to amalgamate one or two of the pp ishes, and give a guardian to Weston as well a 3 to 4PplEt .71. 119 did not 1409 w whether there

would be any objection to the adoption of such a course. Could any reasonable objection be raised to Stockham being added to Norton, which had a population of 345, and a rate- able value of £6,680. Then there was fiekewick, which had only a population of 83, and a rateable value of £3 293; and Daresbury with a population of 139, and a rakeabl. value of £1.581. How often did the representative for Kekewick attend.

The DEPUTY CLERK: He has not attended for three years,—never even put in an appearance. Mr. MelsrvitE! Appleton representative has attended. The DEPUTY CLERK: Yes, twice this year. Last year he attended seven meetings.

Mr. WALLING-toll: lie has "married a wife,and, therefore, be cannot come." (Laughter.) Mr. RIGBY : What power have we, Mr. Dauncey, to remove these Guardians at Stocitham and other places. Mr. DAUNCEY : The Local Government Board will do that.

Mr. RIGBY replied that he did not wish to put anything they cotild help into the hands of tbe Local Government Board, but to do as much of the Ciucirdians' business as possible at that table. (Lauv_hter.) Mr. DAIINCEY : But there are things which you cannot do. you know. I think that Appleton ought certainly to haw another Guardian. •

Mr. LOWE said he was of a similar opinion to Mr. DAllncey. Mr. RIGBY : Yea, hut they ought to grant armther Guardian to Appleton without talOarg one away from another township. Mr. DAENCEY replied that it was a bad thing to have too many Guardians, for they always found that more business was done where the body which had to transact it was not too ponderous. The Runcorn Union had at .present 42 representatives, which seemed sufficient when they took into consideration the size of the Union.

Mr. RIGBY wished to I<now whether the non-attendance of a Guardian at the Board meetings a certain number of times was sufficient to di-qoalify him. The CHAIRMAN: That twitter rests with the ratepayers. Mr. DAUNCEY: But a small parish, containing only 25 inhabitants, does not like to go to the expense of a contested election.
Mr. RIGBY : But still they pay as much as the other places in proportion.

Mr. DARBYSIIIRE said be believed that in order to vote in the election of a Guardian in some of the outlying parishes they must be ratepayers, and if two townships were amalga- mattEl many of the voters would not have a qualification for each parish. Mr. DATINCEY explained that for this particular purpose the division of the townships or prtrishes would be abolished by the Local Government Board. Mr. W. Wiltmovz: It is very ppssiblo that under those circumstances there would be a contest every year. • _
Mr. DAIINCEY IC you give a Guardi;n "to every 25 pope, you might almost as well give one for each large family. Of course, no change could be nude until the next election.

Mr. McisrYnE observed that, in order ts bring the mitte.r to an issue, he would move that for the purposes of Guar dians' election Stockham and Norton should be amalga- mated, and Kekewick and Dareshury ; F.nd also that an additional Guardian should be given to Appleton, and another to Weston.

Mr. IC.ORMAN seconded the proposition. Mr. RIGBY moved an amendment, which was duly seconded, to the effect that the representation of the various townships should be permitted to remain as it was. The original motion was carried by a large majority. Mr. WM. WHITLOW considered it was very unjust to carry such an important proposal without every guardian in the union havin4 notice that the subject was to come up for discussion. In this case even the guardians who would be most aff?c!ed by the carrvin of such a motion, had not oven received notice that it was to be considered! A MEMBER said he believed that the only—matters in regard to the discussion of which each guardian was required to have notice, were those relating to the expendi- ture of money. _ _
Mr. DAuNegY : There is no hurry abut the proposal ; and you might, as a matter of courtesy, let the gentlemen affected know.
Mr. W. WHITLOW accordingly gave notice that at the next Board meeting he would move that the resolution which had been passed, be rescinded,
THE MASTER OF THE HOUSE AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD.

Mr. DAUNCET then said he had another miticr to bring under the ccAsideration of the Board, and it was a rather un- pleasant cue, as it aff,cted the children of Mr. Jones \who lived in the workhouse. He dare say that most of the Guardians knew that it was against the regulations of the Local Government Board for the manage:nent of such in- stitutions, that any children of the master above 14 years of age, should continue to live in the workhouse. The CILAIRMAN : I bog your ptrdon ; we did not know that.

Mr. DAUNCEY proceeded to say, that the rule might appear to the members a hard and fast and cruel one, but it was an order which had only been issued after the necessity for it had been shown to the Local Government Board. Several cases had occurred, and one or two in his own dis- trict, where owing to the residence of a master's children ia the house, great scandal had been caused. He had not, however, one word to say about Mr. Jones's children in particular, as he believed them to be -very well conducted. The Board in London did not wiQi to press unnecessarily bard upon Mr. Jones, and they would be glad to give him any reasonable time in which to make the necessary arrange- ments for the removal of those of his children who wero shove 14 years of age from the house. Having spoken of the various ages and occupations of the children of the master of the house, the speaker went on to say that he believed most such o:ileitis knew, when they accepted-efile?„ that the Local Government. Board had made such an Order. The question in the particular case then under considera- tion, arose on the repoi t of the auditor, and it having been once brought under the consideration of the - Local Oovernment Board, they had no other course left than to deal with it. Mr. NORMAN considered this a very hard'case, as Mr. S,ones had been master of the workhouse over 2 years. In the -couree of that time Mr. Jones had gathered abrmt him a large family, but were they to say that because of this, several of the members of it were to leave the house? If so, ought they not to give the master an equivalent, in the shape of salary, an that he could provide for his'eaildren who were above 14 years of age, out of the house. It was impossible for a man in Mr. Jones's position .to provide for his children outeide the house on a salary of £lOO a year. The proposed arrangement was one which would debar the master's children from visiting their parents, wlrich was a most unfair arrangement, and one which not a-ningle Guardian, or mem• ber of the Local Gevernment Board wor.ld tolerate being made in the case of his own offspring. (Hear, hear.) Not a single word had been said about the way in which Mr. Jones's family had conducted themselves in the workhouse. He did not see how the Guardians oauld rneke any alteration in the present arrangements. . _ . . .

Mr. LOWE remarked that in Mr. Norman's speech he had referred to an arrangement which was made some 18 months ago, as to Mr. Jones paying a -certain sum for the keep of his children in the house. NOS; he must say that the little affair referred to was very cleverly managed indeed! The Blard would remember that he (Mr. Lowe) was the gentle- man who first brought under the notice of the Guardians the reasonableness of the master paying for the maintenance of certain members of his familyin that house. He was quite aware that during the time when the matter was under dis- cussion, tlib master of the house went aboue canvassing the Guardians on the.question, and that be did no speak very respectfully of him during his visits to those gentlemen. He understood that Mr. Jones was instructed to say nothing, on the understanding that if beelid so, "he would be worked through much cheaper," then by any plan which he could personally submit to the Board. Notwithstanding all that had passel on this question, be was not prepared to go as far as the Local Government Board, but, should be quite satisfied if the master's children paid an equivalent for tbe cost or their maintenance.

Mr. HAZLERIaRST quite T.greed with the remarks of Mr. Norman. He would put it to each of the Guardians as a personal matter, and ask how they would feel if they were to be deprived of the society of their children at the age of 14. Though the Board might, to a cPrtain extent, feel powerless _against the Luca Government Board. he hoped they would resist the proposal submitted to theta to the utmost of their a•biiity. Mr. RIGBY wished to ask the Government Inspector if the Board had really no pricer at all in this matter. For his own part, he could see very little use in the members assem- bling there every fortnight, after the interferences which they had to submit to in connection with the Local Government Board. The business of the -Union had better be transacted in London at once, for the Local Government Board mem- bers appeared to pop their noses into everything. (Loud laughter.) Mr. DAuxcrty: That is a matter for your clerk to answer. Mr. HAZLEHURST said it appeared very illogical that be- cause a certain thing had occurred in a particular place the whole country should be saddled with such a regulation. Mr. MCINTYRE was of opinion that it would be quite time enough to enforce such a regulation as the one proposed when some report of irregularity in the house was brought before the Board of Guardi.ins flow was the training or morality of the members of Mr. Jones's family to be looked after if they were removed from his superintendence? He scarcely thought that such a law an the one referred to by the inspector was upon the books of the Local Government Board at the time Mr. Jones entered upon his duties. Mr. HAZLEIIIIItST : It is :1 pity that the question was ever raised. Mr. DA.CNCEY : That is another question. ' •

The Deputy-Clerk read a letter sent some short time previously by tho Local Government Baard on this ques- tion, after which Mr. Rigby maintained that the Guardians had nothing contrary to the plain -meaning of it, as it said they consented to the children of the master residing in the house, under proper restrictions. The CHAIRMAN referred to the lack of power vested in Board of Guardians, owing to "centriliz itiou." Mr. RIGBY c tid the Local Government Board were a perfect nuisance to the Guardians. (Laughter). The money was found hy the ratepovers, and their representatives ought to have the power of spending it according to the best of their The CHAIRMAN said he should scarcely like the expressions of Mr. Rigby as to the Local Government Board to go to the public, as long as he (Canon Barclay) presided over the deliberations of the Guardians. Mr. RIGBY : They arc "tittle tattling at every verse end." Mr. DAtINcEv said he should be glad to forward the observations of the Guardians to the Local Government Board. lo reply to the Chairman, the Inspector also remekcd

that he did not think it was necessary the Boma should pass any resolution upon the subject. Mr. HAzLEnuasr : You can say that in this case you did not see that any change was necessary. Mr. DAUNCEY : No, I cannot do that. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: FARNWORTII GENTLEMAN AND THE CABMAN.
div.p: THE FARNWORTII GENTLEMAN AND THE CABMAN.

At the Widnes Police Court, yesterday, before Mr. Hol- brook Gaskell, Mr. George Walker, who described himself as a cab proprietor living in Liverpool, was charged by a gen- tlemanly looking man, named Mr. Robert Forster, of Farn- worth, with stealing a v.eitch and waistcoat, his property. Inspector Barnett briefly opened the CiSe, after which he called the prosecutor, who appeared to be labouring under a little excitement. Mr. Forster stated that on the previous ,1 evening, about six o'clock, he was in Liverpool, and en- gaged a cab in Clayton Square. Whilst he was talking to ! the cabman, the prisoner came up and they entered into conversation. Ile did not ask the prisoner, who said the driver was his brother, to get into the conveyance, but he did so without being requested, end -drove with him to Fern- worth. Whilst on the journey prisoner struck him. At Farnworth he (witness) found he had not the money with which to pay the cabman, and a disturbance followed, in which the window of the conveyance was broken. He and the prisoner then went into the Ring G'Bells Inn, and be (witness) pulled off his coat and waistcoat. At this time he had his watch in his hand, and it was seen by Mr. George Stead, chemist. He put his match ha his waistcoat again, and some short time after, he looked for the garment in order to put it on, bat could not find it. He and other persons looked entirely through the house in order to find the watch, but they failed to do so. Mr. Lewin, Deputy Magistrates' Clerk: In what state was the prisoner? Drunk.—And what state was you in ? I was as near sober as I could be.—llow near is that? Well, "I had just had enough that was good for me." Prisoner cross-examined the prosecutor, and alleged that be lent the prosecutor 2s. 41. in the cab, and then he told him that if be would see him in Liverpool on the following morning he would give him 55., but he replied that all he wanted was simply the cash he had lent him. P.C. Ross said he was called to the Ring-o'Bells by the driver of the cab, who complained that he had not been paid his fare. Prosecutor complained of his coat having been taken away by someone. He (witness) went outside the house to find the man, but he could see nothing of him, and afterwards went to the Cheshire Lines station at Farnworth. Here he found the prisoner, who was wearing the prosecu- tor's waistcoat over his own. He took him into custody. Prisoner, in reply to the formal Charge by the Clerk, said ha became acquainted with the prosecutor, on the previous night, through his asking him have a drink. Forster afterwards slid, " Come along with Me to Farnwottli," aod he did so, and lent him 2s. 4d. whilst they were in the cab. Forster told him that he bad no money. Prosecutor : Yes, and I paid you back again. Mr. Gaskell (to the prosecutor) : Don't you talk now ; you have had your say. Inspector B Irma said he had not the slightest objection to the prisoner being allowed bail. Prisoner : I can find £5OO bail for that matter. Prisoner was told he could be admitted to bail on finding sureties, himself in £5O, and two sureties in £25 each. The proceedings then terminated.

Ou Thursday evening a meeting of farmers was held at Gisburn, to take steps to improve the Gisburn fortnightly fair, which was formerly one of the best in the north of England. In order to increase the number of stock shown, it Was decided to give LI to the exhibitor who sold the most stock in the market, and also 10s. to the largest seller of sheep. The landowners are supporting the movement. Messrs. IV. Rose and Co., owners of the steamship Pera, which recently foundered off Cape Race, received a telegram from 11,,ont•ea1, yesterday morning, giving the names of those missing. The -crew altogether numbered 33. The Vera, which was engaged in the Canadian cattle trade, was at the tine she struck the iceberg on her way back to Canada. In addition to the crew there were on board six cattle drovers and one foreman, one of the latter and ten of the crew being among the missing. WRECK OF A LIVERPOOL SHIP.

div.head: TWELVE LIVES LOST.
div.p: TWELVE LIVES LOST.

A Lloyd's telegram received from Sydney N.S.W. states that the iron bayque Don Guillermo, 599 tons, homeward bound with a cargo of copra, while lying-in the harbour of Va7au, Tong l Islands, South Pacific, was caught in a cyclone, drPvo'from her anchors, and stranded on a reef of coral rocks and went to pieces. The captain, mate, and two men Were lost. Eight others of the crew put off from the vessel in one of the boats, and not having been beard of are also given up as lost.

div.head: HORRIBLE DEATH FROM HYDROPHOBIA.
div.p: HORRIBLE DEATH FROM HYDROPHOBIA.

Thirteen months ago William Mills was bitten by a dog in Walmer-road, Plumstead. The wound was cauterised and soon healed. A few days afterwards the dog was destroyed, and the circumstances passed out of mind the man continuing his work in the shell foundry of the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich, apparently in good heal,h. List Mon- day he complained of pains, and on Wednesday he showed symptoms of hydrophobia, all the worst features of which painful disorder were rapidly developed, and the man died in dreadful convulsions. He was a married man, about 48 years of age, and bad been 27 years employed at Wvolwich Arsenal.

A Meeting of the Church of End end Funeral and Mourn- ing R4orm Association was held at Grosvenor House, London. yesterday afternoon. The Duke of Westminster piesided, and expressed his approval and sympathy with the objects of the association to promote a better idea of Christian burial, and discourage ostentatious and expensive arrangements. A letter was read from the Archbishop cf Canterbury, who stated the association had his fullest sympathy, and he heartily wishtd it success. All the speakers condemned the pr,s,-nt custom as extravagant an I unprofitable, and a great hardship upon the poorer classes. Resolutions wet() adopted affirming the objects of the asEc- elation.
THE DUBLIN CORPORATION AND THE PREVEN- TION OF CRIMES BILL.

The Corporation of Dublin held a special meeting yester- day, to consider the adoption of a petition to Parliament, protesting against the Prevention of Crimes Bill. Mr. Grays in proposing the adoption of the petition, said prompt action was necessary. Of all coercive acts passed since 1800, this was the most unconstitutional, and the most stringent. He believed they could never have prosperity or peace in Ireland until Irishmen were given the right of self government. Mr. Abraham Stncldeton • seconclei the adoption of the petition. Mr. McEvoy mcv2l an amendment, and said those interested in preserving peace in Ireland were with him in opposing it. Alderm:t.3 Mayers seconded the amet.dment, and said the bill was not intended to hart ass the law-abiding subjees of the Queen, but to punish criminals. After some furthn dis- cussion. the resolution in favour of the petition was carries by 34 votes to 12. The petition will be presented by the Lord Wyor of Dublin in state at the bar of the House of ; Commons.

THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION. RUMOURED LANDING OF TR( ADPS.

WANTED AN IRISH POLICY. (len-ternia Ill.) Sir,—lt is impossible to deny the existence of those under caerrents of individual prejudices, artificial interests, and even bigotry of opinion, alluded to in my last letter, which embarrass the development of impartial and efficient legisla- tion. Add to these that tangible. potent obstructiveness, the question of expediency— by the way, is morelwhich, familiar to politicians of the weak-kneed type than to those bent upon "doing justice though the heavens fall "—and the tardiness of Mr. Gladstone in adopting a courageous out and out nationel policy towards Ireland loses its mysterious- It is his consciousness of these defects in his Parlia- imentary majority, and their consequient delimitation of his ! administrative powers, which impels Mr. Gladstone to seek what the Hon. ;auberon Heruert terms "fresh p iths of light- bearted experimentalism " rather than a trenchant attack upon the vitals of the difficulty. We cannot go so far as Mr. Herbe rt and ironically say that "the larger part of the gray matter coristituting Mr. Gla4stone's brain is still unre- claimed from those views which, whether we speak of them as-protection, socialism, or ecclesiasticism, are three children of one parent, and the eternal enemies of all free action." It is more probable, as already indicated, that he is pre- vented fro,n giving practical scope to the expansive ideas he doubtless has, ideas consonant with the disposition of a states- man so distant from being "an enemy (dab free action," even on the score of ecclesiatticism,as to emphasize at much incon- venience to himself the" rights of the subject "in favour of a notorious atheist. Vindicating the soundness of Mr. Glad - stone's Liberalism does not, however, explain the incom- pletenees of his Irish policy. Some people, who regard the logic of sequencee as invincible in such matters, think, With danger to their trust in the Premier, that he is averse to testing the elasticity of the multifarioue majority which keeps bins in power by introducing a policy premonitory of pr onounctA legislation far the people. in truth, as his party fs constituted at present, daring might hazerd the Premiership and wrisk its supporters' fortunes politically speaking. If Mr. Sladetone is too cautious in t4is respect, who are to blame for its enfeebling effects upon his admitAtration of public affa:rs? Are net those constituencies to blame which have exerciee4 so little wisdom in choosing their political repre- sentatives as to send up milk-and-water watesmen instead of seen fitted by their sympathies with the requirements of their Constituents to watch over aud protect their interests in Par- liament ? It is to be hoped the spread of education will s wipen the intelligence which should supplement the seizure , and strenethen the influence of electoral rights and privi- lege.e—if anything pertaining to the franchise can justly be termed a privilege. In which case the future is preg- nant with vast and desirable changes in the laws of our country. If there is one subject more than another in which a patriot is interested it is the land question. And where is the being, Englishman. Irishman, or Scotchman, who, if be be not the meanest of servile, centempible humanity, is devoid of patriotic feeling ? If there be such, he deserves, as Scott so tritely put it, to "Go down to the vile dust from whence he sprung, !Unwept, uelaonomed. and unsung believe that patriotism is the lever which has raised Eng- land to her height of dazzling greatness. Englishmen love their land, yet how small a portion of it really belongs to L them in the sense of a belonging! They toil with hands and . brain to increase and extend the already imposing—some of them unrivalled—resources of their country. This toil develops wealth; but at the same time it creates revenue, the annual amount of which is an eloqieent tribute to the cumula- tive powers of British industry. Now, bear in mind this rev -nue comes from the people ; it is the outgrowth of national enterprise, and represents labour of proportional ; vastness, therefore enormous effort. It has been farmed by ' political farmers, at a phenomenal cost ; fur the machinery of thegichaqtaer and Revenue Departtnents of the British Empire is as expensive as it is extensive. The product of - public economy, what becomes of it ? It feeds the State, the Government, the army, navy, and our general military • etembinatione, and the other expenses included in timee labelled public expenditure. Our army and navy—the most costly in the world—defend our shores, protect us against invasion, and give stebility to our voice in foreign affairs. We wis'l to underline the fact that the united toil of our people provides the money which defrays the expenses at- teched to the defensives of our land. .The taxation this implies is a burden upon us, yet it is borne with cheerful- ness, more than cheerfulness, when we recollect that of the land protected at our expense the nreater portion is the itionopely of a few, whose actual right to it from a moral point of view is doubtful in the face of history, which in- toms us that it was given to their ancestors by kings who bad no legal, but only assumed authority, to give to their • favourites what was the natural heritage of the people. So that to-day we behold this anomaly : a zealous, indus- trious people paying heavy taxes to sustain an army and • navy for the protection of soil which does not belong to • them, which in thousands of instances is kept from them by the law of pritnoeeniture, and which in numerous of others is unfairly handicapped by unscrupulous landowners, whose s.Yerice bears tyranny and its twin-brothers exaction and abuse. There is no county in England or Scotland where entailed estates do not appeal to our patriotic sympathies as evidences of the injnstice done to us by each and every overnrnent which compels us to pay the class of taxation alluded to. It is a shame that so many beautiful estates should be held under lock-and-key laws, which enforce upon us sn-called moral obligations that prevent a destruction of Obeoxioue statutes made by kings of by-gone, and therefore irresponsible generations. The full import of these facts is slowly but strongly dawning upon Englishmen. Until lately, the wide and generous invitations of commerce and ;manufacture absorbed the attention of our capitalists, and even drew into these arenas of monetary conflict those self- made men, whose sturdy character was all-sufficient substi- tute for capital, as the sacinel exert-milli-Al so frequently tells • tee. Now, however, competition narrows the scepe of the adventurous seeker after wealth, and leaves the plodding moneyless man a victim to the crowd of jostlers who render lila a mimerah!e failure on account of its complexity and Over-whelming difficulties. People are beginning to realise that Government is an over expensive institution as cur- gently administered, while it bolsters up many old and crude Laws that are indeed the "eternal enemies of all free action." ln Ireland matters aseociated with landlordism oppress more distinctly than in England, where, as we have seen, gigantic commercial and manufacturing operations drowned the claims of the land upon the attention of the people. In Ireland, everyone knows, the tenants are the characterietic features of the population. Neither trade nor creative inlustries have a leading impulse with the people.. • Not that trede and manufacture do not flourislnbut that they are in the minority so far as regards the nature of Ireland's procipal incluetries. Irish people depend upon the soil for their living, whether eked out in that miserably forlorn en-inner indicated in thousands of caseswhere the "visitation of Gad" cruelly brought eviction and its attendant evils etzpon them, or in that still more deplorable condition which is weighty with guilt as an illustration of the torments an unjust landlord can inflict upon his tenants. It is patent, therefore, that the soil should be as free as is compatible with the acknowledged right of its owners to receive a rent ,fee its use froni those who use it and that proper restric- tions should he placed upon the landlord's power to abuse his rights, either in raising the rent beyond its nominal value, o in raising it c ma, qaent upon its enhanced value through Improvement on the land made by the tenant at the tenant's expense. That lush landlords have ahneed, grossly abused their se-termed rights is a matter of history ; that the operations of our inequitable laws helped rather than pre- vented them from being unjust is also a matter of history. These reeulted in Irish grievances, which are such incen- tives to agrarian crime in Ireland. As I have encroached tenon your space, I insist restive my concluding remarks till next. week —Yours truly. BENJ. SAWDON. Warrirgton, June 14, 1882.

In the letter Mr. McMinnies says :—'' lam connected 'as trustee with en estatain North Lancashire. Twenty-seven years ago this property was in the possession of a nobleman too poor or too ti,gligent to do his duty as a landowner. The Vaud was logy and comparatively barren, and the farm traildinge dilapidated. It then fell into the hands of a wealthy manufactprer, who immediately began to improve it. Ho put in main drains and dried the beg, rebuilt orrepaired the farmhouses and farmsteads, put In the subsidiary drainage or found Wei for the tenant to do it, and put in order the fences. When he entered upon the farm there were all kinds of mhos e foolish stipulations by which land- lord and their agents harass and cripple the tenants. The age repliett that if the landlord would enlarge his farmstead so that he c-ouhl keep more cattle te would undertake to sell no more hay. Too landlord did ,sn from time to time as was required, and the tenant so increased the productiveness of the land that whereas the farm. under the former tenant maintained eight head of cattle it now maintains 74. Fur all permanent improvements by the landlord the tenant pays 5 per cent. interest. Wino the farmer took the land 16 years ago he had £5OO of his own and be harrowed £2OO. Within the last three or four years he i 1,14 btiht tW,I snail estates out of the profits of Cis farm dui the last 18 y.ears, which together have cost .£12.000. He is not a scientific farmer; hats simply a clever, industrious nan, hirmin4 without restriction, growing anyttiin4 he wishes upon the land, and, of course, growing that which he thinks most profitable."

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 17, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JUNE 17, 1882.

WARRINGTON TRAINING COLLEGE. TRIENNIAL RE-UNION. Visitors to Warrington who happen to make their way to the east end of the town never fail to have their atten- tion attracted by a pile of buildings situated in the park of St. Elphin and in close proximity to the Parish Church. This many windowed and, it may be added, many-gabled structure is a college for training female teachers, who for- merly came solely from the Church of England schools in the diocese of Chester, which at that time included a large portion of Lancashire; but the erection of churches to meet the spiritual requirements of the vast population which thede- velopment of manufactures and the extension of commerce brought within the borders of tee latter county, led to the creation of the bishoprics of Manchester and Liverpool, and these dioceses now also send their teachers to the Warring- ton Training Cellege. Founded in the days when Warring- ton had for its rector the Rev. Horace Powys (who after- wards became the Bishop of Soder and Man), the institution had a very tumble beginning, but it has gradually increased its usefulness until the three pupils with whom the college was opened have grown into 120. Although after receiving their tuition the students are scattered far and wide, by a happy idea on the part of someone, their interest in the institution is maintained by re-unions, which take placs triennially, and one of these pleasant gatherings was held at the college on Saturday last. Entertaining agreeable recollections of their sojourn in Warrington, some 350 former pupils came to revisit the place where they had spent two of the most important years of their lives, to renew their acquaintance with the principals (Mr. and Mrs. Baker), to see once more the rooms they used to occupy, to sit again in the chairs they were wont to call their own, and to stroll with old friends along the paths in which the very trees appeared so familiar that it seemed to them only yesterday since they walked beneath their shady branches, and by the ever-flowing brook. After attending service at the church in which they once regularly congregated, the school-mistresses were entertained at lunch in a large marquee on the lawn. The marquee was erected on the pre- vious day, but the violent winds brought it to the ground, and it seemed doubtful whether it would be possible to re- erect it. However, Mr. Baker thoughtfully wired the Meteorological Departinent for a forecast of Saturday's weather, and, acting upon this, the marquee was successfully erected. The forecast was—" North-westerly to northerly or north'-easterly winds, light or moderate in force; weather fair on the whole ;" and as an illustratioe of the advances made in weather forecasting it must be stated that the above was an accurate description of the day. The marquee had a most inviting, appearance. Immediately on entering the mottoe, " Ich Dien," composed of ivy leaves, met the eyes of the visitors; in the centre opposite a short platform, where the guests sat, was prominently displayed the word " Welcome ;" and furtheon was the assurance that "Union is strength ;" while the tables were agreeably relieved with bouquets of flowers, and the poles supporting the canvas roof were entwined with evergreens. The lunch over, several addresses were delivered, and the company after- wards enjoyed themselves in a variety of ways until evening, when they made their way to the stations, to be conveyed to their respective homes, after having spent another happy day in Warrington. From the ranks of the weaker sex have risen many women who have earned renown for their intre- pidity, and amongst those present was a heroine who occu- pies the distinguished position of being the first woman who has won the bronze medal of the Royal Humane Society. During the heavy gale in October last the stone belfry of Sutton National Schools, near St. Helens, fell through the roof, and Miss Hannah Rosbotham, the assistant schoolmistress, at great risk to her life, rescued her scholars from the falling debris, and for this act of bravery she was presented with the medal, which was exhibited during the afternoon, and the modest and retiring young lady was the centre of an admiring group, who complimented her on the courage she displayed in the hour of danger. The sermon in the morning was preached by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, of Huyton, from the first epistle of Peter, 2nd chapter, i7th verse—" Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the King." The rev. canon said the age in which their lot was cast was, more than any which had gone before, an age of unions and associations, and leagues and meetings, and on the mere hearing of such things one might be inclined to think how happy and united they must be growing. and they might soon be looking for a time of universal peace and concord and good-will. But, in fact, they saw there was nothing of the kind. On the contrary, disputes, dissensions, variance, and party spirit were no less rife than in former days. Why was this? Why was it they were not making some progress towards the reign of Chris- tian love and concord? One reason for it was that in their various unions and gatherings together they were too narrow and selfish. They were either too much dwelling upon their own pleasure and enjoyment, or if they had good and high objects in view which were seeking to gain the benefit for their own or immediate narrow class, and very often in a thoroughly selfish spirit, without any regard whatever to the interests or rights of others. Now, they had a gathering there that day, and he trusted it would be both pleasant and beneficial, and that they would be careful to avoid those dangers of narrowness and selfishness of which he had spoken. It was well indeed, and pleasant and good to come together again in the spot where they had received much of their higher ectueation, and where they had for two years bad that training which was so needful for them to enable them to carry out the practical work of their lives. It was most pleasant to meet again with old friends from whom they had for a thre been parted, and whom they had but few opportunities of seeing ; and returning as they did, after many sef them had had some experience of their practical work, they would be better able to appreciate the benefits of that training. But they would not have to rest contented with the pleasantness of that, their triennial gathering, and the individual re- freshment they might gain. They should try each one to make it a meeting for their mutual benefit. Let it stir up more within them a feeling of brotherhood, and closer sense of union in their work, and interest in one another, and show a greater readiness to carry out the injunction of the text, "Love the brotherhood." While indeed there was a special brotherhood amongst them as members of that college, there was a larger and wider meaning to the words as first uttered by the Apostle. They must extend it to all those who were their brethren in Christ, and strive to show it forth more and more widely when they returnel to their various schools, and impress the duty by example as well as precept upon those committed to their charge. They should learn to take a vet more wide interest in the work they were engaged in and its importance. It was not merely teaching erementary knowledge to a few infants, and girls, but it was the training of those on whom in a great degree the future of England depends. The influence of the workines'class was ever increasing and what their children would be would greatly depend upon the training which they received in elementary schools. They had to do with thiee, and they must give good heed to the first injunction of the text, "Honour all men," and strive to practise it, and to inculcate the duty upon the children, and not allOw them to be growing up in utter carelessness, and be wanting in res- pect for others. They must be aware of taking that narrow view of their profession, which he would allow there was great temptation of, thinking only "how can I increase my grant," and devoting all their energies to those subjects only which they said would pay, and omitting or neglecting those for which the Government would give no payment. Their duty was not merely to teach, but to educate; not merely to instruct them intellectually, but to train them morally and religiously. Not only were they to honour all men, and love the brotherhood, hut also to fear God All should be ; done as unto God. The children should feel continually that they were being brought spin the nurtute and admoni- tion of the Lord. Such had been their training whilst they had been there. They had had the advantage of being brought up in a Church of England training college, and this should re-act upon their schools. If they were faithful to their training, their teaching must be religious teaching, and more than that, distinctly Church of England. If they feared God they would make their Bible les- son of chief Importance, sad not be careless whether or not their children attended it. They would take care the Church Catechism was learned and explained, land that the Prayer Book was not unfamiliar with them. There was toe inueh reason in these days to think church I attendance was diminishing, and until an early acquaint- ance was formed with the Prayer Book it was likely to be so. The Prayer Book must be known if they were to appreciate and joie in their religious services. All this de- pended upon those preeent. It was a matter of great and pressing importance. The Government inspector took no notice of any regard or disregard of religious teaching. Therewas in many ways a tendency more and Mere to Set it aside. In Board Schools, if there was any pretence to religious teaching, it could only be vague and indefinite, and the wish had been clearly expressed to de away with the definite teaching of the Church of England training colleges. But the state of th logs in France had leased; them to hold jealously generation a tguard h ey were ehe rretlei ga teaching teaching.glear learn to fshoutfast and let h and then they reed not he afraid they would be satisfied with with secular teaching only for their children. The last injunction, but scarcely less important to insist upon, was " Honour the King." When Victoria was our Sovereign, there should be little need to impress upon them this pre- cept, but there were some who would sabstitute a republic narml Irishthere w d ome ir m dominions, osnos, sfourbeo'eurrtPoruerseanuttnilioornay in nrci o,who had e who would not shrunk back from most atrocious outrages in pursuance of their policy. There was very much amongst us now a spirit of lawlessness, set f will,an utter contempt for all euthority and unwillingness to show any mark of deference or resneet. It was marvellous how early this spirit showed itself, and it was in the infant school that its steady repression should be first begun, and due subordination and reepect for all authority over them steadily inculcated. At the conclusion of the sermon a collection was made in aid of the Schoolmasters' and Schoolmistresses' Benevolent Fund. At the lunch there were present the Rev. Canon Hopwood, who presided; the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, Mr. Scott Coward (Her Majesty's Inspector), the Mayor and Mayoress of War- rington (Alderman and Mrs Pickmere), Mrs. Beamont, Rev. Canon Nell (Stretton), Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. E. J. Wilcocks, Rev. F. W. Corv, Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Rev. 11, C. Stubbs and Mrs. Stuths, Rev. M. Stevenson, Dr. _ r. Hiles, Dr. Watkins (Newton), Mr. and Mrs B ker, Messrs. W. Sharpe, C. White, J C Thompson, , C. C. E. Rowley, and W Dooley. After proposing the health of the Queen, The rev. CIIAIRMAN remarked that he had ei 1 b did not know why he was asked to take e .1 he chair, IN it was certainly a fact that he'rememberetd seeing the first brick of s that budding laid, and he remembered eeing the first pupil that ever entered its walls 'go into it. (Applause.) That was s,,me 40 years ago. He well remembered that occasion, end he had pleasure in saying that he was then curate of

Warrington, living at Bewsey Old Hall, and serving un,ler Rector Powys—( hear, bear); and if it had not been for the largeness of his heart, and his high courage and determina- tion, and the strength of his arm, not one brick of that building would ever have existed. He well remembered
also their lieginning with three pupils, and, let him say,--for it was rather interesting—they began before Government

began. (Laughter.) They began before there were any Government grants or any inspectors (laughter)— or anything of the kind. They began in this way. That very clever man—whom be knew well—Dr. Kay then, and afterwards Sir James !Kare Shuttleworth, wanted to have a huge central training college to train girls and send them all over England, and it was to be a Government job alto- gether. They saw that meant no religion, and that, be was sorry to say, was what Government jobs did mean now-a- days, and therefore the dioceses were put upon their mettle. One of the very first dioceses, he thought it might be the very first diocese, to set to work was that of Chester, and it resulted in the building of Chester College and then the adjoining college. It was wonderful to know what that little beginning had developed ; but he was sure Bishop Powys saw it all, and that was the reason why he worked. They knew when he began there were excellent men who said "Old Powys will ruin us. He will go on spending money, and, of course' Govern- ment will have its own way, and it will be no good." He did not believe in that, and many of them did not believe in ir, and the consequence !was they saw every diocese had its training, college. The old diocese, now Chester, Manchester, and Liverpool combined, had not been behind in the good work it began first, but it kept up its position. (Hear, hear.) Long might it please God to give them means to do it. (Hear, hear.) Since he saw two or three girls meet there as the beginning of this great movement, be thought he might say without exaggeration they had seen at least from 1,300 to 1,400 certificated schoolmistresses. This was a great work to have lived to see. Like other work, it had not been done without a great deal of labour and trouble, and he must say that he did not think they could sufficiently thank many of the persons who had been engaged in that work. Take for example Mrs. Baker—(applause)—who had been work- ing there for over 30 years, and whose life he hoped would still be spared. There WAS nobody, he would venture to say, that knew anything like as much as Mrs. Baker about conducting a training college. (Applause.) She was con- tent to work her life out there, and Canon Norris in speak- ing about Mrs. Baker said only a woman would do that. (Hear, hear and applause.) He wished also to say that Mrs. Baker had had good helpers, and they ought to be thanked on an occasion of that kind. He alluded to the fact that there was hardly any change of teachers, and said he must mention Miss Goddard—(applause)—whom he had known for 20 years, and a more faithful, honoured right hand no one in Mrs. Baker's position ever had. (Hear, hear.) Miss Goddard had set an admirable example, as there was too much restlessness amongst schoolmistresses. He also beard the servants never changed. Speaking of the pupils who had left the college, he said he had made sundry enquiries, and they had every reason to be thankful that they had done themselves and the institution credit. As to the proportion of parchments they got for the pupils who left the school, he made bold to say that if people would enquire they would find the training college at Warrington was not a whit behind any training college in England. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, be expressed his pleasure in being present, and their thanks to the preacher who gave a most excellent sermon which he hoped they would carry away; and might God bless them, and give them strength, health, wisdom, prudence, forbearance, and patience to enable them fully to carry out the great and important duties of their vocation. (Applause.) The MAYOR did not think the ladies present could leave the tent without thanking Canon Hopwood for the very able and sensible speech which he had delivered. He was sure that if only they would take to heart his advice, and act up to it, they would live not only to be good women but would be good examples to those whom they were placed over to teach. There was no doubt, in his opinion, that teachers were the great mainstay of England. They taught the rising generation, their religion, and they also taught them their morals, and if the teachers Were good women the children were good, they might depend upon that. He rose to propose the health of Canon Hopwood. (Hear, hear.) He was one of the oldest inhabitants of the world, he (the Mayor) thought be said,—(laughter)—but he found out afterwards the Canon said he wa one of the oldest per- sons connected with the origin of that noble institution, the training college of Warrington. He could remember the time when those schools were being built, and he could also remember the time when he saw the Rev. Horace Powys either carrying bricks or mortar (he forgot which) in a hodder, and working, with a spade of help to make the sewer, and if there was one man who helped the rector to carry out that work it was their esteemed friend Canon Hopwood. I His Worship concluded by stating that he remembered the spot where the present college was built being a mound, and he was told when a bay—it was one of the traditions of War- rington—that Cromwell came and planted his canon on the mound and pegged away at the church. He was shown the round holes at the end of the chanel, which he believed were there to-day, as the places where the canon balls hit, but could not enter. That was not true, but was one of the I traditions. They had a noble church, and he was sure that in Warrington they had one of the most noble training ' colleges in England; and he believed as Canon Hopwood had told them it was one of the best managed too, thanks to ! Mr. and Mrs. Baker, and the excellent staff of teachers. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN, in responding, said ho had omitted to ! mention in his proper place Mr. Stubbs,—(applause,)—who he thought had now got a good helper in Mr. Stevenson. Mr. COWARD, who was greeted with applause, said I though many of them were strangers to him, yet to most of I them he was well known, and he hoped to many of them not unfavourably known, for Canon Hopwood rather shame- fully said he must be an object of terror. (Laughter.) He Ibelieved if they oniy knew the interior recesses of his heart, and the hearts of all Her Majesty's Inspectors they wotild ! find •them like sensitive plants, and as meek as lambs. (Laughter.) But that he was sure they would not believe I for a single moment. They all very wrongly and very un- fairly thought he was sent as an engine of destruction, not to build up but to destroy, not to reap a good harvest, but to destroy all possibility of harvest, and to root up the ground. He asked them to put that notion for the next two or three minutes out of their minds, and proceed to expressed the pleasure he felt at being present that day. That was the first occasion on which he had been present, and he thanked ! Mrs. Baker for giving him that opportunity of testifying his regard for teachers generally, and his appreciation of , the work in which they were engaged. He knew no work in which more labour, more time, and mare experoZiture of health and nervous energy were required than in their pro- fession. and it always gave him pleasure to say that of all those engaged in the work of teaching, there were none to his mind who discharged their duty with so much con- scientiousness as the mistresses of England. (Hear, hear.) j Those were not mere words of flattery. They were words that came entirely from his heart. The majority of the , teachers of England were conscientioue teachers, and when he ! said that, what could he say more? In that he summed up ' their religious training and their religious hope, and the I great proof which he thought they bad a right to ark that ' those who were trained in religious training colleges should give them the benefit of that religious training. It gave him further pleasure to be present that day because he found himself amongst those with whom, while differing in many things, yet in the chief things of this life he fully agreed. He found himself amongst those trained in Christian colleges; be found himself amongst fellow christiane; and in thisyarticular age in which we live, an age in which be saw lawlessness undoubtedly growing, and in an age in which that which would make lawlessness still more abound, a materialistic age, an age in which belief in science was taking the place of all religions belief, it was an especial pleasure to see so many hundreds of them whose function and duty it was to go forth in the world and say the great apostle's creed "I believe in God the Father Almighty" atc. The Government were not opposed to that. Their posi- tion of neutrality was one forced upon them. The fact that they so largely encouraged these training colleges, which I were the heart of the whole syetern. and gave them such liberal grants was a proof of that. In that they had an in- stance of the good faith of the Government. What the Government would oin future time alone would show. But let them take advantage to what help they had now. If they went out in that streneth , they would be able to give the raison d'etee for the expense of those colleges. There was every hour a proof that they required on the part of the teachers, when they- 7ert out to their duties in ' life. eh intelligent recognition of the exisenv. of their position. The exigencies of their position were eohtinu.illy and hourly changing; the tencher trained that year must not think she had learned all her business when she left college. She must be prepared for any change. Such changes would never be beyond their reasonable strength and two nd what could be fairly demanded from them. If they did not keep their eyes open, and were not fully alive to the necessities of tiolr pogition, they WGpld tumble down. There was an important stistter to which he would for a few moments call their attention, and that was that. alt' schools in May, 1883, would be examined under the New Code. It would lay a very heavy stress upon the schools and the teachers and introduce the necessity of teaching every single child to repeat poetry by heart, and of answer - -kw questions upon it. But that would break in upon the old organ7zation of the schools. He showed them that they must he alive to meet the necessities of the case, so that they could make the first impression. The Government desired that the New Code should not be an instrument of tyranny, hut an instrument that would benefit the nation without oppressing the teachers, and he hoped in the way in which it was applied they would have nothing to com- plain of. He thanked them for the manner in which they had listened to him, and expressed the hope that their reunion that day would be a pleasant as well as a profitable one. (Applause.)

The Queen has been pleased to approve the appointment of Mr. R. W. Duff, M.P., as a Junior Lord of the Treasury. WARRINGTON CEMETERY.—Returns of interments in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday : Adults, 7; children, 23; total, 30. Mr. Dugald Stuart, son of the late Sir JAhn Stuart, has Just sold the estate of Loch Arron, west of Ross, to Mr. , Murray, M.P. for Hastings.
