They managed to prevent the flames from spread- ing, but the room in which the fire originated was entirely gutted, the roof burnt, and a good deal of leather in an ad- joining room spoilt by the flames and water. The damage I is estimated at at least £4OO and the premises are insured. CREWE RAILWAY WORKS.—An order has been issued by the London and North-Western Railway Company requiring all men employed in the Crewe works who may live more than two-and-a-half miles into the countrY to come into the I town to live. The order will affect rather seriously large ! numbers of working people who live at Nantwich and other outside towns, and who make the journey to and fro every , day. One of the reasons alleged for this requirement is the large number of empty houses in the borough, some of which belong to the railway company, and it is tneeed that the residence of their workmen in the town would relieve them to ate appreciable extent in their rates, besides contributing to their general revenue. THE PROPOSED.DIYISION OF TARPORLEY LOCAL BOARD • DISTRICT.—On Tuesday there was a Local Government Board inquiry at Tarporley, conducted by Captain Hilyard, into the proposal for dividing the district at present under the jurisdiction of the Local Board. The principal reason given by the promoters in favour of the agitatien is the pre- ' sent rating incquality, and they point out that if Eaton and Rushton were annexed to the East Eddisbury Highway ! Board district, the rate would be only 41-d. in the pound in- I stead of 7d., as is the case now. The arguments for the 1 promoters were on Tuesday stated by Mr. J. H. Cook, who said that Lord Tollemache, Sir Philip Egerton, and Lord Haddington were favourable to the separation. Evidence in support of this course was given by Mr. Beckett (Sir Philip Egerton's agent). the Rev. J. H. Cooper, rector; Mr. 1 Finchett, lee., and the inquiry was adjourned. CrIESIIIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY. -- The Cheshire - Agricultural Society have decided to hold this year's exhi- bition at Nantwich, and in the revision of the prize list some important alterations have been made. Mr. Finchett had called the attention of the society, to the prohibition of cheeses which had previously been tested, and suggested that an exhibitor ought in all fairness to be allowed to test his cheese, so as to ascertain its ripeness before sending it to the show. To meet the difficulty the society decided to offer three extra prizes for cheeses over 401bs. in weight, exhibitors to have the privilege of boring them. A fourth prize was added for butter. The age for young stallions was extended from three to four years, and a second prize was added. There haying been no competition in the long- woolled fat whether class last year, it was suggested that the prizes should he omitted; but the suggestion was negatived and the prizes retained. The secretary reported that four five-guinea cups had been promised by local gentlemen for the forthcoming show •, and Mr. Lisle said that in addition they expected to raise £240 locally towards augmenting the general prize list and providing a local fund. It was thought that Dorfold Park would be the best place for the show, but the question was left open till the next meeting' of the committee.

MARRIAGE REJOICINGS AT NANTWICII. - The marriage of Miss Edith Doody, only daughter of Mr. Charles Doody (principal of the firm of Messrs. Doody and Son, wholesale clothing manufacturers, Nantwich), to Mr. Thomas William Ellwood, shipping merchant, Liverpool, was solemnised at the Nantwich Parish Church last week. The town was decorated with flags, arches, ctc., the work being chiefly car- ried out by the numerous hands employed by the bride's father's firm. The church was crowded with spectators,and 1 great interest seemed to be manifested in the marriage pro- ceedings. The bride wore a navy blue satin dress, cream satin bonnet trimmed with cream lace, and wreath of orange blossoms. Her ornaments included a diamond locket, gold chain the gift of the bridegroom, who likewise presented to Mrs. Doody and Mrs. Norman (his mother) handsome pearl rings. The bridesmaids were also presented with silver bracelets. The bridesmaids were Miss Rose Pooler, of Caynton, Shropshire, and Miss Lillie Matthews, of Nant- wich. The wedding party also included Mr. Charles Doody, sen., and Mrs. Doody; Mrs. Norman, Hoylake ; and Mr. Thomas Blythe Sinclair, of Liverpool. The bride was given away by her father, and her brother, Mr. Charles Cyprus Doody, officiated as best man. The marriage ser- vice was conducted by the Rev, M. C. Sanders. Mr, G, D. Harris, the organist, played an aria from Handel when the wedding party entereei the church, and Mendelssohn's "Wedding March " when they left. Twelve young girls, apprentices to the firm, strewed flowers in the pathway of the bride and her husband as they walked from the porch to the carriage outside the gates. The wedding presents were numerous and valuable, and in the evening about 150 em- ployes connected with the firm of Messrs. Doody and Son were entertained at tea in the Town-hall, Nantwich.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

GOLBORNE AND DISTRICT LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—The semi-billiard table recently purchased by the committee is proving a profitable investment, and continues to be the chief features of attraction. In order to provide new balls for the table, two prominent members last week offered a couple of prizes to be competed for, the match being ar- ranged for Saturday and Monday. Twenty-one members entered, and much interest was centred in the event, the room being crowded to excess, especially on Monday even- ing when the competitors were thinned down to the last couple. After an exciting contest the victors were Messrs. J. Dean and W. Eckersley, the former gentleman beating all corners. Some close playing was witnessed, the games often ending 29-31. GIFT TO GOLDORNE PARISH CHURCII.—A handsome brass lecturn, and a Bible and Prayer-book for the use of the officiating minister, have been presented to this church. The lecturn (which is the work of Messrs. Thomason' of Man- chester and Birmingham) stands upon a suitable pedestal at the entrance of the chancel. It bears the following in- scription :—" In memory of Ann Matley, for 25 years a faithful friend in the family of the Rev. C. T. Quirk, M.A., The Rectory, Golborne, who died November 3rd, A.D. 1881. The gift of her sister, Mary Ann Matley."

NEWTON AND EAR,LESTOWN. SEalrotis were preached in Emmannal Church, Wargrave, on Sunday last by Canon Hulme, and collections taken at the three services amounting to some £2B, for the day and Sunday schools connected with the church. 1.0.G-.T.----110PE or EARLESTOWN LODGE.—The usual weekly session of the above Lodge was held in the Lodge- room, Bridge-street, on Monday. evening last, a fair attend- ance of members being present. Reports of a preliminary meeting to arrange for a united temperance 'and band of hope demonstration for Earlestowu and district were given, when it was decided to take part in one, two representatives, with the secretary, being appointed to act on the General Committee for the demonstration. Several members ap- plied to take their second degree, when it was decided to hold the meeting on Thursday next. Readings, recitations, &c, were given by various members, a very pleasant even- SrNDIT SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY AT BHUTONWOOD.—The anniversrry services in connection with the Wesleyan Sun- day School, Burtonivood, were held on Sunday last, when two sermons were preached by the Rey. Aaron Cooper, student from Didsbury College, in the morning at 10-30, and in the evening at 6-39 p.m. An address to scholars, parents, and friends was given in the afternoon at 2-30, by Mr. John Fairhurst, of Haydock. There was a good attend- ance at each service; in the evening the chapel was too small to hold all who came. Collections were made on be- half of the Sunday school, the total receipts being £lO. Special hymns were sung by the choir and children. ing being spent. On Thursday evening last, 21 members of the above lodge assembled at the lodge-room at 7-30, and proceeded, on the kind invitation of Bro. John Little, to the Glass Bottle Works, Crow-lane. On their arrival the mem- bers were conducted through the works by Bro. Little, viewing the different stages in the process of manufacturing bottles, which was most interesting. After spending halt an hour in the works, the members assembled in the house of Bro. Little, and held a degree meeting in the large kit- chen, which afforded ample space for the purpose. The second degree was most impressively conferred on eight candidates by Bro. John Warburton, L.D., assisted by other officers, after which the members were entertained to a coffee supper, kindly provided by Bro. Little. Thorough justice having been done to the good things provided, an entertain- ment was held, Bro. George Warburton, sen., presiding. After a few suitable remarks fro,n the Chairman, an excel- lent programme was gone through, songs b3ing given by Bros. John Taylor, A. Allison, H. Warburton, Geo. Howard, and Sister M. E. Allison. Readings and recitations were also given by Bros. John Watburton and George Clarke. A hearty vote of thanks was tendered to Bro. Little for his very kind invitation and entertainment of the members. Bro. Little responded in a few remarks, after which the meeting was brought to a close about 10-30 by singing the doxology, having been of a most enjoyable character throughout.

LOCAL NOTES. A stranger passing through the streets of Newton .I.ld Farlestowu might well wonder at the number of "stars" to be seen in the shopwindows, and by the help of a lively imagination fancy that there had been some temente. But that would prove their Eayptian darkness of the real cause. The Sup:rintendent of Police has issued a notice offering a reward for information on the subject, and particularly re- ferring to the breaking of a plate glass window in Rob-lane, where the Gothar Tandal must have thrust some pointed weapon through some thick iron bars in order to effect his purpose—mere mischief. It will in this case cost more to replace the window than the whole reward. But if the offender is caught he will serve as an example to other evil doers, and he may thank his stars if he gets off with a fine. We should be sorry to think so, but this practice makes us look too much like our near neighbours to be agreeable, and tha Plate Glass Insurance Company will be chary of accept- ing further responsibility as long as this reprehensible practice prevails. The canvass 'ln favour of Sunda s 'elosing is expected to be completed on Saturday night, and so far the objections have been something like one in fifteen or twenty. In sorra streets there were not more than two or three objecions. Many men from whom but little sympathy with the move- ment was expected signed the petition saying they would be glad if the temptation to drink on Sunday was removed, and they would then have a chance of getting to their work on Mondays. The canvass of the pablicans seems to have been a very curious psycalogical study. Some, to their honour be it said, signed at once. A few temporised and others again were as brusque as if a burglar had entered their threshold, to filch not only,their "good name," but also their purse. The next thing to be done will be to peti- tion Parliament for a new definition of a bond fide traveller. Formerly he was, as the name implies, a real good fellow, and most often of the commercial order, before the days of the penny post. Then he lost his identity during the mythical age, and became a mysterious nonentity who had slept somewhere or other five miles off. But as a sap to Cerherus when Hercules went to woo—you know who— (Alceste) his tether was taken in and he was allowed to sleep like Sisypus just three miles off his beer or beverage. In plain English the Tories thought to reward the licensed victuallers with this act, a piece of legislation of about the same value as the Egypti tn legacy, with the result that in many places public-houses in the suburbs of large towns are crowded from cellar to ceiling with the " bovelfide travel- ler," the genuine article expressly manufactured by a "tram " or " train " journey of some three miles as the crow flies. But as there is no rule without an exception, so the phrase goes, we are glad to re-affirm our statement that the publichouee on Newton Common, thanks to the tenant and the landlord, will be absolutely closed on Race Sunday, as was the case last year. And it is only justice to state that the agent has mitigated if lie cannot entirely remove the evils complained of by the Sunday school teachers, and which are thought to have been overstated. But as this is debatable ground we are content to leave it till next Sunday. Anglo-Scotus speaks up manfully for the timid animal, which, according to Bishop Wilkins (16S8), Noah found a separate compartment for in the Ark, a few thousand years ago, and gives a plan showing where it had its "butch " with the roe, cony and marmott. After all the shooting and running it is quite wonderful to find that it has not yet become extinct. The old cookery books begin by saying "First catch your hare" and then proceed to shave how to cook it. So that there is, so far, historical evidence that for a long time, perhaps Noah's. there has been much interest taken in catching bares. This wonderful work seems to have given "Darwin "a hint as to the survival of the fittest. "A thousand a year" certain, and per centages on the " take " are not inducements to take the same view of this sport as that taken by Anglo-Scotus, though all must agree that it will net diminish the taste for betting on the results of the running. It will be interesting for him to know that in Newton we have legal and illegal betting. And many arc so hare-brained (rash) as to indulge in both.

SCHOOL CASES.-At the Newton Petty Sessions on Satur- day, Charles Gatter, charged with neglecting to send his child Charles to school, pleaded that he " did not see what was the good of sending him." He was fined ss.—William Shen ton, for a similar offence, was fined 58.—Mr. Cawley prosecuted.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

CHOIR SUNDAY AT E. CHAD'S, OVER—The anniversary sermons in aid of the choir of this venerable church were preached on Sunday last, when a moderate congregation listened to the plain, homely, but truthful sermons of the esteemed vicar, the Rev. Gr. Wyatt Ninis. In the afternoon, the venerable looking, though still comparatively young, vicar of Mossley, near Congleton, the Rev. W. E. E. M. Bull, M.A., preached to a full church, from Hebrews, 11 ch. and 30 v., "By faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they were compassed about seven days." From the circum- stances of this capture, the unforgotten preacher evolved a sermon which redounded to his credit, and it will prove doubtless a benefit to the choir and congregation. To the former especially, as it appealed in a practical application of sound advice ;to the latter for a good collection. It came out in the course of the rev, gentleman's sermon that it was likewise the anniversary of his first sermon in St. Chad's nineteen years ago; after which sermon his faithful labours as a curate in connection with his brother-in-law, the late vicar, the Rev. N. Jackson, were continued till he was appointed vicar of his present parish of Mossley. The collections amounted to £7 4s. SI , and though but a small recognition for the services of a good choir, will, with other sums, encourage both organist, Mr. Calderbank, and choir master, Mr. Greenhalgh, to redoubled efforts. BAND OF HOPE MEETING AT OVER.—The new mission room in Detamere-street, Over, in connection with the Free Methodists, is doing a good work. Not only is the Church in this part of Winsford greatly increased since the preach- ing place was obtained, but the spirit of general improve- ment in other fields of morality is apparent. Notably, the temperance aspect. There is now a Band of Hope. A public meeting on Monday last was held there, Mr. J. Slater in the chair, and Messrs. Jahez Hulse and W. Maudslev, two oli and valued temperance workers, acting with arid supported by a third brother, Mr. T. Hough, spoke well in the good work. It need hardly be said that more with such would hardly be required. But, to make it still more successful, the Rev. W. J. Hopper, who is a host in himself, was en- gaged to speak. The joint efforts of five such temperance men produced a very favourable impression on the good attendance present. Some good singing made a pleasant evening which will he long remembered,. A vote of thanks to the evening, by Mr. Richard Hatton was warmly carried, and being suitably acknowledged, the meeting was brought to a close by the National Anthem.

SALVATION ARc, WINSFORD.—This popular movement seems to just suit a host of the Winsfordites; and, of course, the leaders in the movement wisely avail themselves of the disposition and utilize it. A grand convention of workers is making Winsford the rendezvous this week. The ' streets resound with song and prayer. Board School and Town Hall are requisitioned; and great things are expected of " Major " Pearson and the local and neighbouring officers. " Fire and blood " head the large red bills on the walls and in the windows of sundry shops, whatever they mean; and yet they go harmlessly about the work, simply marching in a body, and singing as they go. On Monday night, at a full meeting in the Town Hall, the "Major" denounced in a long speech "tobacco," whereupon some of the leading men, who hare been great smol:ers, smashed their pipes and re- linquished the weed. Thus self-denial from drinking, and smoking, and Sabbith breaking has !narked the introduc- tion of. the " " tn Winsiord in not a few cases ; and where oaths and deg and rabbit courg!ng, pigeon flying, and foot racing used to abound, to the annoyance of many, may now be heard and seen the singing of praises, and the testi- mony of hosts to the power of religion.

RE-OPENING OF UP-HOLLAND OFIURed.----btirifig the pst four months Upholland Church has been undergoing restora- tion, and the work that has been done during this period makes it difficult to recognise the interior. On entering the church one is surpriseirthat any amount of dingy whitewash and mouldering plaster could have prevented one from admiring the etately pillars and grand lofty arches. The greater part of the said pillars and arches are of red sand- 'stone, varied here and there with white, and the effect of the rich tones is very striking. The aisles, too, are now fitted with benches, the framezork of which is of new oak, but the upright ends and the pa Is are of old wood from the oak benches put into the church in 1635. The nave is at present furnished with chairs, and this is certainly an advantrge for ,getting ,a good view of the building. The opening services on Sunday were well-attended, but as the church now affords cqmfortahle seats for nearly two hundred people more than heretofore there was p'enty of room. The hal, of the floor of qr church on the left as one enters (that is to say the north aisle and the northern half of the nave) is quite free and unappropriated. The people of Up-Holland are to be congratulated on baying made such a v(lry excel- lent start in their work of restoration, and it is to be hoped that such a generous response will be made on all sides to their appeal for help, that they may be ableeto build the beautiful chencel Mr. Champneys has designeti for them without being hindered for lack of funds. The committee report that they have only about £BOO as yet towards the £2;000 which the chancel will cost.

TRADE NOTES, END Or THR NORTH WALES COLLIERS' STRIXE.—The strike of the North Wales colliers against the reduction of 5 per cent, in their wages, the termination of which has been so often falsely reported, is at last at an end. On Saturday morning the men remaining on strike—those of the Black Park, Pas Kynaston, and Wynnstay (known as The Green) Collieries—met at Arcefair, and decided to accept the re- duction and resume work, a decision which they have car- red out. Thus has terminated a most disastrous strike, which produced riots, distress among the families of the men, and stagnation of trade in many parts of district. The general resumption of work thus early is no doubt to be attributed to the absence of a substantial relief fund, and to the falsification of the promises made that a large sum of money would be subscribed by the miners of Lancashire and other coal districts. The vigour and promptitude displayed by Major Leadbetter (chief constable) and Deputy Chief Constable Wilde throughout the strike in guarding against disturbances had the fortunate effect of slcuring peace and preventing much damage being done to property, and de- serve prai.e.

THE TRADu DIsPuTE AT Climax:Y.—On Monday evening the master spinners of the Chorley district held a meeting, convened at the request of some of the operatives on strike, to discuss the term, of arrangement with the iepresentatives of the operatives, viz., Messrs. T. Gent, the local secretary, J. Fielding, of Bolton, and W. Maudesley, of Manchesftr, and two or three local spinners. It was understood that the question of payment by indicator should not be discussed. The employers offered to adopt the Bolton hand-mute and self-actor list, with all its conditions, as in force at Bolton. To this the representatives of the operatives demurred, and asked the masters to re-consider the matter. The latter did so, and then offered the old Chorley list. The present Clint- ley self-actor list is slightly higher per lb. on certain, num- bers than the Bolton list, and the employers therefore ob- ject to grant. the increase which the operatives' proposition would entail. After the meeting of the employers the operatives held a mass meeting to discuss the propositions offered, and eventually decided not to accept the masters terms.

THE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark Lane Express says—" During the past week the weather has been, for the most part, cool and rainy. The rainfall has benefited all grain crops excepting wheat, which, from the cool wet weather, looks more sickly yellow than before, and its growth is exceedinely slow. It is, however, coming fast into ear, and some of it is in blossom. The trade, too, is almost at a standstill. The deliveries of native wheat have been remarkably small, excepting at Bristol, and of the small quantities on offer a very inconsiderable portion has been good enough to command the attention of millers. In London the best samples have been difficult of tale, and in several provincial markets the values have ben quoted lower. Country flour moves quietly into consumption, and, as a rule, is rather cheaper to buy. The inquiry for malt is now almost confined to the finest samples. All other descriptions of native produce remain without quotable change in values. Trade for foreign wheat off stands in London appears to get from bad to worse, most descriptions being unsaleable except at a decline. In Liverpeol, on Tuesday, prices were fully id. per cental lower for white sorts, and on Friday these rates were barely supported. Foreign flour has about -maintained the currencies of Monday last." Messrs. Joseekh R. and W. P. Barnes, share-brokers, 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (June 15) :—Several well defined movements are to be chronicled this week, and the-concerns, or batch of concerns, in which the movements have taken place have by far the lion's share of the business of the week. Most speculative stocks, owing to the critical state of affairs in Egypt, have ruled dull and drooping, but to-day figures have shown some improvement.. The business in shares other than rails is of a moderate amount, and as a rule figures realised on transactions coin- pare favourably with those lately obtained. Quotations on the whole are fairly steady, though insurance show distinct, ' and iron, lec., and mining a slight, preponderance of adverse changes. Banks without change of moment. A small general business doing at or about best rates. Alterations in prices is no case noteworthy, and figures quite steady. Higher: National Provinces of England new :f know and d and L), Lancashire and Yorkshire I, and Manchester Joint Stock 1-16. Lower : Manchester and Salford 1-16. Insurance : The quotations herein show a large balance of changes for the worse ' • there are very few, however, whose figures are seiiously altered : Ocean marine and reliable marine; London and North-Western fire shares, which recently have declined severely, are somewhat better, buyers now giving rather better figures than sellers found a difficulty in obtaining only a few days ago, ar.o ffIT lot! Ire offering except at advanced rate 3, Lower : Liverpool and London and Globe. ; 8937a1. .Liverpool), ; Thames and Mereey Marine, '; Eritish. and Foreign Merhiel, Latics- shire, Mencoester Fire, 1-3-- ' • Maritine, 1-16 • ' and Queen, 1-16.—Coal, Iron, ,fc., and Mining: Though in several cases enhanced fi.inres are marked lower, prices are in a majority. Bolckows are again irregular in changes, but this weeff the movements are reversed, fully paid being easier and Ll 2 paid better. In Ehbwa eeveral, fluctuations are recorded. On Friday last, the dividend anuouneernent being disappointing, prices rapidly fell but they have since rallied, and after minor ups and downs to-day show only g below figures of a week ago. Canadian coppers were done as low as 235. on Saturday List, but on Tuesday 255. and 245. Dd. was marked, and quotations now are substantially same as last week's. Bolckows fully paid have been done repeatedly at slightly advancing rates, latest dealing marked being at best rice of the week. Indian gold mines have lost seine of the late advance, those quoted here being all more or less lower. div.head: TENDERS: SPIRITS IN THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: TENDERS: SPIRITS IN THE WORKHOUSE.

During the time the tenders for provisions, &c., for the workhouse, were being considered, and when the question of wines and spirits was before the notice of the Guardians, The Rev. T. FINEGAN asked if those liquors were for the improvement of invalids. If they were they ought to be of the best quality. He merely asked the question—he pre- ferred not to give spirits at all, In case of sickness a thing of that sort ought to be good, but in oiiier cases he vvo! not give it at all. Did the doctor approve of it? The CLERK said the present was not the time to go into the matter. It ought to have been submitted at an earlier meeting. _ _ .
Rev.—T. FINEGAN : Well, I merely mentioned it, it may be out of order now.

The tenders were then proceeded with and the decisions were as follows :—Flour, dz,c,, Mr. Jno. Mr. KERSITAW, iiimoving the- confirmation'of the minutes, said the Committee had redec,rl the Surveyor's estimate of £4.394 by £916 ; and the emomitli-e thought that if the Surveyor would do his work in a preper manner, it would be clone something like £.560 under that sum. It entirely de- pended npon the malopntitinn of hi i men. From what ha ka4-seen going on for the last tw days the -work would not Ike done for -the nuinev. for tione were men doir..g. work under their noses" then which might- to he done for ball ao money they were costing. The- men seemed to waste their time. He did nt consider that four men ought to be emOloyed on work that one could do. Mr.-Sirecrrtswairrit Seconded the motion.

Mr. CAREY said he should like to know for what reason Mr. Hughes wished the Deacon-road to be raised, and why the cominittez had not complied with the request. With reference to street making, the Board had been blamed very , much by the outside public, that while attending to streets ' in the outside parts of the township, they had grossly neg- lected many of the streets in the more frequented parts; and the Health Committee, in the course of their investigation of the neighbourhood, had found seve?al streets which required attention, and had recommended the Highway Committee to have them made—of course, at the expense of the owners. Why was not this work to be done at present? With regard to Upton Quarry, people living in the neighbourhood had told him that the wall was dangerously low for people riding or driving down the road, and he could only hope there would be no accident there, for he was afraid the Board would be blamed if there was one. Mr Kershaw he knew liked friendly criticism, and he was sure the Board sym- pathised with him in trying to keep down the expenditure, but there were one or two points in his highway estimate he , did not understand. In 1881-2 the expense for manual labour was £1,080; this year it was estimated to cost £622. He should like to know from Mr. Kershaw whether the roads had been put in such a condition that they did not require the usual amount of repairing; or whether they were going to do the same amount of work at a cheaper rate owing to the better organisation he had alluded to. The number of carts used for watering the streets had been reduced from four to two; how did Mr. Kershaw propose to do the neces- sary watering, because in dusty windy weather, they were watered too little at present. Perhaps the attention of the committee had been drawn to the fact that a little chloride of lime tnixed with the water made it unnecessary to water the streets so often. A considerable reduction had also 'yen made in the estimate for the repair of gullies and drains. These gullies must be cleaned ; were they to be cleaned, or had some better way of cleaning them without expense been discovered. No provision, either, had been made for extra men for the winter time, and Mr. Kershaw would find he would exceed his estimates if this provision were not made.. Mr. KERSHAW, replying to the questions, said the com- mittee did not wish to make a lot of new streets until they had got the work straight, and felt their footing firmly. It was also a bad time to call upon property owners to pave streets. The wall at Upton Quarry Mr. Carey had not said was dangerous; but dangerously low; but the committee considered it quite secure, and had It been otherwise they would have taken action to make the owners repair it. With reference to the estimate, he had said many times in that room that the Board spent £l,OOO for which they did not get £5OO worth of work, and he thought for £6OO odd they ought to have a great deal more done than they had I sat year for £l,OOO. They had "simply a foreman walking about doing nothing," and men going from place to place also doing nothing. He "saw it dilly," and it "made his hair stand up," sometimes when he did see it. The com- mittee's estimate for the watering of streets was £l5O. while the surveyor's was only £l3B. so that they were pretty well off there. He might say that they had had to swell their estimate for the repair of bridges by £7OO, and to meet any contingencies which might arise; and £620 had been set apart to keep gullies and drains in'a proper state. Dr. O'KEEFFE thought the reply of the Chairman in re gard to Upton Quarry very unsatisfactory. It was danger- ous both to those who rode and those who drove horses there, and if any accident occurred unquestionably the Board would be held re§ponsible for damages. Mr. StacerrnEworent : I don't think it is a highway. Mr. KERSHAW: It is a highway. Dr, O'KEEFEE From time immemorial. Mr. KERSHA.W: If Upton Quarry is dangerous Appleton Quarry is more so. Mr. CAREY : I don't think so. I only wish to warn the Highway Committee about it. r. OIKEEFFE moved that the recommendation as to Upton Quarry be referred back to the committee, so that they might look after the safety of the public. Mr. CAREY seconded. Mr. KERSHAW: it is no use sending it back to the com- mittee.
Only the mover and seconder voted for the amendment, and the minutes were passed.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.

The Gas and Water Committee in their minutes recom- mended that the services of Mr. Robert Robert, storekeeper at the gasworks be dispensed with, the duties as well as those of timekeeper to be undertaken by one man ; and also those of Charles Hammond, employed as a fitter at the pumping stations and gas works be diTensed with. The engineer re- ported that the new engine and machinery now worked satisfactorily with the exception of one or two trifling mat- ters. He stated that as the pipes for the Liverpool Corpora- tion Aryrnwy mains (when passing through Cuerdley and Bold) were being delivered at Fernworth station it was desirable that the corporation should be communicated with as to branches being provided on the mains to enable the Board to take a supply from them in future, if requisite. The committee decided that application be made to have the necessary branches nut in at Barrows-green. The water pumped at Stocks well for the four weeks ending 24th May was 25.00,710 gallons; at Netherley 14.657,046; total 30,666,756: and there had been delivered 40,728,358. There had been manufactured during the same period 3,485 000 cubic feet of gas,atel delivered 3,710,000 feet. Its illuminating po)ver had averaged 16 60 candles. The wages required for the coming four weeks were gas works, £184; waterworks, £144; while the months' accounts, including those slims, were gasworks, £402 ss. 114.; waterworks, £345 15s. sd. Dr. Campbell Brown had made an analysis of the water at Stock's Well and Netherley, the former of which he certified as clear and colourless, and excellent for domestic purposes. Nether- ley water p055e5534 a slight trace of colour, and a ferrugin- ous deposit. This water, though not so pure as that from Stock's Well, was sufficiently pure for domestic purposes. The seal was affixed to the contract of Thomas Lea aud Son for supply of fuel to the waterworks. The tender of Win. Ford, Appleton, to clean and paper Netherley Cottages for £lO Sc. was accepted. PANICHURSP moved the adoption of the minutes, which having been seconded, Mr. KERSHAW said he was pleased to see the committee were making a reduction in their staff. It had been wanted many a year, and he thought the Board would be able to carry it all round.

Mr. CAREY wished to know whether the impurities in the Netherley water were growing, and whether the Water Com- mittee were taking any steps to discover the cause of the impurity. The CHAIRMAN explained that the new analyst, Mr. Brown, calculated on 100,000 parts, whilst Mr. Roscoe spoke of million parts. He, too, was under the impression that the Netherley water was depreciating. Possibly some steps would be taken to investigate' the district, and see whether the water was being poisoned by any sewage works, or any- thing of that sort. Mr. MIDWOOD said he was at the gasworks a day or two ago, and he _thought they could do with disposing of a few engines instead of purchasing a new one. He should like to know the cost, and why they were doing it. P/OTRIICRST said he could only anfiwer as he did last month, that the old Gas Committee considered it necessary a new engine should be erected.
Mr. Minwooto: Looking at the serious loss upon the waterworks last year, I cannot understand the erection of a new engine. _ _ _ _

The -CITAIRMAN said. the Board bad gone into no new expense. They had simply paid for what was ordered three or four years ago. Mr. MIDWOOD We are prepared for the next 50 years, as far as water is concerned. The minutes were then agreed to.

div.head: HOSPITAL COMMITTEE.-THE MATRON COMPLIMENTED.
div.p: HOSPITAL COMMITTEE.-THE MATRON COMPLIMENTED.

The minutes of this committee contained the estimate for the ensuing year of £255 10s. The clerk had been instructed to convey the _thanks of the Board to the Foot- ball Club for their handsome present; and also to inform Miss Downie that the committee was pleased with. the state of the house, and with the economical and efficient manner in which the ,kospital had been managed during the past year. _
The minutes were agreed to on the motion of Mr. SADLER, seconded by Mr. MauTLEY.

Mr. SADLER, in reply to an inquiry by Mr. Midwooft, said the committee had exceeded' last year's estimate, by £l5 10s., chiefly through unforeseen contingencies, and the hos- pital had been a loss to the ratepayers during the year of £284 Cs.

The CILATRMAN did not consider it quite fair to call it a loss. The hospital was there as a useful institution. Mr. SADLER: I should say it is almost a useless article. Mr. KERSHAW : There are no patients in if, and I should be glad if it would cont;nue so. Mr. WEBSTER suggested that collections should be made in the workß, which sent the largest number of patients. The CHAIRMAN,: The people who go to the hospital pay for their accommodation; it is supported out of the rates. I believe it was the first hospital established on that principle after the passing of the Act.

Dr. O'KEEFFE said there was an excellent work before the Hospital Committee if -they would only perform it. If they could save £2BO by collecting from the works, let them do it. Mr. SADLER: I have no doubt we should collect a good deal of that sum if Dr. O'Keeffe will head the list with a liberal sum. (Laue.hter.)
After a little farther conversation the minutes were con- firmed.

HEALTH COMMITTEL At a meeting of the Health Committee accounts amounting to £6B 6s. Id. far health, and £7 12s 64 for market, examined and passed 'for payment. Medical Officer reported to this committee that there had been div- ing the month—birthe 78, being an average of 374 per thousand; deaths 27, being an average of 12 96 per thou- sand; including: children under one year 9, being an aver- age of 43 tier thousand; children, between one anci fire years 12, being an average of 576 per thousand; zyinotic diseases 1, incieests 3. Nuisance Inspector reported one case of enteric fever' which had Proved fatal. The house bad been disinfected. During the month he had destroyed 309 oranges, 33 his, onions, and a cow's lung. Drainage nuisancee : The nuisances on land at Halton View, and bqween Milton-road and poiice station, had been eff-rctually abated. The medical officer and himself had inspected the pools of stagnant water, in which dead animals were thrown in various parts of the district, which they recommend should he either drained or filled up. Replies had been received from owners of vacant land with regard to the fair. hat not being considered sitisfactory it was recom- , mended the fair he held as usual. The estimates for 1832-3 were passed a. follow: Health Committee, £1,132; Market Committee, £34 124. 64. The Market Superintendent reported that the receipts for May were £2l 16s. 11d., being a d. cream complred with last year of £3 124. 11d. The total receipts from the fair this year were £22 Os. 14., or £ll less than the corresponding fair last year. Five shops were now let, and the oath bad done fairly. , The minutes were agreed -too' the motion Of Mr. Carey.

Mr. CAREY taid the majority of the landowners were not agreeable to prevent the holding of a fair, but the:re was a large minority who were not willing to bind themsd vet, and the Health Committee under those circumstanc, s felt it was hopeless to carry tht., discussion further, and decided to It the matter drop for the present. —Replying to questions froin Mr. Midwood, Mr. CAREY Said the tioard received an income of £36 per annum from the weighing machine, and expended £7 in keeping it in repair. In answer to Mr. Webster, he stated the market during the year had been a loss to the pu‘dic of .£578.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 179 1882. SCOTTISII LEGAL LIFE ASSURANCE! SOCIETY. MR. RANKINE'S REPORT. Mr. John Rankine, advocate, who was appointed by the Registrar to examine into the affairs of the Scottish Legal Life Assurance Society, has just issued his report. After dealing with the preliminary objections, he states that the grounds of the application were (1) That no notice in terms of seciety's rules were given prior to a special general ,meeting, held on 14th February, 1881, Of an amendment of rule 26, whereby the day, month, and hour of the annual general meeting was then altered from the second last Thursday of March at half-past seven o'clock p.m. to the second last Thursday of June at four o'clock p.m., and that in spite thereof the said amendment WAS declared by David Hoer, the secretary of this society, to have been duly made and by him, with the approval of the directors and other office-bearers, sent in to be re- gistered. (2) That all important meetings of the society for a con- siderable time past, and in particular at those held in March, 1880, and in February and June, 1881, largo numbers of persons had attended and voted who were not members of the society. (3) That to aid said persons in so atrending arid voting various office-bearers of the society,' and in particular the said David Horn, bad taken part in the issue of bogus or sham contribution books to such persons. (4) That the said office-bearers, and in particular the said David Horn, had induced members and non-members to support them by treating them with drink and paying their fares from their houses to the places of meeting and back. (5) That the office-hearers of the society had, without due cause, in a large number of cases, permitted servants to retain and appropriate funds belonging to the society with- oct either dismissing these servants or causing them to be punished. 1. The facts on which the first complaint, which relates to the alteration of the day and hour of the annual general meeting, is based are rot in dispute. They are fairly set forth in the complaint. At the same time it is stated by the office-bearers, admitted by the applicants, and clearly proved, that the amendment in qaestion was admitted, declared, and sent in for registration in the honest belief that it had been competently proposed and passed,a belief which was all the more naturally held, seeing that this amendment was only an retditional alteration on a rule of which a duly notified amendment was already before the meeting, The office- bearers have deponed that it was only when the blot was pointed out to them in this application that they discovered their mistake, and I see no reascn to doubt that such was the case. 2. The second charge is also admitted. There can be no doubt that for some length of time, and especially during the years 1880 and 1881, large numbers of non-members were present at the general meetings of the society. The question whether the directors and office bearers or any of them were cognisant of or responsible for this irregularity, is mixed up with the further qnestion of responsibility for the issue of bogus books, and may be deferred. It may be here remarked, however, that even if these persons indi- vidually and as a body were desirous, as would seem to have been the case from the terms of the circular No. 4 of the productions, to pat a stop to such practices, the means of checking admisaions, though perhaps the best available, are proved to have been inadequate in practice. No attempt was made to traverse the allegation that the evil increased subsequent to the exclusion of collectors from meetings through the operation of the 30th section of the Act o: 1875, and that it was partly accounted for by the uproarious character of the meetings which kept respectable members of the society from attending. The collectors naturally have considerable influence with the members. These facts if proved, as I think they must be held to be, along with others which indicate a certain amount of fellowship among the Glasgow collectors, tend to show the power exercised by those local servants of the society. The question remains behind whether when illegitimately used, as was un- deubtedly the case, their influence was used spontaneously and for their own ends, or at the instigation and with the knowledge of their superiors. 3. The greater part of the investigation was taken up with the charge against certain directors and office-hearers, and in particular agaiest David Horn, the secretary, of taking part in the issue of sham contribution books for the purpose of enabling partisans who were not members to attend general meetings. With regard to this charge it was ad- mitted that from a very early period in the history of the society this fraudulent practice had been in existence; that it was notorious, and that certain collectors had in the years 1880 and 1881 made use of the facilities at their cemmand for continuing the same. It was further admitted that they did so in the course of their canvass for members of the Board and office-bearers who were aware that they were so canvassing for them or. for their policy. It -is further admitted that the official accused of participation in the fraud had a considerable interest in the result of the meet- ings in question in March, 1880. Blair, the president, Horn, and Clarke were up for-election. In February, 1881, it was proposed, contrary to the views of an important body- of collectors and others, to doable the length of time during which offices might be held. And in June, 1881, large additions to the salaries of officials were in contemplation. These admissions are of importance in estimating the evidence bearing on the question of complicity of the officials. It was only faintly suggested, and was not proved, that the whole body of officials, directors, and office-bearers, combined to pack the general meetings with non-members either through the manufacture of sham books or by the improper use of genuine books. The case of each person accused must therefore be taken separately. The first i Allan Blair, now and for 10 years president of the society. George WEl:annoy who alone speaks to any connection between him and the issue or use of bogus books, is a discharged servant of the society, of not unblemished character, and he cannot &pone to any conversation with Blair about honks, or to having actually received from him the books produced. It WAS no doubt a serious indiscretion on the part of Blair to employ such a man at all in the deli- cate work of canvassing, and: Very little evidence in corro- boration would have availed to set up M'llbanney's story. An it is. I must hold it out-weighed by the clear denial of Blair himself, and that the charge is not proven. The case of James Nicholson, a director, is in the same position in one respect, that his use of bogus books is only spoken to by one witness, Patrick Hughes. I was favourably impressed with the demeanour of the witness. He was not cross-examined beyond a single question. He seemed to have no interest one way or another, unless it was as being a member of the Prudential. The disappearance of the collector Hart, who was said to be present when the hooks passed, is not ex- plained, and cannot, at least, be laid at the door of the applicants. On the other hand, I could not help regarding the evidence of Ninholson himself as palpably uncandid. He therefore rests in my judgment under the gravest suspi- cion of having resorted to the fradulent device in question, though upon a lamentable penury of testitnonv it cannot be said that his complicity is legally proved. The atternpt to connect William Clark, a director, with the distribution of boons hooks has failed entirely. David Horn, the secretary, is specially mentioned in the application, and an exam ina- than into his conduct bulks very largely in the evidence adduced. I refrain from entering into particulars. The conclusion I came to during the inquiry has been confirmed by further .study of the evidence. I think it proved sufficiently that Horn was cognisant of and a consenting party to the sham contribution books as passports to meetings, and that on two occasions at least he himself issued such books in considerable numbers. Even if the evidence for the applicants were put out of the ac- count altoewther, it still would be incontestable that he went on employing men as canvassers who were to his knowledge ready to seek their ends by fair means or foul. The explanation elven by the agent for the society was that Horn cettld not afford to lose the services of such men as John M'Brearty and Barclay, which seemed to me a some- what dangerous admiseien. The episode in which Mr. Jas. Grant, a publican in "tinning Park, figured, made a very uefavourable impression on my mind. On the second thy (Wednesday) of the inspection. Jas. D. Jack deponed that Grant had told hint of his having written up a number as books, given him by Horn for the purpose, shortly before the meeting in March, 1881. Jrant bad been desired by the agents for the applicants to appear for ex- amination on the preceding day. but had detlined. On the last day-of the inspection (Friday)' the agents, the short- hand writer, and I visited him at his shop. -He declined to &pone until he had seen Horn according to promise. It then appeared that during the whole course of the investigation Gent and Horn hail had meetings on several occasions. One who conducts hit-.a-self in a way an foolieh cannot wonder if he awakens suspicion. When Grant appeared in the wit- ness box at haat it was after having seen Horn. His denial, and the manner in which it was made, dissipated any doubt miolit have had—first, whether he had ever told the story, and, secondly, whether it was true. I had no longer any doubt that the other stories told by John Milirearty, Bar- clay, M'Ewen, and Robertson, were also substantially accu- rate. ,4. It was admitted by the agent for the society to be the universal practice before elections for election committees to meet at public-houses, and to be there treated to drink at the expense of the candidatea. It was also admitted tjaat tickets entitling tnetnbers to travel by rail or tramway to Glasgow from the neighbourhood and back on the dates of general meetings were gratuitously distributed by candi- dates or hatches of candidates or (where a course of policy had been adopted ty the Board and ()ffice-laperers) out of a common fund. It was denied that treating of members not- belonging to election cemmittees had been brought home to the B iard and officials or to any individual office-hearer. Without minutely going into the tvidence. I must hold it proved that the practice in question was too common, both before and after general meetings, both -as an inducement to attend and as 'a reward for attendance thereat. The evidence as to knowledge of treating relates ,to Malcolm the treasurer, Horn the secretary, and to Cl akeand Shaughnessy. directors. With reference to Malcolm the utmost that is p-oved is that he was aware of treating having taken place on two occasions in the course of 1881. It is, I think, preyed that Horn wae aware at the time that treating was going nit upon both these occasions, and that he afterwards paid the hill either out of his own pocket or by drawing on the common fund. and that he was ale° aware of the treating:given by Clarke end Shaugh- nessy. Clarke admits having treated supporters to Orink after the meetings of March, 1880, and February, 1881. Sheuohneesv i,lei admits having furnished drink to members not belonging to his committee on two occasiana ; and he Makes the siunificant remark, "I think you racy take it that you must, stand trsatt to tboso whom you wish to sup- port you." 5. No argument woe tendered on either side regarding the treatment of defrauding servants. The rule is proved to

have been to keep on such servants as merely fell behind it their payments through innocent misfortune provided there were a reasonable prospect of their being able to re-pay by instalments, and to dismiss and in some cases to hand over to the public prosecutor such as had been guilty of em- bezzlement or dishonest modes of concocting defalcations. I beg to add one or two observations on matters which are not embraced within the application. The object of certain undoubted interpolations in the two collection books of John M'Brearty was not sufficiently proved on account of the omission to examine M'Brearty on the subject. All the witnesses who were examined on the matter concurred in describing the general meetings of the society, and especially those at which elections took place, as [Rine. of the most riotous and disorderly character. I regarded it as my duty to allow any suggestions to be made for remedying this unfortunate state of matters I find that there is nothing like unanimity among the witnesses in this respect. Something has already been done in the direction of obtaining more orderliness by the alteration in the hour of meeting from seven o'clock to four o'clock p.m. But this change has the drawback of practically excluding working nam from attendance, since they cannot afford to throw up a day's work for the purpose. I also beg to call attention to the extraordinary though not unprecedented increase which took place in the salaries of the board and office- ' hearers at the meeting which took place in June, 1881. Prior to that date the salary of the secretary was £250 per annum. The directers had agreed to raise it to £350. At the said meeting it was augmented to £5OO. Similarly, the salary of the treasurer, which had been £3OO, and had been increased by the directors to £330, was at the same meeting also raised to £5OO. The pre- sident's salary was raised from £lOO to £250; and each of the directors, instead of £25 a year, obtained £125. There is no doubt that the duties of some at. least of these persons are not only arduous but responsible, but I sought in vain for any explanation of the sudden rise indicated above. No explanation was offered at the meet- ing, and none seems to have been thought necessary. It seems to have been this sudden increase in the expenses of administration which first aroused the active suspicion of the promoters of the application. These persons have deponed that they have been animated by no feeling of malice against the managers of the society, but only by a sincere desire to expose certain evils which had crept into its administration. That such is the case I I,,ave no manner of doubt, and the result of the investigation has been fully to justify them in demanding it. The agent for the society was so sensible of the propriety of the application that Ile expressly admitted that the costs of the applicants and of the inspection should be borne by the funds of the society.— Humbly reported by me, (Sgnd.) Jolts RANKINE, Inspector. 10, Melville-street, Edinburgh, 16th May, 1882.

Note in Supplement to the Report on the Affairs of the Scottish Legal Life Insurance Society. I am of opinion that no part of the evidence of the wit- nesses called on either side was superfluous. I venture therefore to certify for the costs of all those who. being so called, attended merely as witnesses. It will be for considers- ti, n whether the same privilege be applicable to the three attestors of the application, and to the directors and office- bearers examined, all of whom were really parties, and most of whom were present during the course of the investiga- tion as such. The case of James Grant is exceptional. He did not attend as a witness for either side. It is doubtful whether he would have appeared at all had he not been speci illy required by me to do so, both by a formal requisi- tion and at a personal interview. His evidence was extremely unsatisfactory. lam accordingly of opinion that he is not entitled to be included in the certificate.—Humbly reported by,
(Signed) JOHN RANKINA Inspector. Edinburgh, sth June, 1882.

div.head: BUTCHERS AND THE INSPECTION OF MEAT.
div.p: BUTCHERS AND THE INSPECTION OF MEAT.

Mr. WEBs-rEa said the butchers had a great grievance that it required three men for the inspection of meat. They thought an inspector ought to be appointed, and the heavy expense incurred in bringing some person from outside dis- pensed with. Dr. BOOTH: If the butchers keep bad meat they deserve to pay for it. Dr O'KEEFFE remarked that if the butchers would wilfully sell bid meat they deserved net only heavily fining but im- prisonment, and if the sanitary officers were attending well to their duty, as he thought they were, they deserved the thanks of the public.
TUE NEW RATE.-LAWYERS' RILLS.

At an adjourned meeting of the Finance Committee, held on the 7th inst., the following accounts were ordered to be paid :—Gas account, £402 5s lid ; water fund, £345 15+ 51; hospital, £l9 184 2d; heaith, £6B 6 ld ; market, £7 12561; highway, £463 2+ 10.1; finance, £BO4 10+ 101; gas sinking fund, £525.78 6.1; sundry gas deposits, £64 19+ 11—£589 6+ 9d; water sinking fund, £L355 13s 10,1; Ec..nornc Life Assurance Society, £356 19+ lid—£l.7l2 13s ; water extension _account, £777 ; main sewerage account, W. W. Copeland, £l6 13+ 4.1. A letter was read from Mr. H. Mather asking for the payment of £4OO on account of Moss Brook road, and it was recommended that he be paid £2OO, and r:q.:ezted to complete the work at once. Another meeting was held on the 9 ,net., when the estimates of the various committees were examined, and the committee recommended that a rate of 2s Olin the £ be laid. Accounts amounting' in , the aggregate to £2.322 64 were ordered for payment. Mr. HANDLEY, in moving the passing of the minutes, re - (erred to the new rate, stating that 2+. 6.1. rate for the last year only realised £9.101 2s. 61., while there was expended £1.158 3s. 21. in excess of that sum ; and there was also a deficiency on the rate of £1.895 14+. 31. How was this to be made up P But there was the bright side to the question. The profita on the gas works, after providing interest on cipital, of £3,145 9+. 7d., but deducting £1,085 is. 64, of a loss on the waterworks, would be a total of £2060 B+. id. The committee proposed to appropriate £1.895 14s. 3d from that amount, anti wipe off the ddiciency on the rates. The estimates for the coming year amount to £8.790 14s. 2d.; last year they were £10,416 is. 6d.; but as the 21 6d. rate did not then produce much more than £9,0(.0, the committee proposed to lava 25.61. rate again. Assuming that the rate brought in £9OOO, there would be a surplus over the estimate of £204; but at the time the new estimates were made, that new hll of Mr. Beasley's for about £7OO, and the surplus would be s walk, v,d up and something added to it. He did not think it would be wise to lay a less rate than the one recommended. -

Mr. MiDwoota said the Highway Committee had reduced their estinie.te by about £1,200, and considered they could do th 2 Work well and have a balance if the money was Healy spent; but when he went to the Finance Committee Lest week, he found the chairman determined to lay a rate of 2s. 61.; and he (Mr. Midwood) could not get his own way as he should like to have done. He protested against the rate, and would like it to be referred back to the corn. nit for further consideration. Had the same prudence been exercised in the Finance Committee that was done in the Highway Committee, they could have dune with a leas rate. He noticed that Mr. Oppenheim's bill from the 10 h January, 1881, to the 6, h October amounted to £635 Os. 41. It was estimated that Mr. Oppenheim should recover £6.000. while only about half of that amount had been received. In one day Mr. Oppenheirn charged the ratepayers of ii;idnes for letter writing, Sze., £29 9s. ; and seven days afterwards he charged £23 34. for a similar thing, making a total of £52 12e 9d within that short space of time. And these things had been allowed to pass that Board and sent for taxing without any person attending en behalf of the Board to pro- test against any items ! (Hear, hear.) The cost of taxine, was £5, and the Board got deducted from the bill the stem of 35.! He thought this a great hardshtp on the ratepayers, and that the Board was to blame in not sending a deputation to go into the taxing of the bills. He did not think a 2s. 61 rate was required. The estimates amounted to £8796 14e. 2d, and that rate would produce over.£lo,ooo. The CHAIRMAN : You see you can never get the money , within the estimate.

Mr. Mtuwoon said the Finance Committee were asking for considerably more than would be wanted, and in these straitened times it was important that the rate be kept. as low as possible, and at tne same time have enough to pay their way and retain a balance. Mr. SADLER agreed with Mr. Midwood with respect to Mr. Oppenheim's accounts. There was one interesting item Mr. Midwood did not refer to. In nine months it had cost the ratepayers £35 for letters Mr. Oppenhehn had over- hauled.
Mr. MIDWOOD: I can pite understand his letter coming. It has been all cream with him.

Mr. HANDLEY said Mr. Midwood bad charged him with not taking particular care in going through the estimates of the Finance Committee. He had spent some time during the last month considering these things, and he thought they could not possibly do with a less rate. He should only be too glad if they could do so, but looting at the acc,dents which might take place. it would he impossible then to meet the engagements of the Baud. Mr. Oppenheirn's bill every- body must acknowleflve was large, but he had a great affair in hand. There was £G.OOO owing to the Bard, and the only thing the Board could do was to employ a solicitor.

to try and get the money in. [he bill had been pissed by the taxing master, and the Board was bound to pay it. In his letter the taxmaster said the bills seemed fairly made out, and he could not see any items that eould be taxed off. A deal of the £6.000 which was owing had been received. Mr. CAREY: H w much more do you expect to receive Mr. HANDLEY : Not much more.
Mr. MIDWoOD moved that the proposal to lay a rate of 2e GI in the £ he referred to a special meeting of the Board, to go into particulars. Mr. MARTLEY seconded the propoNal, which was agreed to. •
THE SEWERAGE WORKS AND THE HUTCHINSON TRUSTEES.

I At the meeting of the Sewerage C onmittee on the 25th I ult., a letter was read from Mr. T. Kirk, the contractor for the main sewer, giving notice that he had stopped the work and would hold the Board responsible for damages; and it was recommended that Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., Warrington, be consulted. and instructed to reply to Mr. Mr. Kirk on the Board's behalf. At an earlier meeting Mr. Kershaw had been unanimously elected chairman of the Board. The clerk was instructed to ask whether the trustees of the late Mr. Hutchinson would- negotiate with the Board without referring to arbitration, and, if they consented, to ascertain the amount or yearly rent required. The minnteswere agreed to on the motion of Mr. Kershaw. Mr. MIDWOOD remarked that, in answer to a question, he was informed at the last meeting that Hutchinson's trustees had not offered to accept any money amount (GI- way-leave through their land. Since that meeting he had found nut that the Board was in possession of letter from Hutchin- son's trustees, dated January; 1581, nfflring to allow the way-leave through 1.765 yards of their land for £5,500; and he wished to know why he received the answer referred to at the last meeting. Also if the easement for the way- leave was included in the estimates to the Loc d Government Board, and if the trustees had notice served upon them that the Board would take a sewer through their land ?

Mr. KERSITAW replied that he was not cognisant. of the money offer, as h was not a member or the Board when it was made. The eas.ment, he believed, was n.)t included in the estimate to the Local Government Board ; and with regard to the question as to notice, that was a matter far dismision in committee, and not in the Board room. The Board had to protect themselves.

Mr. CARRY observed that Mr. Midwood had forgotten what took place at the last meeting. Mr. Midwool then asked if the Boarl had made any off-r to Hutchinson's trustees, and he (Mr. Carey) explained that the Board had had an offer from them which amounted to £5 000. Mr. Mrnwoon : We are in a fez as regards the contract and the whole thing.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Wm. Bankes (chairman) and Charles Reynolds.

ASSAULT.—A labouring Main, inariid Richard Reene, was su:nmoned for assaulting Martha Taylor, and there was also a cross summons in which the woman was charged with having committed an assault on Reece.—Mrs. Taylor's statement, which was supported by a witnees, was to the 'effect that she lived in Windmill-streat, and on the evening of the sth inst., was sitting at the door of her house, when she heard a scream. She itent to the door and found that Reece had bit her sister. She asked him why he had done this, when be ran at her, and struck her with something heavy, so that she fell to the ground senseless.—Reece said he came home and found Mrs. Taylor in the house drunk. He told her she could not be permitted to remain there. She called him a thief, used other strong language, and hit him on the side of the face. He then gave her a blow on the m3uth. Since the 26th November -last, he had been an ab- stainer, with the exception of taking three pennyworth of brandy, which had been ordered him by a medical man.— Mrs. Reece was called, and gave a graphic picture of the violent conduct and language alleged to have been indulged ' in by her sister.—The magistrates said they considered there was very little difference between the conduct of the persons in the case; and each of them would have to fiwl sureties, himself, or herself, in £lO, and one in £5, to keep the peace six months. Reece had 10s. EU. and Taylor 12s. Gil. costs to pay. OFFENCE AGAINST THE POACHING PREVENTION ACT.— Thomas Clarke, about 40 years of age, was summoned under the Poaching Prbvention Act, with having, at Halton, on the 4th December, 1831, been found on the highway with a rabbit and five nets in his possession.—Sergeant Lowndes and P.C. Cooper gave evidence to the effect that on the date mentioned they were in Sutton-lane, when they heard the shriek of a rabbit. They remained secreted for 26 minutes, and then saw four men come from behind the wood. A live rabbit was found under the prisoner's coat, and a number of nets in his possession.—Clarke, who has been previously convicted for a similar offence, waa fined 295., and costs IAN. 61. OFFENCE AGAINST THE CANAL BOATS' ACT.—MeS4r9. ernes and Williamson, of near Middleton, Manchester, were summoned by Mr. Farrington, inspector to the Runcorn Board of Guardians, for using as a dvrellinghouse a beat named the Thomas, on the river Weaver, upon the 2nd inst., the vessel, not being lettered, marked and num- bered, as required by the Act. Evidence having been given in the case by Mr Farrington, the defendants were fined 2s. 61 and costs 12s. Gd.

VIOLENT CONDUCT IN A BEE RHOUSE.—A young man named John Brown was charged with assaulting Miss Mary Ann Page, of the Nag's Head beerhouse, and also with having been guilty of disorderly behaviour, anil refused to quit the premises.—Miss Page, a neatly dressed young woman, said she was the niece of the man who kept the beerhouse. On the 20th M,y, the defendant visited the house, ansi commenced fighting in the kitchen. Her uncle asked him to go out, but he refused. She was told to open the door, so that Brown could be put out, upon which he kicked her on the side.—ln the first case defendant was fined 10s. and costs 10s. 'Cd., or in default, 14 days' imprisonment; and in the second, 205., and the costs 10s. 6d., or one month's imprisonment. THE BEGGING Nutsaacbaa—Thomas Johnson, a rough looking man, was fined ss. and costs Ss. 4d., or seven days' imprisonment, on the evidence of P. C. Cooper for begging in High-street on Saturday night. SELLING MATCHES WITHOUT A HAVrKER'S CERTIFICA.TE. —Richard Tilly, an old man was charged with selling matches without having a pedlars' certificate.—Evidence was given to the effect that the prisoner had been found hawking matches in the public streets without having a licence.—Snperintendent Williamson said he had cautioned the old man some months ago against hawking without licence, and let bim go.—Prisoner was fined 2s. Cd. and cosas. A WEAK CASE.—John Abbott, a grey headed man, was charged, on remand from Saturday, with stealing a kettle, a frying pan, a saucepan, tub, rope, a jockey bar, and two bolts, the property of Mr. R;chard Abel, of finncorn, from a flit lying on the beach near the Belvidere, on the 9th insa— ne prosecutor stated that the articles were all safe upon the flat in question, which was called The Alice, on Thursday evening.—Sergeant Walley said that about eleven o'clock on Friday morning, he went to the prisoner's house in Mill- street, and there found the things produced. Henry Hard ley, carpenter, said that on Thursday evening, he, with the assis- tance of the prisoaer and six other men, put the boat on tha beach near the Belvidere. He pail all the men off with the exception of Abbott, and gave them orders to leave the vessel. He also told them they would have to receive fresh orders before they started again, and instructed the prisoner not to put a foot on board until ho was tOid to do so.— Prisoner P3i,l he took enme of the things he found on the vessel to Hirdley, and he was about to remove the others ,when a thunderstorm came on. The gonds were no use to him —The, Bench said they believed the old man's statement and divn:sAed the summons. - - -

_....... . APPLICATION B V A STEPPATIIER.—JnhtI Smith, iron turner, of 39, Surrey-strPet. applied for the committal of his stepson. Wm Frederick Gib:on, aged 13. under Section 16 of the Industrial Schools' Act. He complained that the lad was ung.ov,!rnable, and in the habit of staying out two or three nights a week.—The magistrates said they thought it would be better for Solith to bring further evidence before them. and make another applicAtion, as the boy's mother was at present unwell.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Bruadrit and S. B. • 'Chadwick.

ALLEGED SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A POCE WEIGHBR.— James Stanton, dock porter, was charged under a warrant, with having, on the previous day, unlawfully assaulted John Nelson, a weigher.—Complainant said he was in a hat at the'ddoks, preparing an account of a cargo, when the pri- soner came to him, and said there four men who were de- termined "to do for him." After using various threats, pri- soner struck him a violent blow on the eye, which knocked him down. Some abort time ago, he was a witness in a case whgre A man named Conway was charged with unlawfully wounding, and afterward.' convicted at the Sessions. Siam that time the prisoner and other members of his family had been inethe habit of annoying him in the street—John Kelly and John-Dyer gave corroborative evicrinee, and the prisoner was ordered to be bonnd over, himself in £lO, and two in £5, to keep the peace for six months, or, in default., be sent to gaol three months.—Prisoner, who found the sure- ties, had also Ms. 10d. ensts to nay. AN ADVENTURE BY TWO CITESTRR who gave .the names of Elizabeth • Dutton (15) and Ellen Jones (14), bat whose real names were suppressed in court nut of kindness to 'them, were charged, on remandf with stealing two rings, value 9d., the Froperty of Louisa Evans. who keeps a shop for the sale of fancy goods in tligh- street. On Monday night, the prisoners went into tin abop,

and asked to see the two rings, but they only purchased a brooch. When they had gone, she found the rings were gone. Elizabeth Lee, aged 11, who lives next door to the prosecutrix, was in the place when the prisoners entered, and saw Jones put one of the rings on her finger, and go away with it. Ou the girls being searched at the police station by Mrs. Withington, Dutton dropped the ring pro- duced behind her. The prisoners were apprehended by In- spector Hollingworth, and had been remanded until Wednes- day morning, on the application of Superintendent Wil- liamson, so that he might communicate with the police at Chester. One of the girls had pawned a dress for the pur- pose of paying the railway fare from Chester.—The mother of the girl Dutton now appeared, and stated that she had run away from hoine.—Each of the prisoners' parents was ordered to pay a tine of 55., or, in default, be imprisoned one day.
7.lllrxsDAY.—Beforo Messrs. John Bruudrit and Henry Reynolds.

ASSAULTING A POLIJII:0-F-171-C.ER.—David Roberts and Harris Snell, two seamen, were charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Now-road; Roberts was further charged with assaulting P.C. Devenport in the execution of his duty. The men were seen fighting on the previous night, at about eleven o'clock. Roberts had his coat off. Deveriport separated them, and with the assistance of P.C. Mellor, took them into custody. Roberts became very violent, got hold of Devonport's leg, struck at him several times, and tried to throw him down. Snell, in de- fence, said he was walking to his vessel when Roberts attacked him, and all that he did was to defend himself. Snell was discharged, and Roberts was fined 20s. and ss. costs for the assault, or, in default, one month. He was also ordered to enter into his own recognisances of £5 to keep the peace for six months.

This Board held their monthly meeting on Tuesday afternoon, at Dutton Workhouse, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Bat clay.

AUDITOR'S REPORT. The DEPUTY CLERK read the auditor's report, dated the 9th inst., and signed by Mr. John Dolby. It stated that he bad examined the accounts with the balance sheet, and had compared the sevral payments credited to the treasurer with the vouchers; and he certified that the entries appeared correct and legal, and that the balances of the treasurer's accounts, viz., £406 ha. 101, agreed with the balance whic-n by his own book appeared to have been in his hands at the time of closing such accounts. He found, from the informa- tion laid before him, that the amount of the outstanding liabilitiea.of the Rural Sanitary Authority at that time was £5,620 ss. 4d.
